ci: Stories are shared in different ways.
lo: Imagining stories together; Ways stories are shared; Connecting with stories

s.d: Students record a short story about a lost toy using voices, footsteps, claps and classroom objects. Hearing a story without pictures shows how sound can carry characters, settings and events. Pairs swap recordings and draw what they imagined before seeing each other's original story plan. Students then ask a family member to add a familiar song, saying or sound from home. Each pair finishes with a sound story that can be played to the class with everyone's eyes closed. GarageBand makes it possible to record voices, layer sounds and compose simple music in one place.

Students paint three digital pictures showing the beginning, middle and end of an imagined story. They see that colour, shape and expression can tell events without written words. Partners exchange the middle pictures and invent different events that could connect the same beginning and ending. Students choose one version and explain how the pictures helped them understand it. Each child finishes with a three-picture story displayed in sequence. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with separate layers that can be changed as ideas grow.

Students lay coloured tiles across the carpet to guide Sphero Indi through the beginning, middle and end of a familiar story. The ordered path makes story sequence something children can build, walk beside and test. Another pair receives the same character and ending but chooses a different tile route to show a new version of the story. Students move, replace and reorder tiles when the car's journey does not match their planned events. Each group finishes with a working story path and an oral telling timed to Indi's movement. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students record three short scenes showing a family story, using drawings, toys, movement or spoken words. They explore how the same memory can be shared through pictures, actions and voice. Families can suggest one important detail or home-language phrase for children to include in the retelling. Students arrange the scenes in order and choose simple titles that help viewers follow the events. Each child finishes with a short family-history film for a class viewing. IMovie allows the clips, titles and transitions to be edited together in one tool.

Students choose puppet characters and record an imagined story that begins with two characters wanting different things. This helps children tell stories together while listening to another person's ideas. Halfway through, pairs swap their unfinished puppet show with another pair, who decides what happens next. The original storytellers then record an ending that connects both groups' ideas. Each pair finishes with a narrated puppet show containing a clear beginning, problem and ending. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students design and build their own mini shadowbox theatres using shoeboxes, coloured cellophane, paper cut-outs, and craft sticks to create characters and backgrounds from their personal or family stories. They then use a simple torch or LED puck light to project shadows onto the box 'stage', animating their tales with movement. To add a digital twist, students record short audio narrations of their stories on a classroom iPad, syncing their live shadow puppet show with their voices. This project celebrates imagination, sequencing, and diverse storytelling styles—helping students express identity and culture through both hands-on making and digital storytelling.

ci: Everyone has a role to play in the community.
lo: My communities; Contributing to the local community; Connections in my community

s.d: Students photograph school staff and record each person explaining one way they help the school community. This shows that the school works because many people carry out connected roles. Children choose one helpful question to ask, then play their page to the person they interviewed so they can check it together. They end up with a class book that families can use to meet the people and places in the school. Book Creator keeps photographs, recorded voices and children's drawings together on each page. Pairing children for the recording keeps screen time brief and makes the interview the main experience.

Students add drawings of familiar school people and places to a shared Freeform board. They draw lines between people who work together, such as the teacher, office staff and nurse helping a child who feels unwell. Pairs study another pair's connection and ask them to explain why it matters. The class ends up with one large visual web showing how the school community fits together. Freeform's open canvas gives the web room to grow as children notice more connections. The teacher can revisit the board after each community walk and add children's new ideas.

Students draw a cutaway view of the school and place staff members where their work usually happens. This helps children connect community roles with the places that support them. Each child hides one visual clue in the drawing, then a partner works out which staff role it represents. They end up with a detailed illustrated school scene for a classroom display. Sketchbook's drawing tools let children revise colours, shapes and details without starting again. Printed drawings can prompt conversations with visiting staff and families.

Students paint a digital portrait of a school community member doing one important part of their role. This makes each person's contribution visible rather than showing only a face or uniform. Children choose a meaningful object to include, such as a library book, garden tool or first-aid bag, and classmates work out what it tells them. They end up with a gallery of original role portraits. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with separate layers for the person, place and helpful object. The class can arrange the portraits by places or by the ways people help others.

Students lay coloured tiles across the carpet to guide Sphero Indi between picture cards showing connected school roles. This models how a message, object or request moves through the school community. Groups swap routes and work out which tile needs changing when Indi does not reach the next person. They end up with a tested physical pathway that tells a simple story, such as a lost hat travelling from the playground to lost property and back to its owner. Indi follows the coloured tiles without an app or screen. Children explain each stop as the robot car travels through their community story.

Students design and build a giant collaborative train set from recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, and craft materials, with each carriage representing a different person or role in the school community (like the Principal, Nurse, or Librarian). Using simple coding with Sphero Indi robots placed in the 'engine', students program routes along their handmade tracks to visit each carriage and learn about the connections between roles. This hands-on project blends creative construction with basic robotics, helping students visualise how everyone's contributions keep the school 'train' running smoothly. The design cycle guides them through imagining, planning, building, testing, and sharing their interactive school system model.

ci: Scientists follow a method to discover new things.
lo: The scientific process; Observing my world; Drawing conclusions

s.d: Students magnify an ice cube every two minutes and draw the tiny cracks, bubbles and puddles they observe on paper. This makes careful observation the starting point for predicting, testing and drawing a conclusion. Partners compare drawings and decide which change happened first, next and last. They repeat the test with one cube in shade and one in sunlight to see whether their prediction holds. Each pair ends with a sequenced observation strip beside the two melting trays. The magnified view reveals changes that are difficult to notice with eyes alone.

Students record balls, blocks and toy cars moving down ramps, then watch each movement in slow motion. This helps them observe closely before deciding which object moved fastest or travelled furthest. Pairs swap one ramp feature, predict what will change and film the test again. Another Prep class watches the clips and votes on which evidence best supports each conclusion. Students end with paired slow-motion recordings showing what changed between two fair tests. Slow playback makes brief movements available for repeated observation.

Students photograph plants, animals and fungi during a nature walk and use Seek to suggest what each living thing might be. This shows that scientists observe carefully, use tools and check possible answers. Children compare two suggested identifications with the real colours, shapes and textures they can see. Each pair chooses one identification they trust and one they think needs more checking. The class ends with a paper display of observed living things labelled as checked or still wondering. Seek's camera-based identification gives children a useful starting point rather than a guaranteed answer.

Students record short weather reports after observing clouds, wind, sunlight and puddles outside. This gives them a clear routine of observe, predict, check and explain. Each group records a morning prediction, then returns later to add what actually happened. Families can watch the paired reports and hear children explain whether the evidence matched the prediction. Students end with a short weather clip containing both the prediction and conclusion. Live captions make their spoken scientific words visible for early readers.

Students program a character to move through four scenes showing a simple ice-melting investigation. This turns the scientific process into a sequence they can see, test and fix. Partners exchange projects and check whether observation, prediction, testing and conclusion appear in a sensible order. Children then change one scene so the character explains a different possible result. Each pair ends with a tappable animated explanation of how scientists find out new things. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young children debug the order without needing to read long instructions.

Students design and build spinning weather wheels using cardboard circles, split pins, and craft materials to represent different weather types (sun, rain, wind, clouds, snow). They decorate each section with textured materials like cotton balls, foil, tissue paper, and felt to bring each weather type to life. Using a simple stop-motion app on iPads, students animate their wheels to show changing weather patterns and record short audio explanations of their predictions for each type. This hands-on project supports observation and communication skills, connecting scientific inquiry with creative storytelling and visual representation.

ci: Living things share our world and have an important role in nature
lo: The different living things around us; The roles living things play in nature; How humans and other living things share space

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students choose an animal character and record its voice explaining the important job it does in nature. This helps children notice that even small living things can pollinate plants, spread seeds, make soil or provide food. Each pair listens to another pair's character and asks one question from the animal's point of view. Students then improve their recording by adding one detail about how humans can share space with that animal. They end with a short talking-character explanation for another Prep class to watch. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to each child's recorded voice.

Students make a close-up digital drawing of a local living thing and the place where it finds food, water and shelter. This shows how plants and animals depend on the spaces around them. Children swap drawings and look for one helpful connection, such as a bee beside a flower or a worm beneath leaf litter. They then add that connection to their picture using a new layer. Each child finishes with a detailed habitat illustration that can prompt an oral explanation. Sketchbook's drawing tools and layers let children revise without covering their first ideas.

Students sort teacher-provided pictures of local plants, animals, fungi and people on a shared Freeform board. This helps them work out which living things share the same places and how their roles are different. Small groups draw lines between things that help one another, such as flowers and bees or trees and birds. Another group checks each connection and moves a picture if they can explain a better place for it. The class ends with one large visual web showing how life around Elsternwick is connected. Freeform's open canvas lets children move, group and connect pictures together.

Students arrange teacher-provided pictures to compare a healthy shared space with one that is difficult for living things. This makes human choices visible, including planting flowers, leaving water, dropping litter or removing shelter. Each pair chooses the three changes they think would help wildlife most and adds short spoken-to-the-teacher captions. Pairs exchange collages and point to one choice that could work at school. Students finish with a two-part visual display showing before, after and the changes between them. PicCollage's grids and captions keep the comparison clear for early readers.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a large floor mat showing trees, flowers, water, nests, paths and buildings. This lets children explore how animals and humans move through the same space to meet different needs. One group places an animal card at the starting point, while another chooses a safe destination and explains why it belongs there. Children press the directional buttons, run the route and debug it when the Bee-Bot stops at an unsafe or unsuitable place. Each group finishes with a tested sequence that connects a living thing to food, water or shelter. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make every route a hands-on sequence planned in advance.

s.t: Family Heritage Homes: Miniature Memory Villages
s.d: Students design and build a miniature 'home' that represents something special about their family's heritage using cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, natural materials, and recycled bits. They decorate their homes with personal touches, then use Sphero Indi robots to 'visit' each other's creations, mapping a route between homes with coloured tiles and sharing stories as the robot travels. This hands-on project weaves together physical making, digital navigation, and storytelling, helping students celebrate identity and community while exploring how we all share and shape our planet together.

ci: Relationships impact our wellbeing.
lo: Developing relationships; How those around us impact our behaviours and interactions; Keeping ourselves healthy and safe

s.d: Students draw a self-portrait, photograph it in ChatterPix Kids and record it saying what helps them feel safe, calm and welcome at school. This shows that relationships can change how someone feels. Children swap portraits with a partner and add one kind action they could offer that person. Each child ends with a short talking portrait for a class belonging display. Drawing a mouth on the photograph lets the portrait speak in the child's own voice. The teacher can replay selected portraits when the class reviews its agreements.

Students code two characters to show a playground interaction where one action changes how another character feels. This helps children notice how behaviour can support or harm wellbeing. Partners swap projects and suggest a different kind response for the second scene. Each pair ends with a short animated story that shows a problem and a helpful choice. Simple blocks let children sequence movement, speech and scene changes. The class can watch the stories and name the choices that build positive relationships.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a familiar character giving one clear tip for making friends or asking an adult for help. This gives children a safe way to talk about relationships, feelings and personal safety. Each child chooses whether the character speaks to a new Prep student, a worried friend or someone left out of play. The result is a short talking-character message for another Prep class. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to the child's voice. Teachers can replay the messages before transitions, buddy time or playground sessions.

Students build a class book by adding a drawing and recorded sentence about someone who helps them feel healthy, safe or included. This makes the link between caring relationships and wellbeing visible. Families can contribute a short child-recorded page about a caring routine used at home. The class ends with a narrated book showing many different ways people care for one another. Book Creator keeps pictures, text and voice recordings together on each page. Children can revisit the book when they need ideas for helping a classmate.

Students photograph a partner-made block scene of a friendship moment and record what each person might be feeling. This helps children connect visible actions with feelings that may not be easy to see. The partner listens, then records one helpful action that could improve the scene. Each child ends with a photo-and-voice reflection showing how behaviour can affect wellbeing. Seesaw keeps the photograph and both spoken reflections together in a portfolio entry. The teacher can use the entries to notice which children can name feelings, safe choices and sources of help.

s.t: Feelings Forest: My Emotion Explorer Map
s.d: Students design and craft their own 'Emotion Explorer' map using large sheets of paper, felt, cardboard scraps, and natural materials like leaves and twigs. Each student creates a unique forest path representing their feelings and important people in their lives, decorating their map with hand-drawn symbols, pop-up trees, and crafted emotion creatures. Using Bee-Bots, students program simple journeys along their map's path, stopping at key spots to share a story or feeling with classmates. This hands-on adventure helps students express their identity, understand emotions, and celebrate how different relationships shape who they are.

ci: Emotions can be expressed in different ways.
lo: Recognising our own and others' emotions; Responding to and interpreting our emotions; Different ways we express emotions

s.d: Students record and arrange short sounds to express calm, worry, joy and anger without using words. This shows that emotions can be communicated and interpreted through music. Partners swap soundscapes, name the emotion they hear and explain which sounds shaped their response. Students then revise one sound so their message is clearer to the listener. Each pair ends with four short emotion soundscapes for a class listening gallery. GarageBand lets students layer recorded sounds and musical loops.

Students build a face from paper shapes and photograph it changing from one emotion to another. This helps them notice how eyes, eyebrows and mouths can communicate feelings. Partners watch each animation without being told the emotion, then suggest what may have happened between the first and last face. Students add or remove frames to make the emotional change easier to interpret. Each pair finishes with a short stop-motion story showing an emotion developing over time. Stop Motion Studio combines their photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students record a short video showing an emotion through facial expression, posture and movement while keeping their voice silent. This helps them recognise that people can express feelings without words. A partner watches the video, records an interpretation and suggests a kind response to the feeling they noticed. The original student then adds a voice reflection explaining what the partner understood accurately or differently. Each student finishes with a portfolio entry containing an expression, an interpretation and a response. Seesaw keeps video, voice and reflection together in one journal post.

Students sort drawings and words for emotions onto a shared Freeform board. This helps them see that the same situation can lead to different feelings and that one expression can have several meanings. Small groups connect each emotion to possible body clues, facial clues and helpful responses. Groups then visit another section of the board and add a different interpretation rather than copying the first answer. The class ends with a connected emotion map that can support later picture-book and drama discussions. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and link ideas together.

Students draw the same simple face twice, using colour, line and texture to express two different emotions. This shows how visual choices can communicate feelings even when the facial features stay similar. Partners view the drawings without labels and describe what each colour or mark makes them think the character feels. Students choose one piece of feedback and adjust a layer to make their intended emotion clearer. Each student finishes with a paired digital artwork and a short spoken explanation given to the class. Sketchbook's drawing tools and layers make it easy to test changes without losing the first idea.

s.t: Feelings Bot Parade: Emotions on Wheels!
s.d: Students design and craft expressive robot costumes using cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, paper plates, and art materials to represent different emotions (like joy, sadness, or excitement). They decorate Sphero Indi cars with their creations, then use simple color code tiles to program their 'Feelings Bots' on a parade route that tells a story of changing emotions. Along the way, students stop at 'emotion stations' to act out and discuss feelings, blending hands-on building, digital coding, and dramatic expression. This project helps students embody and communicate emotions through movement, art, and technology, making emotional literacy a joyful, memorable experience.

ci: Services are established to help the needs of people in the community.
lo: Local services; Why we need local services in our community; How services meet personal and community needs

s.d: Students train Teachable Machine to recognise picture cards showing ambulances, fire engines and library services. They test whether the computer can match each image to a service that meets a community need. Students choose difficult pictures, swap them with another group and work out why the model makes mistakes. They improve the model by adding more varied examples and testing it again. The class ends with a working image classifier and a record of its correct and incorrect guesses. Similar image recognition helps council monitoring and emergency-dispatch systems identify vehicles and respond to community needs.

Students build a visual community-needs survey on a teacher-prepared Freeform board using labelled sections for services such as the library, doctor, fire station and public transport. They respond to picture scenarios by dragging a coloured shape or digital sticky note beside the service they would contact. Pairs add a drawn scenario based on a need they notice at school or in Elsternwick, then invite classmates to classify it. Students count and annotate each cluster to identify which services were selected most often. They discuss how different services are organised to provide particular kinds of help. The completed board becomes a colourful class map of needs, choices and local support systems.

Students record a puppet conversation between a community helper and a person asking for help. They show what the service provides, why it is needed and what happens when someone contacts it. Students swap planned situations so another pair must decide which helper belongs in the scene. They record clear questions and answers, then replay the show to check that the service process makes sense. Each pair finishes with a short animated puppet show for a younger class. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students record a short interview with a visiting community helper about the people, places and steps involved in their service. This makes the organisation behind a familiar service visible, rather than showing only the helper's job. Students choose the most useful answers for families new to Elsternwick and remove repeated or unclear sections. They arrange the clips so the film moves from a community need to the service's response. The class finishes with a set of short interview films featuring real local voices. IMovie lets students trim clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students collect a class tally of local services they have used, such as libraries, doctors, public transport and emergency services. On Geoboard, pairs stretch different coloured virtual rubber bands up the grid to construct a column for each service. They count the grid spaces carefully so every column matches the class tally, then add a simple colour key. The resulting pictorial column graph reveals which services meet frequent needs and which are used only in special situations. Pairs compare column heights and explain one surprising pattern using language such as more, fewer and equal. They finish with a clear visual model showing how often different community services support the class.

Students will design and build a 3D maze representing a miniature town using cardboard boxes, tubes, recycled containers, and craft materials to create roads, buildings, and local services (like fire stations, hospitals, and post offices). Using Sphero Indi cars, children program simple routes to 'respond' to community emergencies, navigating their crafted maze to reach different services. This hands-on project lets students explore how community helpers are organised and work together to meet needs, blending creative construction with basic coding and teamwork. It brings the theme to life as students imagine, build, and test their own organised community systems.

ci: Patterns help us to interpret the world around us.
lo: Patterns and cycles in our lives; Different patterns around us; How patterns can be created, interpreted and extended

s.d: Students record repeating movements around the school, such as swaying leaves, dripping water and a bouncing ball, then watch them in slow motion. Slowing each movement helps them notice the small steps that make a pattern repeat. Partners compare clips and choose the moment that best shows where one cycle ends and the next begins. They test whether the same pattern continues when the movement becomes faster or slower. Each pair ends with a short slow-motion clip and a spoken explanation of the repeating cycle. The slow-motion playback makes changes that are usually too quick to see available for close observation.

Students become pattern detectives by training a teacher-guided Teachable Machine image model to recognise stages of a natural cycle, such as egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly. They capture examples using the built-in webcam, then sort each image into a labelled class. Students test the model by holding up new drawings or photographs and observe when it identifies a stage correctly. When the model is confused, they improve its training set by adding clearer or more varied examples. Partners discuss which visual features helped the model notice differences between stages. The finished classifier becomes an interactive sorting station that reveals how careful observation helps people interpret patterns and change.

Students program a ScratchJr animation showing a repeating natural pattern, such as day and night, the seasons or a butterfly life cycle. Repeated blocks help them see that a cycle follows an order and returns to its beginning. Students swap projects, predict what should happen next and check the animation to test their prediction. They then debug any stage that appears in the wrong order or does not repeat clearly. Each student ends with a working animated cycle that classmates can interpret. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young students sequence movement and repetition without needing to type code.

Students build repeating colour and shape patterns on Geoboard by stretching virtual bands around the pegs. They explore how a pattern can change in size or direction while keeping the same repeating rule. Partners exchange unfinished patterns and work out which shape should come next. The original designer checks the extension and explains the rule using words such as repeat, turn, bigger and smaller. Each pair ends with a completed geometric pattern and a clear explanation of how it grows. The virtual bands can be moved quickly, so students can test several possible extensions before choosing one.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist to identify plants, animals or fungi found during repeated walks through the same part of the school grounds. Returning to one place helps them notice seasonal patterns and changes in which living things appear. Pairs choose one identification they are unsure about and compare the living thing carefully with the app's suggestion before accepting it as a guide. The class compares observations from different days and discusses which living things appeared again. Students end with a checked set of local species observations that can be revisited later in the term. Seek uses the camera to suggest identifications, but students still need to look closely because a suggestion may not always be correct.

s.t: Seasons Spinners: Cycle of Change Dioramas
s.d: Students design and craft a rotating diorama that shows how a tree or animal changes through the four seasons. Using cardboard circles, paper plates, felt scraps, recycled materials, markers, and child-safe fasteners, they build a spinner where each turn reveals a different seasonal scene. Students then use Sphero Indi (or similar simple robot) to 'travel' to each season, triggering their spinner to display the matching change. This hands-on project helps students visualize repeating patterns in nature and connects digital movement with tangible model-making, deepening understanding of cycles in the natural world.

ci: Plants are a life sustaining resource.
lo: Products derived from plants; Plants all around us; The interconnectedness of plants

s.d: Students record 360-degree views beneath a tree, beside a garden bed and near plant-based materials around the classroom. Seeing the whole space helps them notice that plants support life and appear in places they may overlook. Pairs choose one view and challenge another class to find every plant, plant product and living thing that depends on plants. They replay the spherical footage and turn the view to check anything they missed. The class ends with an immersive tour of plants and plant products across the Elsternwick campus. The camera captures the full surroundings, so viewers can look in every direction.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a floor mat showing a plant's journey from seed to familiar product. This makes the links between plants, people and products such as paper, bread, cotton clothing and wooden furniture visible. Groups swap mats and work out the intended journey before checking it with the designers. They debug any route that skips a stage or places the stages in the wrong order. Each group finishes with a working sequence that connects a growing plant to something people use. Bee-Bot's directional buttons let students enter and revise each route step by step.

Students magnify leaves, seeds, wood, paper, cotton fabric and a piece of fruit to look for tiny patterns and structures. Close observation helps them compare plants with the products that come from plants. Each pair chooses one surprising detail and invites classmates to find it without first naming the object. Students sort the specimens by visible features such as fibres, veins, layers, pores or repeating shapes. They finish with a labelled comparison display of specimens arranged beside their magnified details. The magnification aid makes details visible that young eyes could not easily inspect unaided.

Students build a narrated digital book that follows one plant resource from where it grows to how people use it. This shows that food, fibres, paper, medicines and building materials begin with living plants. Each child chooses a different reader, another Year 1 class, a family member or a younger buddy, and explains unfamiliar words for that audience. Partners listen to each page and ask one question that the author answers in a final revision. Students finish with a class library of plant-to-product stories containing text, images and recorded voices. Book Creator keeps the writing, visuals and narration together in one book.

Students photograph leaves from three common school plants and train Teachable Machine to recognise each group. They look closely for patterns in shape, edge, colour and vein structure that help distinguish plants around them. Groups exchange one mystery leaf and test whether the model recognises it, then add better examples when it makes a mistake. This works like plant-identification apps such as Seek, which compare camera images with patterns learned from many examples. Students finish with a tested image-classification model and a record of which leaves confused it. Teachable Machine lets them retrain the model so they can see how the examples they choose affect its decisions.

s.t: Rainmaker Robots: The Water Cycle Adventure Track
s.d: Students will design and build a vibrant 3D water cycle adventure track using cardboard, felt, blue cellophane, cotton balls, and recycled materials to represent clouds, rivers, rain, and sunshine. They will then program a Sphero Indi robot (or similar age-appropriate robot car) to journey through each stage of the water cycle, pausing at student-created stations that explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection. Along the way, students collaboratively decorate and label their track, using simple code cards or color tiles for navigation. This hands-on challenge helps students visualize natural cycles, fosters teamwork, and blends creative making with early robotics in an unforgettable, active learning experience.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Homes reflect our culture and environment.
lo: Different types of homes; Characteristics of a home; The importance of sustainable living spaces

s.d: Students photograph a model or drawing of a home and record the home explaining how its culture and environment shaped it. This makes features such as raised floors, thick walls, courtyards or steep roofs easier to connect with real needs. Students choose one feature the home is proud of and one change that could make it more sustainable. They swap recordings with a partner, who listens for clues about where the home might belong. Each student ends with a short talking-home recording based on researched details rather than stereotypes. ChatterPix Kids makes the image talk by adding a drawn mouth and a recorded voice.

Students sort teacher-provided pictures of homes from different places into a visual comparison grid. They add short captions showing how climate, local materials, family life or traditions may affect each home. Pairs then exchange grids and add one surprising similarity between two very different-looking homes. Students also choose one sustainable feature they would borrow for a Melbourne home and explain why. Each pair ends with a labelled collage that can be displayed as evidence for the central idea. PicCollage makes it quick to arrange pictures, captions and simple backgrounds on one page.

Students build a small home from classroom construction pieces and photograph each stage in Stop Motion Studio. Their animation shows the home changing from an older design to a present-day version with one sustainable improvement. Another group watches the unfinished animation and suggests a change that better suits the weather or the people's needs. Students revise the model, add the new frames and check that viewers can see why the design changed. Each group ends with a short stop-motion film showing how homes respond to place and time. Stop Motion Studio joins the photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students stretch virtual bands to make a simple bird's-eye floor plan of a home. They use shapes to show spaces for sleeping, preparing food, gathering, washing and staying safe. Partners swap plans and work out whose needs the layout meets well and whose needs may have been missed. Students then move one wall or doorway to make the home more welcoming, useful or efficient. Each student ends with an original floor plan that shows deliberate choices about the characteristics of a home. Geoboard allows bands to be moved quickly so students can test several layouts without redrawing everything.

Students lay coloured tiles to guide Sphero Indi through a large floor plan containing key parts of a sustainable home. They sequence a route past features such as a water tank, shaded window, recycling area and shared family space. Another pair changes the order of the tiles, and students work out how the new route affects Indi's journey through the home. They revise the path so every chosen feature is visited without unnecessary travel. Each group ends with a working coloured-tile route and a spoken explanation of its design choices. Sphero Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen.

Students will research and build miniature models of homes from different cultures and environments using recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, craft sticks, and natural materials. They'll integrate simple LED circuits (with coin cell batteries and copper tape) to add glowing 'lights' inside their homes, representing how people adapt to their surroundings and needs. Using age-appropriate apps like PicCollage on iPads, students will photograph their creations and digitally label unique features, linking each model to its place and time. The finished light-up village becomes a collaborative display, celebrating diversity, sustainability, and the creative ways people build homes around the world.

ci: The actions we take influence our safety and wellbeing.
lo: Safe environments; How our actions affect ourselves and others; Keeping our body and mind healthy

s.d: Students record two versions of the same doorway, playground or handwashing moment, one with an unsafe choice and one with a safer choice. Comparing the clips makes it clear that small actions can change everyone's safety and wellbeing. Each group chooses a real school routine that younger students or families would find useful. They finish with a short safety film that pauses before the choice and invites viewers to predict what should happen next. Live captions, stickers and titles help Year 1 students make the message easy to follow.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a heart, brain, stomach or pair of lungs explaining one daily action that helps it stay healthy. Giving the body part a voice helps children connect eating, movement, sleep and calming choices with how their bodies and minds feel. Students swap recordings and check whether the advice is clear, kind and possible for a Year 1 child to follow. They finish with a short talking-character health message for a class body display. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the character's mouth with each student's recorded voice.

Students paint a layered self-portrait showing how their body and mind might feel before and after a healthy action such as sleep, movement, water or quiet breathing. The two versions show that choices can affect both physical feelings and emotions. Each student chooses colours, marks and shapes that make sense to them, then asks a partner what changes they notice. They finish with a paired digital painting that can prompt a class conversation about different ways people care for themselves. Layers let students change the background, body outline and feeling marks without starting again.

Students watch a teacher-selected video about body care, emotions or staying safe and answer its built-in questions as they go. Stopping at key moments helps them notice how one person's action can help or harm themselves and others. Pairs compare one answer, replay the matching scene and decide whether the video gives enough evidence. They finish with a completed set of responses and one healthy or safe action they can test during the school week. Clickview's curated clips and built-in questions keep the viewing focused and manageable.

Students build and record a short puppet scene in which a character faces a choice about playground safety, personal space, rest or asking for help. Showing both the choice and its effect makes cause and consequence visible to young learners. Groups exchange unfinished scenes, predict the safest next action and let the original creators choose the ending. They finish with a narrated puppet show that models clear words and helpful actions. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

Students design and build a vibrant obstacle course that represents a 'day in the life' of a healthy person, using cardboard, popsticks, fabric scraps, recycled containers, and markers. Along the track, they create interactive stations (like brushing teeth, eating fruits, exercising, and resting) with moving parts or flaps. Using Sphero Indi cars, students program simple routes to guide their cars through each healthy habit station, reinforcing cause-and-effect and the importance of daily routines. This hands-on project helps students physically map out and share their understanding of how healthy choices keep our bodies and minds strong.

ci: Artistic appreciation and expressions inspire our imagination and creativity.
lo: Forms of expression; Expressing thoughts and ideas; Understanding and appreciating art

s.d: Students compose a short soundscape that expresses the colours, shapes and feelings they notice in a chosen artwork. This shows how one art form can spark imagination in another. Students swap artworks without explaining their choices, then compare how differently their partners translate the same image into sound. They choose and arrange sounds to create a clear beginning, change and ending. The class finishes with a listening gallery where the artwork is revealed after each composition plays. GarageBand makes this possible by letting students record and arrange music and sound effects.

Students draw an everyday object in Sketchbook, then transform it into something imagined through colour, pattern and added details. This helps them see that artistic expression can begin with close observation and grow through creative choices. Partners exchange unfinished drawings and suggest one surprising possibility without taking control of the artist's idea. Each student decides whether to accept, adapt or reject the suggestion. They finish with a detailed digital illustration and a short written artist statement. Sketchbook's drawing tools support careful sketching, colouring and visual experimentation.

Students animate cut-paper shapes to show the feeling and imagery in a short poem they have written. This lets them explore how words, movement and visual art can express the same thought in different ways. Another class watches the animations without seeing the poems and describes the feelings or ideas it notices. Students use that response to adjust the timing, movement or final frame. They finish with a short stop-motion poem that can be screened for the school community. Stop Motion Studio captures the paper pieces frame by frame so small changes appear to move.

Students record a short interview with a classmate about an artwork, song or poem that inspires them. This builds appreciation by asking children to listen closely to another person's ideas and feelings. Interviewers must include one follow-up question based on something their partner actually says. Students then edit the conversation so the speaker's voice and meaning remain clear. They finish with a brief podcast episode featuring an introduction, interview and closing reflection. Podcasting using Canva supports recording and editing the complete audio story on an iPad.

Students draw or write responses to several artworks on a shared Freeform canvas. This makes different forms of expression and personal interpretations visible in one place. Each student connects their response to a classmate's idea that surprises them, then adds a note explaining the connection. The class looks for artworks that produced similar feelings as well as completely different reactions. They finish with a connected visual wall of drawings, words, questions and appreciation notes. Freeform's infinite collaborative canvas lets ideas sit beside one another and grow over several lessons.

Students work in teams to design and build colourful mini 'forts' or 'tunnels' using big cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, recycled materials, and child-safe art supplies. Inside their creations, they place a simple iPad with the Voice Memos app, recording and playing back their own poems, songs, or stories about feelings and imagination. Each fort is decorated to express an emotion or idea (like 'joy', 'curiosity', or 'peace'), blending artistic choices with physical construction. This project lets children express themselves through both building and audio storytelling, sharing their creative spaces and messages with classmates.

ci: Marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities.
lo: Needs and wants; The changing needs of communities; The design process

s.d: Students record a 360-degree view of a classroom marketplace while classmates buy, sell, queue and restock essential and optional items. The whole-space recording helps them notice how layout and organisation affect whether community needs are met. Students watch from different directions and choose one change that would make the market easier for a young child, an older person or someone carrying several bags. They rearrange the stalls, record the market again and compare the two versions. They end with before-and-after 360-degree recordings of a redesigned marketplace. The spherical view captures the stalls, signs, queues and movement at the same time.

Students build a short survey that asks another Year 2 class to choose between community needs and wants in marketplace situations. The responses show that marketplaces change according to what people value, use and can afford. Students include one question about what a local support organisation should stock first when space is limited. They compare the live results, discuss surprising choices and revise any unclear questions. They end with a real set of community preference data and a ranked list of priorities. Microsoft Forms automatically collects the answers and displays simple charts.

Students turn class votes about essential and optional marketplace items into a visual stock-planning board in Freeform. They use sticky notes or duplicated picture symbols to represent items such as bread, soap, warm clothing, toys and treats, then arrange them into labelled needs and wants zones. Groups use the drawing and shape tools to circle high-priority items and add tally marks showing how many people selected each one. When the teacher announces hot weather, reduced funds or a new baby group, students move, remove or duplicate items to revise their plan. Pairs compare boards and discuss who their choices support and who might miss out. They produce an annotated community stall plan that makes changing priorities and limited resources visible.

Students watch selected clips showing supermarkets, street markets and community food services, pausing to sort what each place provides into needs and wants. This helps them see that marketplaces are organised around the people who use them. The teacher adds questions that ask students to notice who is served, what is easy to access and what may be missing. Students revisit one clip after hearing about Sacred Heart Mission and change an answer when new evidence changes their thinking. They end with completed responses comparing several kinds of marketplaces. ClickView's built-in questions keep the viewing focused and make student thinking visible to the teacher.

Students build possible floor plans for a small community market by stretching bands around the virtual peg grid. They explore how stall shape, pathway width and available space influence what the market can offer. Partners swap plans and test whether every essential stall can be reached without crossing another stall. Students revise their shapes when a new community need requires a food table, quiet waiting area or donation point. They end with a clear geometric market plan that balances limited space with community priorities. The virtual bands make it quick to move boundaries and compare area and perimeter.

Students design and build their own mini marketplace stalls using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, and craft materials, representing different community needs and wants (e.g., food, clothing, toys). Each group creates physical 'goods' for their stall, then codes a Bee-Bot or Sphero Indi to visit other stalls following a marketplace map they draw and decorate. Along the way, students practice exchanging 'needs' and 'wants' tokens and reflect on how their choices impact the community. This project blends creative building, basic robotics, and real-world marketplace concepts, making the design cycle hands-on and meaningful.

ci: Forces and motion are all around us.
lo: Forces around us; Scientific laws of motion; Innovations in technology

s.d: Students photograph pushes, pulls and still objects, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images into three groups. This helps them work out how a computer can recognise evidence of force and motion. Pairs swap image sets to test whether each model can recognise unfamiliar examples from the playground. They finish with a working image-classification model and a list of mistakes that helped them improve it. Teachable Machine retrains the model when students add clearer or more varied examples. This works like sports-coaching apps that recognise movement from images to give feedback on technique.

Students photograph a playground object and record it explaining the pushes, pulls, gravity or friction acting on it. This gives young scientists a playful reason to use force and motion vocabulary accurately. Another class watches the talking objects and sends back one question each group must answer. Students finish with a collection of short explanations from swings, slides, balls and climbing equipment. ChatterPix Kids lets students draw a mouth on a photo and add a recorded voice. The short recording limit encourages one clear scientific explanation rather than a long script.

Students build a digital investigation book by adding results from rolling the same object across different surfaces. This shows how friction changes motion and why fair testing matters. Groups exchange books and repeat one another's investigation to see whether the results are similar. Each group finishes with a narrated book containing predictions, measurements, labelled evidence and a conclusion. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page. Families can use the finished books to try one safe force experiment at home.

Students film and edit short comparisons of objects moving down ramps with different heights or surfaces. This makes changes in speed and distance easier to see and discuss. Groups choose one surprising result and ask another group to explain it before revealing their own conclusion. They finish with a short science documentary using titles, spoken explanations and carefully selected clips. IMovie provides titles and transitions for joining several tests into one clear film. The final films can run beside the physical ramps during a community display.

Students arrange coloured tiles to make Sphero Indi start, change direction and stop along a floor path. This shows how technology can control motion through a planned sequence of causes and effects. Groups swap paths and work out the intended sequence before letting the car run. They finish with a tested route that carries the car between labelled examples of pushes, pulls, gravity and friction. Sphero Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen. Students improve the spacing and order of tiles when the movement does not match their plan.

s.t: Marble Run Mayhem: Forces in Action!
s.d: Students will design and build their own wild marble runs using cardboard tubes, recycled boxes, popsticks, paper plates, and masking tape. They will explore forces like gravity, push, pull, and friction as they experiment with different ramps, tunnels, and obstacles. Using iPads and the free 'Stop Motion Studio' app, students will film their marbles in action, creating short movies that highlight how their inventions work. This project brings the science of forces and motion to life through creative engineering, hands-on building, and digital storytelling.

ci: Taking care of our Earth starts with the choices we make.
lo: Earth's resources; How our actions affect the environment; Ways we can care for our planet

s.d: Students sort photographs of everyday lunchbox items into 'use once', 'use again' and 'recycle' groups. This makes the link between daily choices, Earth's resources and the rubbish we produce easy to see. Pairs then redesign one waste-heavy lunchbox by replacing three items with lower-waste choices. They swap collages and check whether each suggested change is realistic for a Year 2 family. Each pair finishes with a clear before-and-after lunchbox collage. PicCollage's grid layouts and short captions keep the comparison simple and visual.

Students complete a teacher-created bin-audit form to count paper, food scraps, soft plastics and recyclable containers found in the classroom rubbish. Microsoft Forms' choice questions and automatic response charts reveal which materials the class discards most often. Groups study the visual summaries, predict which type of waste they could reduce and choose one realistic action, such as using both sides of paper or packing reusable containers. After a week, students repeat the same form to collect comparable data. They examine the updated charts and decide whether their action made a measurable difference. The class finishes with an evidence-based waste goal for the following week.

Students photograph a clean discarded object and record it explaining where it came from and what could happen to it next. Speaking as a bottle, wrapper or cardboard tube makes the path from resource to rubbish easier to understand. Students swap recordings and suggest one better choice that could change each object's ending. They then revise the voice clip so the object asks listeners to take one clear action. Each student finishes with a short talking-object message for a class recycling display. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and recorded voice directly to the photograph.

Students code two short animations showing what happens when a character makes a wasteful choice and a caring choice. The side-by-side outcomes show how one action can affect land, water, animals or the amount of rubbish produced. Partners exchange projects, follow each sequence and identify where the environmental outcome changes. Students debug any unclear movement or message so a younger class can understand the cause and effect. Each pair finishes with an animated choice story containing two different endings. ScratchJr's blocks let students sequence characters, speech and movement without needing to type code.

Students record short interviews with classmates about one Earth-friendly choice they already make and one they could improve. Hearing several answers shows that caring for the planet depends on many practical choices rather than one perfect solution. The class selects a few questions for a staff member who helps manage waste, gardens or resources at school. Students listen back and choose the clearest answers rather than recording every idea again. They finish with a set of brief audio interviews that can be played at a class action meeting. The microphones and recorders capture voices clearly enough for students to compare ideas and notice repeated themes.

Students design and build miniature animal habitats using recycled materials like cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, bottle caps, and natural elements such as twigs or leaves. They then program a Sphero Indi robot (or similar age-appropriate robot) to navigate between the habitats, 'delivering' eco-friendly solutions—like tiny recycling bins or water drops they've crafted—to each one. This project lets students explore how caring for different environments supports life on Earth, encouraging creative problem-solving and teamwork while linking local actions to global environmental responsibility.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Landmarks and places of significance tell stories about our history.
lo: The significance of places to different people and cultures; The connection between landmarks and identity; How landmarks and symbols represent our history

s.d: Students explore teacher-selected Australian and Aboriginal places of significance in Street View, looking closely at signs, symbols, paths and memorials. This shows how a place can hold stories that are not obvious from its appearance alone. Pairs compare two sites and choose which details help visitors understand each place's identity and history. They then guide another pair through the view and explain one visible story and one story that would need to be learned from Traditional Owners or trusted sources. Each pair finishes with an oral guided tour of a significant place. Street View lets students move through the surroundings without signing in or changing the map.

Students build a simple 3D scene showing a significant Australian place at two moments in time. This helps them show how landmarks can stay important even when their surroundings or uses change. Students swap scenes and ask whether the symbols, people and objects make the place's story clear. They revise one detail after hearing what their classmates understood or missed. Each student finishes with an interactive virtual scene that can be explored from different viewpoints. Delightex lets students place and arrange objects inside a three-dimensional world.

Students record a short puppet conversation between two people who value the same place for different reasons. This makes the significance of places to different people and cultures easier to hear and compare. Students choose a carefully researched local or Australian place, while teacher-approved sources guide any Aboriginal perspectives. Another class watches the puppet shows and identifies the clues that reveal each speaker's connection to the place. Each pair finishes with a narrated puppet show containing a clear setting, two viewpoints and a respectful ending. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a landmark or symbol speaking in the first person about one true event, memory or cultural connection linked to it. This gives them a clear way to explain how landmarks carry stories from the past. Students choose whether their speaker addresses a new visitor, a future child or someone who wants to change the site. Partners listen and check that the recording separates known facts from imagined words. Each student finishes with a short lip-synced character explanation suitable for a class exhibition. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the on-screen character's mouth with the student's voice.

Students make a digital field guide with one page for each significant Australian place they investigate. This brings maps, stories, symbols and reasons for preservation into one clear collection. Families or another Year 2 class can listen to the pages and leave students with questions to answer in a revised edition. Students include their own words, a labelled image and a recorded explanation of why each place matters. The class finishes with a narrated digital book that compares several places without ranking one culture's significance above another. Book Creator supports text, images and student-recorded narration on the same page.

Students will choose an Australian or Indigenous landmark, then craft a 3D diorama using recycled boxes, tissue paper, and natural materials (like stones, sand, and leaves) to recreate its landscape and features. They'll embed a simple battery-powered LED (with adult help) to illuminate a 'story stone'—a decorated rock that symbolizes the site's unique story or Dreaming. Using iPads, students will record a short audio narration about their landmark's significance, then attach a QR code to their lightbox so visitors can listen to the story. This project combines hands-on building, storytelling, and digital skills to celebrate the connection between place, culture, and history.

ci: Our relationships with others impact our lives.
lo: Importance of relationships; Developing and maintaining healthy relationships; The impact of relationships on wellbeing

s.d: Students record a short interview with a trusted person about how their relationship has changed over time. This shows that caring relationships grow through shared experiences, listening and repair. Each student chooses one answer that could help the class build stronger relationships and records a voice reflection explaining why. Families can listen and add another example from home. Students end with a collection of short video or audio interviews and personal reflections. Seesaw keeps the recordings together in each student's portfolio.

Students photograph three clear body poses for calming down, such as stretching, star breathing and hands on heart, then train Teachable Machine to recognise them. This helps students explore how self-regulation can support healthy relationships during difficult moments. Pairs swap models and test whether each pose is recognised from different positions, then add better examples when the model makes mistakes. Similar pose recognition is used in physiotherapy and accessibility tools to notice body movements and give useful feedback. Students end with a tested model that identifies their chosen calming poses. The model improves as students add varied and accurate training examples.

Students plan and record a puppet scene in which two friends face a small disagreement and try two different responses. This makes the impact of words, listening and taking responsibility easy to see and discuss. Another pair watches the unfinished scene and chooses which healthy response the characters should try next. Students then record an ending that shows how the choice affects both characters' wellbeing. They end with a short animated puppet show that can be used during a class meeting. Puppet Pals lets students move characters across a backdrop while recording their voices.

Students paint two layered portraits showing how a person might feel before and after a caring interaction. This helps them notice that relationships can affect feelings, confidence and wellbeing. Students exchange paintings without explanations and ask a partner what colours, shapes or details helped them read each feeling. They then revise one layer so the emotional change is clearer without adding words. Students end with a paired digital artwork showing the impact of kindness, exclusion, apology or support. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting with separate layers that can be adjusted during revision.

Students photograph small classroom figures frame by frame to show a friendship changing over time. This makes maintaining relationships visible through actions such as inviting, listening, apologising and checking in. Groups swap half-finished animations and suggest one caring action that could change what happens next. The original group chooses whether to use that suggestion and explains its choice in the final scene. Students end with a short stop-motion story showing a relationship problem, a response and its effect on wellbeing. Stop Motion Studio joins the photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students work in teams to design and construct colourful 'Friendship Bridges' from cardboard, craft sticks, yarn, and recycled materials, representing the connections between people. Next, they decorate simple Sphero Indi cars as 'Emotion Bots', coding them with coloured tiles to travel across each bridge, pausing at 'emotion stations' where students add hand-drawn emoji signs or calming textures. As the bots journey, classmates explain how different feelings and actions can strengthen or weaken relationships, making the abstract idea of connection tangible. This playful project blends physical building, basic robotics, and social-emotional storytelling to help students understand and reflect on the bridges they build with others.

ci: Celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community.
lo: The ways personal and cultural events are celebrated; Our appreciation of the diversity of cultures; How celebrations shape community identity

s.d: Students arrange objects, colours and handmade signs that show how a family or cultural celebration brings people together, then record each display with the Insta360 camera. Seeing the whole setting helps them notice that space, decoration and gathering are part of how traditions shape community identity. Groups swap recordings and look around each other's displays, asking respectful questions about details they do not recognise. Families can also suggest one object or message that should appear in the display. Students finish with an immersive 360-degree gallery of celebrations represented across the class. The spherical recording lets viewers turn and explore every part of each setting rather than seeing one chosen camera angle.

Students write and send a short survey asking families which events they celebrate, what they do and why those traditions matter. The responses show both shared customs and important differences within one school community. Each group chooses one pattern in the auto-charts that surprised them and writes a new question to investigate. The class discusses how to report small cultural groups respectfully without treating one answer as typical of everyone. Students finish with a class data display showing how celebrations help shape the Elsternwick community. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and turns them into charts that Year 3 students can read and compare.

Students record a short interview with a family or community member about one celebration, including what has stayed the same and what has changed. Listening to a real voice helps students understand that traditions are carried, adapted and valued by people. Partners exchange recordings and choose one respectful follow-up question that would help the speaker explain the tradition more fully. Students edit the interview so the speaker's words remain the centre of the episode. They finish with a class podcast collection featuring different cultural and personal celebrations. Podcasting using Canva works on iPads and supports recording and editing the complete episode in one place.

Students design an exhibition panel comparing two celebrations through food, music, clothing, symbols, gathering places and purpose. The comparison helps them see diversity without deciding that one way of celebrating is normal and another is unusual. Each panel includes a question for visitors, such as 'What brings people together in both celebrations?' Visitors add spoken responses during a class gallery walk, and students revise any wording that could create a stereotype. Students finish with a clear visual display for families or another Year 3 class. Canva provides layouts for combining short text, images and headings on one exhibition panel.

Students paint a layered digital artwork that combines symbols, colours and patterns from celebrations that matter to their family or community. Choosing what to place in the foreground and background helps them show which parts of identity are public, shared or personally meaningful. Students exchange paintings without explanations first, then compare what viewers noticed with what the artist intended. The artist can change a layer when a symbol needs more emphasis or a clearer relationship to the whole image. Students finish with an original digital portrait of cultural identity for a class gallery. Brushes Redux supports layered painting, so students can revise one part without repainting the entire work.

Students will work in teams to design and build vibrant 3D 'towers' representing a celebration or tradition from their own or another culture. Using cardboard, fabric, recycled materials, clay, LED tea lights, and decorative craft supplies, they will construct physical towers featuring key symbols, artifacts, and elements of their chosen celebration. Then, students will embed simple programmable micro:bit messages or sound bites (recorded on micro:bit or Makey Makey soundboards) into their towers, sharing stories or greetings in different languages. This project fuses hands-on making with digital storytelling, encouraging students to express cultural identity and diversity in a memorable, interactive way.

ci: The rights and responsibilities of citizens are determined by the rules and laws of a community.
lo: The differences between rules and laws; People responsible for enforcing rules and laws; Rights and responsibilities of citizens; The consequences when rules, laws and rights are not met

s.d: Students program Sphero BOLT to travel through a floor course where signs represent community rules, laws and restricted areas. They work out why some instructions keep everyone safe while others simply help a group run smoothly. Teams exchange courses and test whether another group's instructions are clear, fair and possible to follow. When a route fails or breaks a stated rule, students revise the code and explain the likely consequence for the community. Each team ends with a working coded route and a short spoken explanation at each checkpoint. Sphero BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid let students show actions such as stop, wait and proceed.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion about whether a fictional community decision should be a rule or a law. This helps them examine who makes decisions, who enforces them and how citizens' rights may be affected. Halfway through, students must choose one new piece of information that could change their position, such as a safety risk or an unfair consequence. They compare their reasoning with a partner and identify where their answers became stronger. Each student finishes with a written conversation and a justified recommendation for the fictional community. The teacher can set up a Socratic Tutor scenario that asks open-ended questions without giving students the answer.

Students enter class responses into Microsoft Excel about which rights and responsibilities matter most at school. They turn the responses into charts and look for patterns, disagreements and responsibilities that support several rights. Small groups choose one surprising result and ask another class whether the same pattern appears there. They add the new responses and check whether the larger sample changes their conclusion. Students finish with a labelled chart and a short evidence-based statement about one right and its matching responsibility. Excel tables and charts make changes in the class data easy to see.

Students record and edit a short news report showing what happens when a community rule, law or right is not respected. Their report must explain the rule or law, identify who responds and show consequences for more than one person. Groups film two possible endings, one where the response is fair and one where it creates a new problem. Another class watches both endings and chooses which response best protects people's rights. Students finish with an edited news report containing titles, interviews and two contrasting outcomes. IMovie lets them combine recorded clips, titles and transitions in one film.

Students write a Kahoot quiz that asks classmates to decide whether each everyday example is a rule, a law, a right or a responsibility. They must explain the correct answer after each question so the quiz teaches rather than only tests. Groups swap quizzes and flag any question where the wording or answer seems unfair or unclear. The authors then revise those questions using the feedback and run the improved quiz with another group. Each team ends with a playable quiz built from realistic school and community situations. Kahoot's timed questions and response summaries quickly reveal which distinctions still need discussion.

s.t: Rule City: Build & Govern Your Own Mini-Town
s.d: Students work in teams to design and construct a model town using cardboard, recycled boxes, craft sticks, and fabric scraps, creating roads, buildings, parks, and community spaces. Once built, each group invents a set of town rules and laws (displayed on hand-made signs), then programs a Sphero Indi or Bee-Bot as a 'citizen' to navigate common scenarios—like crossing streets or visiting the library—while following these rules. Teams test, revise, and reflect on how their rules shape daily life in their town, connecting physical making with digital problem-solving and the real-world impact of systems, laws, and citizenship.

ci: Humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take action.
lo: The work of scientists; The process of learning; How science brings about new understandings and changes

s.d: Students program a micro:bit to measure light levels and show an LED warning when a classroom space is using more light than it needs. This shows how scientists turn measurements into action that can reduce wasted energy. Groups test different thresholds, compare sunny and cloudy conditions, and swap devices to check whether another group's code works reliably. They adjust one variable at a time and debug warnings that appear too early or too late. Each group finishes with a working light-monitoring device and a tested recommendation for the classroom. The built-in light sensing, LED grid and battery pack allow the device to collect information and run away from the computer.

Students measure the time taken for ice cubes to melt under different fair-test conditions and enter their results in Microsoft Excel. This helps them see how controlled variables and repeated measurements lead to stronger scientific explanations. Groups exchange data so they can decide whether one unusual result should change the class conclusion. They make charts that reveal patterns across locations, coverings or container types. Each group finishes with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based conclusion about heat transfer and changes of state. Excel's tables and charts make patterns and unexpected results easy to compare.

Students build two small homes in Minecraft Education, changing one design feature at a time to show how shade, windows and building materials can affect heating and energy use. This makes scientific principles visible as choices that can improve how people live. Another group inspects each pair of homes and identifies the variable that changed before suggesting a more sustainable redesign. Students then rebuild one section to respond to that feedback while keeping the comparison fair. Each team finishes with a matched pair of models and signs explaining the scientific reason for each design choice. Minecraft's shared block-building world lets students construct, inspect and revise the models at full scale.

Students photograph clean examples of paper, plastic and general waste in Teachable Machine and train an image model to sort them. This shows how repeated examples help a computer learn patterns and how science can support responsible consumption. Groups test one another's models with crumpled, partly hidden and differently coloured items, then add better training examples when the model makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way by recognising materials before directing them into different streams. Each group finishes with a tested classification model and a record of which objects confused it. Teachable Machine's image classes and live camera testing make each improvement visible straight away.

Students record a narrated screencast that explains one fair test, drawing the setup and moving labels to show the independent, dependent and controlled variables. This makes the process of learning in science as important as the final result. Partners pause the explanation at the prediction stage and decide whether the test is fair before hearing what happened. Students revise any unclear section and add an annotation showing how the evidence changed or strengthened their thinking. Each student finishes with a short recorded explanation that can play beside the experiment at the science fair. Explain Everything records the student's voice, drawing and on-screen movements together.

Students design and build a spectacular Rube Goldberg-style chain reaction machine that demonstrates different types of energy transformation (e.g., potential to kinetic, motion to sound). Using recycled cardboard, marbles, dominoes, balloons, string, plastic bottles, and more, teams prototype each step and connect them for a dramatic final effect. They record their machine in action using an iPad, then use the Clips app to add voiceovers explaining each energy change and how scientific principles make their carnival contraption work. This hands-on challenge immerses students in the design cycle and links scientific understanding to creative problem-solving and real-world innovation.

ci: Adaptation and sustainability ensure the survival of living things in changing environments.
lo: Adaptations and structural features of living things; Roles of living things in an ecosystem; Actions that benefit or harm ecosystems

s.d: Students photograph and identify Victorian animals they can find around the Elsternwick campus. They check each identification against the app's species information and list the structural or behavioural features that may help the animal survive. This makes adaptation visible in places students usually walk past without noticing. Pairs compare animals found in sunny, shaded, built and planted areas, then suggest why each animal was there. They finish with a set of local species records and evidence-based survival explanations. The app's Victorian fauna guide keeps the investigation local and age-appropriate.

Students explore climate and terrain layers to compare the changing environments where selected animals live.
