They annotate regions with the adaptations that help each animal find food, shelter or safety there. Groups then swap maps and add one possible environmental change, such as reduced rainfall, warmer conditions or habitat loss. The original group decides whether its animal could survive that change and adds a supported prediction. Students finish with an annotated map showing how place, adaptation and survival are connected. MapMaker's layered geographic data lets them look for patterns rather than view a static map.

Students record a short digital field guide entry explaining how one living thing fits into an ecosystem. They combine text, labelled images and narration to show its adaptations, food relationships and role in keeping the ecosystem healthy. Each student also adds a page showing one human action that would help and one that would cause harm. Another class listens to the entries and records a question that the authors can answer through revision. Students finish with a narrated class book linked to Life on Land or Life Below Water. Book Creator keeps writing, images, audio and video together in one book.

Students design an infographic that follows one animal through an environmental change. They show the animal's useful features, its ecosystem role, the new threat and an action people could take to improve its chance of survival. Students choose whether their message is aimed at families, park visitors or other children, then adjust the words and images for that audience. Partners test each infographic by explaining its message after viewing it for only ten seconds. Students finish with a clear conservation display for a classroom or corridor exhibition. Adobe Express provides simple layouts for combining short text, images and diagrams.

Students build a 3D ecosystem containing producers, consumers, shelter, water and a human action that changes the environment. They code selected objects to move or respond so viewers can see relationships such as feeding, hiding or habitat loss. Groups exchange scenes and predict which living things will benefit, struggle or disappear after the change. The builders then revise their scene so the cause and effect can be understood without a long explanation. Students finish with an interactive ecosystem that compares a harmful choice with a more sustainable one. Delightex's CoBlocks make movement and responses part of the model rather than decoration.

Students will design and build a unique animal using clay, recycled materials, and craft supplies, inventing imaginative adaptations to help it survive in a chosen ecosystem. Next, they'll construct a matching 3D habitat diorama using cardboard, fabric scraps, and natural elements, ensuring it includes features that support their animal's needs. Using Sphero Indi robots, students will code a simple 'migration' route for their creature—laying out coloured tiles and obstacles within their habitat diorama to simulate real-world challenges like finding food or shelter. This cross-disciplinary project brings adaptation and sustainability to life, connecting creativity, coding, and hands-on making to the big ideas of Sharing the Planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration leads to new discoveries that can shape and change society.
lo: The factors that motivate exploration (Causation); How people reflect on discoveries from the past to inform change (Change); How exploration brings about change and new understandings for people, places and society (Change)

s.d: Students map the First Fleet route and add notes showing key decisions, risks and motivations along the journey. They switch between terrain, climate and population layers to work out how place may influence exploration. Groups compare the British route with evidence of the ancient travel, trade and navigation networks of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Each group chooses one point where a different decision might have changed what happened next. Students finish with an annotated map that separates evidence, questions and possible consequences. MapMaker's geographic layers let them test ideas against real features of the Earth.

Students collect images, short notes and source details about an Australian journey or discovery on a shared canvas. They connect each motivation to an action and then to a change for people, places or society. Groups swap boards and add a question wherever the evidence does not fully support a claim. Students then rearrange the material to show that the same event can look different from British and First Nations perspectives. They finish with a visual evidence web ready to guide historical writing or discussion. Freeform's infinite canvas makes relationships and gaps easy to see.

Students build paper scenes and record a stop-motion explanation of how one discovery changed everyday life. They show the sequence from a problem or motivation, through exploration, to a discovery and its later effects. Another group watches the unfinished animation and identifies any missing cause or unexplained change. Students revise the sequence by adding frames, labels or a contrasting perspective rather than simply making the film longer. They finish with a short historical animation that makes cause and change visible. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame recording lets students slow down a complex chain of events.

Students interview a teacher-set historical character about why they supported, joined or were affected by an exploration. They ask follow-up questions about motives, choices and consequences while remembering that the chatbot is not a fact-checked source. Halfway through, students exchange their strongest question with a partner and use it to push the conversation beyond dates and events. They check important claims against class sources and note where the character's viewpoint may be limited. Students finish with a saved written conversation and a short list of claims to verify. The Character Interview scenario keeps the discussion structured while the teacher controls its rules and support.

Students watch selected clips about the First Fleet, Aboriginal histories and later Australian exploration, pausing to record what each clip says changed. They sort their responses into motivations, discoveries, benefits, harms and unanswered questions. Pairs compare two clips and look for differences in language, missing voices and evidence. Each pair chooses one claim that needs a different perspective before it can be accepted. Students finish with completed responses that show how accounts of the past can shape decisions today. ClickView's curated video library and built-in questions support close viewing without requiring students to make another media piece.

Students will design and build their own 'exploration rovers' using recycled materials, wheels, and craft supplies, then program Sphero Indi robots to navigate a giant collaborative map representing different historical exploration routes (like the First Fleet or Indigenous trade paths). Along the journey, students will create and hide miniature 'time capsule artifacts' inside their rovers—handmade items or messages representing discoveries or moments in history. As they test and refine their rovers' journeys using the Design Cycle, students reflect on how exploration changes societies and what messages or objects might matter to future generations. This project fuses hands-on building, digital navigation, and historical imagination, making learning about past explorations a memorable adventure.

ci: An inquiry into the nature of the self; beliefs and values; personal, physical, mental, social and spiritual health; human relationships.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a future version of themselves giving advice about handling a setback, change or friendship problem. This opens a safe conversation about resilience because students can speak through a character rather than perform on camera. Students swap characters with a partner and record a second message showing how advice may change for different people. They end with two short character videos that model helpful self-talk and responsible choices. The character automatically lip-syncs to each student's recorded voice. A class viewing can begin a list of strategies students already use when life feels difficult.

Students build a shared map of actions that help or harm friendships online and face-to-face. This makes the links between choices, feelings, safety and trust easy to see. Small groups connect similar actions, then respectfully challenge one connection made by another group. They end with a colour-coded class canvas showing friendship problems, possible responses and likely outcomes. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes. The teacher can return to the board after stories or discussions and ask students to revise earlier ideas.

Students compose two short soundscapes showing how a setback can feel before and after someone uses a coping strategy. This helps them notice that feelings can change without labelling any emotion as wrong. Partners listen without seeing the title and explain what change they hear, prompting the composer to refine the music. Each student ends with a paired recording that moves from tension towards calm, courage or hope. GarageBand lets students arrange loops and record original sounds in separate tracks. A listening gallery gives the class many word-free ways to represent resilience.

Students post short responses to friendship and online-safety scenarios, naming a safe action and why it could help. This makes personal responsibility visible through everyday choices such as pausing, asking permission, including others or seeking adult help. Students reply to two classmates by offering another respectful option rather than judging the first response. The class ends with a practical wall of strategies that can be revisited when real problems arise. Padlet supports brief posts and peer replies in one shared space. The teacher can add new scenarios during the inquiry to see whether students' responses become more thoughtful.

Students create a choose-your-own-response story about a character facing a setback, change or friendship difficulty. This shows how one decision can affect safety, trust, feelings and what happens next. Students exchange books and record advice for the character at one important decision point. Each student ends with a multimodal book containing two possible responses, their consequences and a final reflection. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration on the same pages. Families or another Year 3 class can read the stories and discuss which choices protect both self and others.

s.t: Resilience Road: Build Your Own Journey Board Game
s.d: Students design and construct a 3D board game that represents a journey through life's challenges and triumphs, using cardboard, recycled materials, clay, and craft supplies for pathways, obstacles, and character tokens. They integrate simple interactive elements with Makey Makey or micro:bit to trigger sound effects or messages when players land on key spaces, blending physical making with digital creativity. Each game space features scenarios about overcoming setbacks and building friendships, encouraging students to reflect on their own strategies for resilience and safety. By inventing and playing their unique games, students collaboratively explore growth mindset and positive relationships in a memorable, hands-on way.

ci: Technology transforms how we create and share ideas.
lo: How technology expands creative possibilities; The evolution of communication tools; The impact of technology on expression

s.d: Students record and arrange one short message as Morse-style rhythms, a radio jingle and a modern electronic soundscape. They hear how changing technology can reshape the same idea and influence how an audience responds. Each group gives another group only the audio and asks what message or mood they understood. Students then revise the least clear version after hearing that feedback. They finish with three contrasting recordings that show the evolution of audio communication. GarageBand's instruments, loops and audio tracks let students compose and record in one place.

Students draw and record a narrated timeline showing how one communication tool changed from an older form to a digital form. This makes the evolution of communication visible while students explain what each change made possible. Partners swap timelines and identify one benefit, one loss and one new responsibility created by the change. Students add these responses as a final annotated section. They finish with a short screencast that combines drawings, labels and spoken explanation. Explain Everything records the screen and voice while students draw and annotate.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short speech for an animated character explaining a cybersafe choice to younger learners. They explore how an on-screen speaker can make an important message clearer, friendlier or more persuasive. Each student tests two versions with different wording, then asks a younger peer which one is easiest to understand. Students revise the script so it avoids fear, blame and private information. They finish with a brief animated message ready to use in the student-led technology workshops. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students build an interactive 3D gallery showing how a single idea might be expressed through symbols, text, sound-related objects and virtual movement. This shows how digital spaces expand creative choices beyond a flat page. Groups exchange galleries and code one object to respond differently after visitors make a choice. Students test whether visitors can move through the scene and understand the intended message without spoken instructions. They finish with a coded virtual exhibition for classmates to explore. Delightex's CoBlocks let students program objects to move and respond inside the 3D scene.

Students build a survey asking how classmates create, communicate and decide what is safe to post online. The responses show how technology affects expression across their own school community. Students invite a younger class and an adult class to answer the same carefully worded questions. They compare the automatic charts and work out where age groups agree or differ. They finish with a survey and a set of evidence-based recommendations for their technology workshops. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and turns them into charts.

s.t: Wearable Message Makers: Light-Up Expression Bands
s.d: Students will design and craft their own wearable 'expression bands'—wristbands or headbands made from felt, recycled fabric, and cardboard—that light up to share a personal message or mood. Using simple circuits with LEDs and coin cell batteries, they'll integrate their chosen symbols, words, or emojis into the band, learning about both creative self-expression and basic electronics. Students will sketch, prototype, and refine their designs using the Design Cycle, then share how their wearable tech communicates ideas in new, interactive ways. This project brings together technology, hands-on making, and the evolving ways we express ourselves to others.

ci: Systems connect us.
lo: Human systems; The interconnections that exist within and across systems; The influence of systems on communities

s.d: Students photograph clean examples of paper, plastic and landfill items, then train an image model to sort them. This shows how a recycling system depends on clear inputs, rules and decisions. Groups swap unfamiliar items and find out where their models make mistakes or disagree. They improve the training examples, retest the model and decide which items still require a human choice. Students end with a working waste-sorting model and a record of its most revealing errors. It works like the camera-driven sorting systems used to direct materials inside recycling facilities.

Students map one school system, such as lunch orders, borrowing books or moving waste from classrooms to bins. They add each person, place, action and resource, then draw arrows to show how the parts connect. Groups swap boards and remove one important part to predict what would slow down, stop or affect another system. They then invite a staff member involved in the system to correct missing links and explain real constraints. Students end with a detailed system map showing normal operation, a breakdown and a possible improvement. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move ideas and redraw connections as their understanding changes.

Students collect daily counts of rubbish, recycling and compost produced by their class across one school week. They enter the numbers into a table and create graphs to spot patterns in the waste system. Each group chooses one practical change, such as moving a bin or improving a label, and gathers a second set of data after the change. Groups compare which change had the clearest effect rather than simply choosing the most popular idea. Students end with before-and-after graphs and an evidence-based recommendation for the school. Excel makes it easy to update charts when new measurements are added.

Students program Sphero BOLT to carry a small item through a model collection route linking a classroom, sorting point and reuse station. This makes the movement and timing inside a human system visible and testable. Another group changes one route condition, such as closing a path or moving a collection point, and the programmers must debug their solution. Students compare whether one long route or several short routes moves items more reliably. They end with a working program, a tested route and a short live demonstration of how the system responds to change. BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid can show both the route and the item's destination category.

Students record a 360-degree view of one school system in action, such as the library return area, compost station or busy bag-storage space. The full view helps them notice how people, signs, objects and pathways affect one another. They position the camera twice, once during a quiet period and once when the system is busy, while protecting people's privacy. Another class explores the recordings and identifies a bottleneck or missing instruction that Year 4 did not notice. Students end with two immersive views and a specific proposal for improving the space. The spherical recording keeps the whole surrounding system visible rather than showing only where a camera operator pointed.

s.t: Eco-Systems in Motion: Sphero Smart City Challenge
s.d: Students design and build a vibrant miniature cityscape using recycled cardboard, bottle caps, fabric scraps, and natural materials, mapping out roads, parks, and key 'system' zones like recycling centres and compost stations. Working in teams, they code Sphero robots to represent 'waste trucks', programming routes to collect and deliver materials through their interconnected city systems. Along the way, they must troubleshoot breakdowns or blockages, redesigning physical features or code to keep their city running smoothly. This hands-on project highlights how human-made and natural systems interact, and empowers students to creatively explore sustainability and organisation in their own community.

ci: Scientific investigations help us understand interactions within systems.
lo:
Interactions between objects, materials and living things
Gathering and analysing evidence
How scientific knowledge develops

s.d: Students program a conductivity tester, then test classroom objects and materials with crocodile clips. This shows how a controlled investigation can reveal interactions between electricity and different materials. Each group chooses one surprising object for another group to predict before testing it. Students finish with a working tester and a checked table of conductors and insulators. The micro:bit's pins provide the input, while its LED grid displays the result. Students repeat uncertain tests, change one condition at a time and debug their code when the evidence does not match.

Students measure how changing one part of a system affects another, such as ramp height and travel distance or water temperature and dissolving time. Entering repeated results into a table helps them gather enough evidence to spot patterns rather than trust one trial. Groups exchange data sets and check whether another team's conclusion is supported by the numbers. Students finish with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based conclusion. Excel turns the measurements into charts that make patterns and unusual results easier to see. Students add further trials when the graph shows gaps or results that do not fit.

Students build and record a frame-by-frame explanation of an interaction such as pollination, erosion, dissolving or a chain reaction. Moving one part at a time makes cause and effect within the system clear. Groups swap unfinished animations and predict the next change before the creators reveal it. Students finish with a short scientific animation that includes observations, evidence and a revised explanation. Stop Motion Studio combines the individual frames into a moving sequence. Students remake any section where the model suggests something that their investigation did not support.

Students photograph and sort material samples, then train an image model to recognise categories such as metal, plastic and paper. Comparing correct and incorrect classifications shows why scientific knowledge improves when more varied evidence is added. Each group challenges another group's model with crumpled, partly hidden or unusually coloured samples. Students finish with a tested classification model and a record of which examples confused it. This works like the camera-driven sorting systems used to direct materials along different paths in recycling facilities. Students retrain the model with better examples and check whether its decisions improve.

Students record a digital casebook showing how one scientific explanation changed after repeated investigations. They add written predictions, images, tables, recorded narration and corrected conclusions to show how evidence changes what we think. Another class reads the casebooks and leaves the authors with one question that the evidence should answer. Students finish with a multimodal book that compares their first explanation with their final one. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page. Students include one result that did not fit and explain whether it led to another test or a changed claim.

s.t: Marble Mayhem: Build a Chain-Reaction Carnival
s.d: Students follow the Design Cycle to investigate, design, build, test and improve a tabletop chain-reaction carnival where a rolling marble tips a cardboard seesaw, releases a popstick domino trail and raises a fabric flag. Using recycled cardboard, paper tubes, popsticks, string, bottle caps and clay, they prototype connected mechanisms that reveal how forces and material properties interact within a system. An iPad's slow-motion camera becomes their investigation tool: students replay each physical trial, identify where motion stops and record successful runs out of five while changing just one feature, such as ramp height or surface texture. Teams use this evidence to revise their designs and explain how their scientific ideas developed, finishing with a spectacular linked carnival demonstration.

ci: Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people.
lo: The diversity of First Nations people; The importance of community, family and kinship; The importance of Country to First Nations people

s.d: Students build an interactive 3D exhibition showing how Country, language, family and community connect in one teacher-approved First Nations case study. Each part shows a relationship rather than treating culture as a collection of separate facts. Teams swap exhibitions and identify one connection that needs to be clearer. Students then revise their scene using feedback and check every detail against approved sources. The finished virtual exhibition gives visitors a path through linked places, people and ideas. CoBlocks can make labels or objects respond as visitors move through the scene.

Students map the diversity of First Nations peoples across several Australian regions using teacher-provided, authoritative information. They add careful annotations while recognising that cultural boundaries can overlap and are not the same as state borders. Students switch terrain, waterways and population layers on and off to work out how geography may shape connections to Country without claiming that geography determines culture. Partners compare maps and question any label that makes all First Nations communities seem the same. The finished map includes regions, language names, geographic evidence and a note about the limits of mapping living cultures. MapMaker's data layers let students test which geographic features help explain each place.

Students record a short podcast comparing two teacher-approved examples of First Nations language maintenance or renewal. They explain why language carries connections to Country, family, knowledge and identity. Each group plays a draft to another class and records one question that the first version did not answer clearly. Students edit their wording so they distinguish between the communities rather than speaking about one Indigenous culture. The finished episode includes an introduction, two specific examples, a comparison and a respectful closing reflection. Canva provides the recording and editing space needed to complete the episode on an iPad.

Students design a visual guide showing how to ask respectful questions when researching First Nations Country, language and community. They turn local protocols and teacher-approved guidance into clear actions such as checking sources, naming the specific community and avoiding copied cultural symbols. Groups exchange drafts and test whether a younger student could follow each instruction without extra explanation. Students choose which advice deserves the strongest visual emphasis and explain why. The finished guide can be displayed beside classroom research stations or sent to another Year 4 class. Adobe Express combines short text, images and graphic layout in one poster or infographic.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion that tests the claim that all First Nations peoples share one culture, language and experience. The chatbot asks open questions that prompt students to use specific examples of diversity, kinship and connection to Country. Students pause midway, reread their answers and replace any broad generalisation with more accurate wording. Partners compare transcripts and select the response that changed their thinking most. The finished transcript shows each student's first idea, supporting examples and revised conclusion. The teacher controls the chatbot's questions, timing and level of support, and students do not use it as a fact source.

s.t: Story Stones & Talking Maps: Ancestral Pathways Quest
s.d: Students design and craft 3D landscape maps using recycled cardboard, clay, natural materials (leaves, stones, sand), and fabric to represent significant places and features from local First Nations stories or global Indigenous cultures. Using Ozobot robots, students program journeys along 'paths' they create, with each stop marked by hand-painted 'story stones' that share language words, symbols, or short audio recordings (via QR codes) about the site's cultural significance. The hands-on process blends digital coding, map-making, and tactile art, helping students explore the importance of land, language, and storytelling in connecting communities and sharing the planet. The project culminates in a guided walk-through where peers 'travel' the map, learning about diversity and respect through interactive storytelling.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human migration is a response to challenges and opportunities
lo: The reasons people migrate; Migration throughout history; Effects of migration on communities, cultures and individuals

s.d: Students map migration journeys caused by bushfires, floods, earthquakes or the search for work and safety. They add terrain, climate and population layers to work out why people left one place and chose another. Pairs swap maps and test whether the evidence supports each route and destination. Students then revise any route that ignores a mountain, river, hazard or settlement pattern. They finish with an annotated map showing causes, choices and effects on both communities. MapMaker's real geographic layers let students explore how several factors can shape one migration decision.

Students build two connected settlements, then change one with a flood, bushfire or earthquake that forces some residents to move. This shows how migration can begin with a challenge but lead towards new opportunities. Another group enters the world and chooses a safe migration route, a temporary shelter site and a place for a new community. The builders watch these choices and improve roads, services or warning systems that did not work as expected. Students finish with a world that shows the original community, the journey and the changed destination. Minecraft's shared building space makes the consequences of each planning choice visible.

Students watch curated clips about historical and recent migration, pausing to record reasons people moved and the challenges they faced. This helps them separate forced movement from migration shaped by work, family or other opportunities. Small groups compare answers and look for voices or viewpoints that the clips include or leave out. They then answer teacher-selected questions using evidence from exact moments in the videos. Students finish with a set of evidence-based responses comparing migration across time. ClickView's built-in questions keep viewing active and give the teacher a quick check of understanding.

Students draw and narrate a migration story from departure to arrival, using one researched historical example. They show the challenge or opportunity that prompted movement and the effects on individuals, cultures and communities. Partners exchange drafts and identify one point where the cause or consequence needs clearer evidence. Students revise the sequence while recording arrows, labels and spoken explanations on the screen. They finish with a narrated screencast that makes the journey and its effects easy to follow. Explain Everything records students' voices and on-screen drawing together.

Students program a portable decision device for a family preparing to leave a community threatened by a natural hazard. Button A displays an essential need, Button B displays a travel challenge, and shaking the board produces a changing event such as a blocked route or new shelter. This makes students weigh safety, limited choices and opportunity rather than treating migration as a simple trip. Groups swap devices, test each other's event sequences and suggest changes when a decision is too easy or unrealistic. Students finish with a working coded device and a short live demonstration of the choices it creates. The micro:bit's buttons, movement sensing and 5x5 LED grid make the decision process physical and repeatable.

s.t: Rescue Rover Rally: Navigating Nature's Obstacles
s.d: Students design and construct 3D models of landscapes affected by different natural disasters (like bushfire-scorched forests, flooded towns, or earthquake-crumbled roads) using cardboard, fabric scraps, clay, and recycled materials. They then code and decorate a Sphero Indi or similar programmable rover to navigate rescue routes through their handmade terrains, simulating emergency response journeys. Along the way, students must problem-solve real-world challenges, like blocked bridges or unstable ground, and iterate on both their physical models and robot code. This project brings systems thinking to life, showing how environments and communities adapt to change, while blending digital skills with hands-on creativity.

ci: Leaders shape communities.
lo: Roles and responsibilities of effective leadership; The purpose of leadership in communities; Qualities of influential leaders

s.d: Students hold a written conversation with a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about a school leadership dilemma. They must decide what an effective leader should do, explain who is affected and respond to questions that challenge their choice. Each student receives the same dilemma but may reach a different decision. Students then compare their conversation with a partner and identify where listening, fairness or courage changed the outcome. They finish with a saved discussion showing how their thinking developed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support.

Students build a survey asking classmates which leadership qualities help a community most. This gathers real evidence about why people trust some leaders and not others. Small groups choose their own qualities to test, such as fairness, courage, listening and responsibility. They invite another Year 4 class to respond and look for surprising differences between the groups. Students finish with a survey and auto-generated charts that can guide leadership applications at school. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and displays the results automatically.

Students build a digital handbook showing how a student leader should respond to real school situations. Each page links a responsibility, a leadership quality and a practical action. Students ask a current school leader to choose one situation that needs the clearest advice, then revise that page for a younger audience. They add recorded explanations so younger students can hear why each choice matters. Students finish with a multimodal leadership handbook that can be read during class meetings. Book Creator combines text, images, audio and video within one book.

Students write scenario questions that ask players to choose the strongest response to a leadership challenge. This makes them apply leadership qualities rather than simply list them. Each group tests its questions on classmates and rewrites any item that causes confusion or has more than one reasonable answer. A buddy class then plays the finished quiz and discusses why the best answer would help the community. Students finish with a playable quiz that teaches responsible decision-making. Kahoot gives immediate responses after each short question.

Students post evidence showing how different leaders have shaped communities through decisions and actions. They connect each example to a quality such as persistence, empathy, fairness or clear communication. Classmates respond by adding a counterexample, a question or another leader who used the same quality differently. Students choose one post to revise after reading the responses rather than treating the first answer as final. The class finishes with a shared evidence wall that shows leadership can look different across communities. Padlet keeps notes, images, links and peer responses together on one wall.

Students work in teams to design and build imaginative miniature communities from recycled cardboard, craft materials, and LEGO figures, each representing different leadership roles (mayor, coach, captain, etc.). They then program simple Ozobot robots to follow custom-drawn paths through their community, stopping at key 'leadership stations' where students place interactive signs or mini-challenges that showcase leadership qualities in action. The project blends hands-on construction with basic robotics, encouraging students to reflect on how leaders guide and shape the places we live. This creative journey lets every child bring their vision of leadership to life—both in what they build and how they direct their LeaderBot through it!

ci: People can create or manipulate messages to target specific audiences.
lo: The devices used to target audiences; Critical evaluation of messages; How we know we have been influenced

s.d: Students question a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about how the same message could persuade a child, a parent and a school principal. They examine how word choice, evidence and emotion change when the target audience changes. Students then swap one persuasive claim and ask the chatbot to challenge its missing evidence and possible bias. Each student decides which chatbot prompts helped them think critically rather than simply accepting an answer. They finish with a written conversation showing how their judgement changed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support.

Students design two advertisements for the same imaginary product, with one aimed at Year 2 students and the other at adults. This makes audience targeting visible through changes in images, colour, layout, claims and calls to action. Another class views the advertisements without being told the intended audiences and guesses who each one targets. Students revise any design whose intended audience was unclear or whose claims were misleading. They finish with a matched pair of advertisements and a short designer statement. Adobe Express supports posters, social-style graphics and short promotional videos.

Students build a survey that shows two differently worded messages about the same school proposal and asks which one is more convincing. They collect anonymous responses to find out whether emotion, evidence, popularity or urgency has the strongest influence. Students send different versions to separate groups, then compare the auto-generated charts for signs that wording changed people's choices. They also identify questions that may have pushed respondents towards a particular answer and rewrite them more fairly. They finish with a survey, response charts and an evidence-based conclusion. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and displays summary charts.

Students record two short jingles promoting the same imaginary product to different audiences. They change tempo, instruments, repetition and vocal delivery to test how sound can shape attention and feeling. Classmates listen without seeing the product and identify the audience and emotion each recording appears designed to target. Students revise one jingle after hearing which musical choices influenced listeners most strongly. They finish with two contrasting recordings and a spoken explanation of their choices. GarageBand lets students compose, layer and record music in one place.

Students draw a persuasive message on the whiteboard and record themselves changing it while explaining every choice. They circle loaded words, exaggeration, missing evidence and visual tricks to show how a message can be manipulated. A partner pauses the screencast at key moments and suggests where the audience might be misled or influenced. Students then record a revised version that remains persuasive without hiding important information. They finish with a narrated before-and-after screencast. Explain Everything records the screen and voice while students draw and annotate.

s.t: Persuasion Pinball: Build & Code Your Message Machine
s.d: Students design and construct interactive pinball machines from cardboard, recycled materials, and craft supplies, embedding key persuasive messages or advertisements throughout the playfield. Using micro:bit boards and simple sensors, they program sound or light effects that trigger when the ball hits specific targets, reinforcing their intended message to the player. Each group selects a target audience and crafts both the physical and digital elements to maximise impact, blending creativity, engineering, and persuasive communication. This hands-on project lets students critically explore how design, technology, and messaging work together to influence audiences.

ci: Entrepreneurs have a responsibility to develop, market and sell sustainable products and services.
lo: The power of giving back; How our environment is impacted by the products we create; Sustainable business practices

s.d: Students photograph examples of recyclable, compostable and landfill packaging, then train an image model to sort each item. This shows how entrepreneurs can plan packaging that creates less waste after a product is sold. Teams swap test objects and record which packaging their model sorts incorrectly. They then choose whether better training images or clearer packaging design would improve the result. Students end with a working classifier and a short demonstration for market-stall visitors. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, using trained image systems to direct waste into different streams.

Students enter expected material costs, selling prices and quantities for their sustainable product. This helps them see that responsible choices must work alongside a realistic business plan. Teams test different decisions, such as paying more for recycled materials or donating part of each sale. They compare scenarios and choose one that balances profit, environmental impact and giving back. Students end with a cost table and graphs showing income, expenses, profit and donations. Spreadsheet formulas let them change one number and immediately see how it affects the whole plan.

Students measure their product and model a reusable holder, stand or packaging insert that could be 3D-printed in plastic. This asks them to reduce unnecessary size while still protecting or displaying what they sell. Partners exchange models and check whether the measurements, openings and wall thicknesses suit the intended product. Each student revises the shape after the measurement check rather than accepting the first design. Students end with a print-ready 3D prototype that can support their market stall. Tinkercad's solid-shape tools let students adjust exact dimensions before printing.

Students build a digital product story with text, images and recorded narration explaining where their materials come from, how the product is made and where the money will go. This makes environmental responsibility and giving back visible to potential customers. Another Year 5 team reads the book as a customer and leaves questions the creators must answer in the next version. Students revise unclear claims and add evidence for any sustainability promises they make. They end with a narrated digital book that can be opened beside their market stall. Book Creator keeps writing, images, audio and video together on each page.

Students program a micro:bit to count market-stall sales when one button is pressed and display the running total on its LED grid. This gives each business a clear way to track progress towards a profit or donation goal. Teams choose a target and code a different LED image to appear when it is reached. They swap devices, test the counting instructions and debug any totals that increase incorrectly. Students end with a battery-powered sales counter they can operate at the market stall. The two buttons, variables and 5x5 LED grid make the counter work without another app during the event.

Students design and build miniature market stall 'pods' from recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, and upcycled plastics, creating both the physical stall structure and display elements for their sustainable product. They integrate a simple micro:bit or Makey Makey circuit to add an interactive feature — such as a light-up sign, movement sensor, or sound effect that activates when a customer 'visits' their stall. This project brings entrepreneurship to life as students prototype, iterate, and test both their stall's design and customer experience, closely mirroring real-world market innovation and sustainable business practices. It ties directly to the unit by blending hands-on making, digital technology, and systems thinking about ethical production and marketing.

ci: Design processes enable people to respond creatively to challenges in the natural world.
lo: The nature and impact of natural hazards (Causation); How design processes are used to generate and test solutions (Function); The ethical and practical considerations in human responses to natural challenges (Responsibility)

s.d: Students build a 3D neighbourhood facing a bushfire, flood or earthquake, then code objects to move or respond when a safety design is activated. This shows how one design choice can change the effects of a natural hazard. Groups swap scenes and try to find weaknesses in each other's evacuation routes, barriers or safe spaces. They revise their scene after hearing which people or places were still at risk. Each group finishes with an interactive hazard simulation that shows a problem, a response and an improved design. Delightex's block coding lets students control how objects move and respond inside the 3D world.

Students explore terrain, climate and population layers to mark Australian places that may face floods, bushfires or earthquakes. This helps them work out why the same hazard can have very different effects in different communities. Each group chooses one location and decides where a shelter, warning point or safer route should go. Another group checks the map from the viewpoint of children, older residents or people without cars. Students finish with an annotated hazard-response map supported by evidence from several layers. MapMaker lets them switch layers on and off so they can test whether their design decision still makes sense.

Students program a micro:bit to detect strong movement and show a warning symbol for a model earthquake alert. This turns hazard monitoring into a design problem that can be tested and improved. Pairs exchange devices and shake them gently in different ways to check for missed alerts and false alarms. They adjust the movement threshold, timing and LED message after each test. Each pair finishes with a working alert device and a short on-screen sequence explaining what people should do. The built-in accelerometer senses movement, while the LED grid displays the warning.

Students interview a teacher-set chatbot representing a resident, emergency worker or council planner affected by a proposed flood or bushfire response. This makes them consider whose safety, cost and environmental needs may be helped or harmed by a design. Students ask follow-up questions, then compare how the stakeholder's answers change their first idea. Partners challenge one another to identify a practical limit or an ethical concern they had missed. Each student finishes with a written conversation and a revised design brief naming the people, problem and constraints. The teacher controls the chatbot's role, rules and level of support.

Students record a 360-degree view of a school evacuation route while classmates move from a classroom to an assembly area. This helps them examine how space, crowd movement and obstacles affect emergency planning. They move one barrier, sign or meeting point, then record the route again to test whether the change improves the flow. Another class views both recordings and identifies places where younger children or people with limited mobility might struggle. Students finish with two immersive recordings that show a design before and after testing. The spherical view captures the whole surrounding space, including problems that an ordinary forward-facing video could miss.

s.t: Disaster-Proof Dream Homes: Shake, Rattle & Rebuild!
s.d: Students design and construct model houses using recycled cardboard, balsa wood, fabric, and a variety of everyday materials, aiming to withstand simulated natural hazards like earthquakes, floods, or bushfires. They use a micro:bit with sensors (e.g., accelerometer, moisture sensor, or temperature sensor) embedded in their structures to test and record how their designs perform under stress—such as shaking platforms, water spray, or heat lamps. Guided by the design thinking cycle, students iterate on their prototypes, analyze real hazard data, and reflect on how their innovations could help communities stay safe. This hands-on challenge connects STEM concepts to real-world resilience, ethical design, and sustainability.

ci: Finding peaceful solutions to conflict can make a difference in the world.
lo: Types of conflict; Causes and impacts of conflict; Conflict resolution

s.d: Students map one playground conflict by placing each person's words, needs, actions and feelings on different parts of a shared canvas. This shows how the same event can have several causes and several honest perspectives. Groups swap canvases and add two possible solutions without deleting the original thinking. They draw connections to show which solution could reduce harm for everyone involved. Each group ends with a visual conflict map and a short agreed plan for peaceful action. Freeform's infinite collaborative canvas keeps every perspective visible while ideas are moved and connected.

Students compare photos of everyday homes, meals and belongings across different countries and income levels. This helps them question assumptions that can cause misunderstanding or conflict between communities. Each pair chooses two families who appear different at first, then looks for needs and routines they may share. Pairs show their comparisons to another group and revise any claim that relies only on appearance. They end with an evidence-based comparison showing differences, common ground and questions that still need respectful research. Dollar Street's photographs make global lives visible without reducing people to statistics.

Students build a short frame-by-frame story showing a conflict, its impact and two possible endings. Comparing a harmful response with a peaceful response makes cause and effect easy to see. Groups exchange unfinished animations and ask another group to choose which small action should change the ending. Students then reshoot the key frames so the solution includes listening, compromise or repair. They end with a stop-motion film that makes one turning point in conflict resolution visible. Stop Motion Studio lets students adjust the story one movement at a time.

Students record and arrange a soundscape that moves from disagreement through tension to a peaceful resolution. This lets them explore how conflict affects wellbeing even when no spoken explanation is used. Another class listens without being told the intended sequence and identifies where the relationship begins to change. Students revise the timing, volume and choice of sounds after hearing that feedback. They end with a short original composition and a clear explanation of the peaceful action represented by its turning point. GarageBand's recording and music-arranging tools let students shape mood through sound.

Students make a digital book that retells one conflict from two different viewpoints before offering a fair resolution. This shows that peaceful solutions often begin when people understand needs beyond their own. Students record each viewpoint in a different voice, then invite a classmate to check whether both sides have been treated respectfully. They revise the ending so it includes a specific action such as an apology, agreement, compromise or act of repair. They end with a narrated book that can be read by younger students during a class visit. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration in the same book.

s.t: Peace Pathways: The Conflict Resolution Board Game Lab
s.d: Students design and build their own large-scale, 3D board games that explore conflict and peaceful solutions, using cardboard, recycled materials, clay, and craft supplies for game pieces, pathways, and obstacles. They integrate Makey Makey kits or micro:bit sensors to add interactive elements—such as sound effects or digital 'chance' cards triggered by landing on special spaces—bridging physical play with simple coding. Each game challenges players to navigate real-world-inspired scenarios, encouraging empathy, perspective-taking, and creative problem-solving. Teams follow the Design Cycle to brainstorm, prototype, test, and refine their games, making learning about peacebuilding both hands-on and memorable.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Colonisation has shaped society.
lo: The impact of colonisation; Colonisation stories; The effects of colonisation ? past, present and future

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record two short avatar narrations that describe the same colonisation event using two teacher-selected historical sources. Each narration clearly separates quoted evidence from the student's explanation. Hearing contrasting accounts shows how colonisation stories change according to whose voice was recorded and preserved. Pairs swap their clips and identify one agreement, one difference and one unanswered question. Students finish with two concise source-based recordings that can open a class discussion. Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs each character to the student's voice.

Students map a colonisation journey and add labels at places where land, people, plants or power were changed. They switch between terrain, population and climate layers to work out why particular routes and settlements developed. Each group then removes one layer and asks another group what important part of the story has disappeared. Students revise their labels so the map includes consequences for First Nations peoples as well as settler aims. They finish with an annotated map showing that colonisation reshaped connected places rather than a single location. MapMaker's data layers let students compare geographic patterns directly.

Students build three adjoining versions of one researched Victorian place, before colonisation, during early settlement and a carefully considered future. They use teacher-provided sources to decide which buildings, paths, plants and land uses belong in each version. This makes changes to Country visible while avoiding invented details about sacred places or cultural practices. Groups exchange worlds and check whether every major change can be traced to evidence. Students finish with a walk-through model and short in-world labels explaining what changed, who was affected and what could happen next. Minecraft's shared building space lets several students construct and revise the same model.

Students edit a two-minute documentary from teacher-provided source images about one colonisation story. They record narration that names the source, explains its viewpoint and identifies what the source cannot tell us. Another class watches an early cut and sends back the question they most want answered. Students revise the sequence so Indigenous perspectives are not treated as an afterthought or a single shared experience. They finish with a short documentary that contrasts evidence from the past with an issue still visible today. IMovie's voice-over, titles and transitions keep the whole edit in one place.

Students draw a layered view of one landscape before and after colonisation, showing changes such as fences, introduced species, roads or altered waterways. They use one drawing layer for each period so individual changes can be hidden and revealed. Partners exchange drawings and suggest one missing cause or consequence supported by class research. Students then add a future layer that shows either continued harm or a realistic repair choice. They finish with a detailed three-stage illustration that can be read as visual evidence rather than decoration. Sketchbook's layers make changes across time easy to compare.

s.t: Time Capsule Storyworlds: Augmented Diorama Adventures
s.d: Students design and build immersive dioramas representing a location before, during, and after colonisation, using cardboard, fabric, clay, natural and recycled materials. Each diorama includes hidden QR codes or AR markers created with Delightex Edu or AR Makr, which, when scanned with iPads, overlay student-made digital stories, Indigenous perspectives, or imagined future scenarios onto the physical scene. The project fuses hands-on model-making with interactive digital storytelling, encouraging students to think critically about change over time and diverse viewpoints. This tactile-tech hybrid brings history to life and empowers students to reflect on place, memory, and the ongoing impact of colonisation.

ci: People's choices are influenced by their beliefs and values and can impact others.
lo: How values and beliefs impact choices; How people's choices and actions impact others; Responsible decision-making

s.d: Students record paired interviews about a difficult choice and the belief or value that shaped it. Hearing two answers to the same question shows how different values can lead to different choices. Each pair then invites a family or community member to add a short response to one agreed question. Students choose one moment where an action affected another person and explain what a more responsible choice might have been. They finish with a three-minute podcast episode containing the interview, reflection and closing question for listeners. Canva lets students record and edit the whole episode on an iPad.

Students design a branching infographic that follows one everyday choice through several possible consequences. This makes the link between personal values, actions and their effects on other people easy to see. Partners swap drafts and choose the path they think is most responsible, then explain which value guided them. Students revise any path where the consequence is unclear or unrealistic. They finish with a decision map that can be displayed beside a real class agreement. Canva's infographic layouts help students organise choices, arrows and outcomes clearly.

Students build an anonymous survey using realistic dilemmas about friendship, fairness, honesty and belonging. The responses show how beliefs and values can lead people to make different choices in the same situation. Another Year 5 class completes the survey so students can compare their expectations with a wider set of views. Students study the automatic charts and discuss why the most popular answer is not always the most responsible one. They finish with a set of survey results and three evidence-based recommendations for class decision-making. Microsoft Forms collects responses and creates charts automatically.

Students post a short decision scenario with two possible actions and the people who could be affected. This helps them look beyond the person making the choice and consider the wider impact. Classmates respond from different viewpoints, such as a friend, family member or person left out, without pretending there is one perfect answer. The original writer then changes one action after reading the responses and explains the reason for the change. Students finish with a wall of revised scenarios showing how listening can improve a decision. Padlet keeps each scenario and its peer responses together in one visible thread.

Students write quiz questions based on choices involving fairness, loyalty, honesty and responsibility. Creating the answer options makes them decide what responsible action looks like and why tempting alternatives may harm others. Small groups test one another's questions and flag any item where more than one answer could be justified. The writers revise those questions or add clearer context before running the final class quiz. Students finish with a playable quiz and a record of the questions that caused the strongest disagreement. Kahoot gives immediate response results that can open a short class discussion after each dilemma.

s.t: Identity Automata: The Choice & Consequence Chain Reaction
s.d: Students design and build elaborate chain reaction machines (inspired by Rube Goldberg devices) that visually represent how personal choices, shaped by beliefs and values, ripple out to affect others. Using cardboard, recycled materials, marbles, popsicle sticks, and LEGO gears, students craft each segment to symbolize a decision point or value (e.g., honesty triggers a positive domino effect, while selfishness creates an obstacle). They integrate BBC micro:bit sensors or Makey Makey to trigger sounds or lights at key moments—bridging the physical with the digital. The process encourages deep reflection on cause and effect in decision-making, while celebrating the diversity of each student's identity and the collective impact on their community.

ci: Thinking beyond ourselves empowers us to act.
lo:
How we evidence our process
How taking action helps us grow our understandings
How we provoke others to make meaningful change

s.d: Students record a screencast that shows how one idea for helping others changes from first thought to final action. This makes their choices, setbacks and new understanding visible instead of showing only polished work. Students swap screencasts and pause at key moments to suggest a different decision the creator could have made. Each student then adds a final section explaining which feedback changed their next step and why. They end with a narrated record of drawings, evidence, revisions and decisions. Explain Everything records their voice and screen while they draw and annotate.

Students build a shared board that connects school or community concerns with evidence, people affected and actions that Year 6 students could take. This helps them think beyond their first reaction and work out which actions could make a meaningful difference. Another class adds questions and places a marker beside the ideas most likely to influence them. Students reorganise the board after reading this response, keeping rejected ideas visible so the process can still be examined. They end with a connected map of evidence, audience questions, possible actions and final choices. Freeform's infinite canvas lets groups move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes.

Students collect weekly numbers that show whether a chosen class action is changing behaviour, such as reusable-container use, library donations or participation in a kindness challenge. This gives them evidence to decide whether taking action is actually growing understanding or only creating attention. Groups exchange spreadsheets and try to explain one another's results before hearing the original group's interpretation. Students use the questions raised to adjust their action and collect a second round of data. They end with a table and graphs showing what changed, what stayed the same and what they will try next. Excel turns their recorded numbers into charts that make patterns easier to spot.

Students compose a 30-second jingle that asks a specific audience to make one realistic change. This requires them to think beyond what they personally enjoy and consider what might move someone else to act. They test two versions with classmates, changing the pace, instruments or repeated words according to which message is remembered accurately. The class selects several jingles to play for the intended school audience. Students end with a short piece of original campaign music that carries one clear request. GarageBand lets them arrange musical loops and record their own sound.

Students build a frame-by-frame animation showing an action, an unexpected obstacle and the change in thinking that follows. This makes growth visible as a process rather than treating action as a perfect final moment. Pairs exchange unfinished animations and choose where the story needs stronger evidence or a more convincing response. Students photograph revised scenes and add frames that show how feedback altered the outcome. They end with a short animation that can provoke discussion about what meaningful change really requires. Stop Motion Studio joins individual photographs into a moving sequence that can be refined one frame at a time.

s.t: The Ripple Wall: Build a Blooming Sculpture for Change
s.d: Students build a giant interactive wall sculpture from recycled cardboard, popsticks, fabric scraps and folded paper flowers, expressing a shared message about an issue they want to change at Elsternwick. Using micro:bits programmed in Microsoft MakeCode, foil touch pads and servo-powered linkages, they make visitors' touches trigger unfolding flowers that reveal student artwork and practical action challenges. Following the Design Cycle, teams investigate community perspectives, imagine and plan mechanisms, create prototypes, then test and improve their designs using visitor feedback, recording sketches, photos and test results as evidence of their process. During a public exhibition, visitors activate the sculpture and contribute paper pledges, helping students reflect on how creative expression can provoke meaningful change and how taking action grows their understanding.

ci: Student-led exhibition (PYPEX) ? Students develop and present their own units of inquiry.
lo: Student-led transdisciplinary themes; Approaches to learning; Research and presentation skills

s.d: Students build a public-budget ballot that asks visitors to allocate mock funding across the student-led PYPEX inquiries. This shows how voting rules and stated values can shape what a community supports. Each group chooses whether voters select one priority, rank several priorities or divide a fixed number of votes. Another Year 6 class completes the ballots, then students compare how each ballot design changed the result. Students finish with a working exhibition ballot and automatically collected response charts. Microsoft Forms gathers every response in one place and produces instant charts.

Students build an interactive 3D model showing how an idea moves through Australia's Parliament to become a law. This makes government structures and decision points easier to explore than a flat diagram. Groups swap scenes and test whether they can follow the process without spoken instructions. Students revise any stage where testers become lost or misunderstand who makes the decision. They finish with a coded virtual tour for visitors to explore during PYPEX. Delightex lets students code objects to move or respond within a 3D scene.

Students enter mock election results and work out the winner under first-past-the-post and preferential voting. This shows that the same votes can produce different outcomes when the system changes. Groups exchange identical vote data but apply different counting rules, then compare which result seems fairest and why. Students can also change a small number of preferences to find the point at which the winner changes. They finish with tables and graphs that support an evidence-based exhibition explanation. Excel makes it practical to calculate totals, organise preferences and graph the results.

Students record a short episode that tests one question from their PYPEX inquiry through a structured civic debate. This strengthens research, persuasive speaking and the careful use of evidence. Each episode includes two different viewpoints and a final section where students identify the strongest claim rather than simply choosing a winner. A partner class listens and sends back the one question that still needs an answer. Students finish with an edited podcast episode that can play at the exhibition. Podcasting using Canva allows students to record and edit the complete episode on an iPad.

Students record a narrated explanation of how a proposed school rule could move from an idea to consultation, revision, voting and review. This connects law-making structures with a process students can examine in their own community. Another group pauses the explanation whenever a decision seems unfair or unclear, and the authors revise their model. Students must show where evidence, competing values and community feedback can change the proposal. They finish with a concise animated screencast for their PYPEX display. Explain Everything records students' voices while they draw, move and annotate ideas on the screen.

s.t: Govern-Bot City: Build & Code Your Own Nation
s.d: Students design and construct a miniature nation using recycled cardboard, popsticks, and craft materials to create government buildings, courtrooms, and community spaces. They then program Sphero robots to act as 'citizens', navigating the city according to rules and laws collaboratively designed by the class—experimenting with different systems (e.g., democracy, monarchy, dictatorship). Through iterative prototyping and coding, students physically experience how values, structures, and laws shape the daily life and fairness within their nation. This hands-on simulation makes the abstract concepts of governance and civic organisation tangible, memorable, and fun.

ci: Energy may be converted, transformed, and used to support human progress.
lo: Different forms of energy and how they are used; The impact of different energy sources on the planet; Sustainable energy practices

s.d: Students program micro:bits to gather data about energy use around the classroom, following https://microbit.org/teach/lessons/?selected=energy-awareness. They use the data to work out when electrical energy is being used well and when it may be wasted. Groups choose different classroom locations and compare results before recommending one realistic change to another Year 6 class. They finish with a working data logger and an evidence-based energy-saving recommendation. Students can adjust and rerun their programs when the first set of readings raises new questions. The micro:bit's built-in light sensing and programmable LED grid make the investigation visible in students' hands.

Students explore hydropower, wind power and waste-to-energy systems in the Alternative Energy lesson at https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/alternative-energy. They follow how mechanical and electrical energy are transformed before power reaches a community. Pairs compare the three systems, then choose the best mix for a community with needs set by another pair. They finish with an annotated Minecraft record of their chosen energy system and the reasons behind it. Students must account for environmental effects as well as the amount of useful energy produced. The Minecraft world lets them move through each power system and examine parts that are difficult to visit in real life.

Students photograph and sort clean classroom waste, then train an image model to recognise items such as paper, containers and non-recyclable packaging. This shows how identifying materials correctly can reduce the energy and resources lost when recycling is contaminated. Teams swap test objects and check where each other's models make mistakes. They finish with a trained classification model, test results and a short list of changes that improved its accuracy. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way by recognising materials and directing them into different streams. Teachable Machine lets students add examples, retrain the model and immediately test whether it has improved.

Students design a precisely measured plastic housing or stand for a Solar Buddy light in Tinkercad. They consider how the shape could protect the light, keep controls accessible and position it for practical use. Each design is handed to another group, who checks its measurements and suggests one change for a nominated user or setting. Students finish with a refined 3D model that can be rotated and inspected from every side. They label the design choices that support safe, durable use without claiming the software can test materials or solar performance. Tinkercad's solid-modelling and measurement tools let students adjust dimensions before any later physical printing is considered.

Students build an interactive 3D scene that shows an energy chain, such as sunlight becoming electrical energy and then light in a home. This makes each conversion visible and helps students distinguish the energy source from the useful output and unwanted heat. Groups exchange scenes and try to identify a missing or inaccurate conversion before the designers revise it. They finish with a coded virtual model that viewers can move through and activate. Students can add a second pathway to compare a renewable source with a non-renewable source supplying the same need. Delightex's CoBlocks let objects move or respond so the energy sequence unfolds one stage at a time.

Students design and build a working model of an amusement park ride (such as a Ferris wheel, carousel, or roller coaster) powered by their choice of renewable energy, like solar, wind, or hand-crank. Using recycled cardboard, wooden skewers, plastic bottles, gears, and motors, teams prototype their ride, integrating a micro:bit or Makey Makey to monitor energy input or trigger ride movement. Learners apply the design cycle to test, refine, and showcase how energy is converted and transformed to create motion and fun, drawing real-world links to sustainable engineering. This collaborative project challenges students to creatively solve problems while making energy concepts tangible and memorable.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: How community values shape the management of the natural environment; The need for sustainable practices; Taking action for environmental stewardship

s.d: Students layer population, climate and terrain data to compare how two communities manage nearby natural environments. This shows why the same environmental challenge can lead to different choices in different places. Each group chooses where it would protect land, allow development or restore habitat, then adds annotations explaining the trade-offs. Groups swap maps and challenge one decision using evidence from a different layer. Students finish with an annotated map that shows how community needs and environmental care can compete. MapMaker's geographic data layers let students test whether their first ideas still make sense when new evidence appears.

Students record 360-degree views of places around the campus where people affect soil, water, plants or wildlife. Seeing the whole setting helps them notice how paths, bins, gardens and buildings shape the environment. Each group asks another class to explore one recording and identify a stewardship problem the filmmakers missed. Students then record a second view that points out a practical improvement and explains who would need to support it. They finish with a pair of immersive recordings showing a place before and after a proposed community action. The camera captures the complete surroundings, so viewers can look beyond the feature the group first noticed.

Students interview a teacher, Camp Mallana staff member or invited community expert about a practice that protects the natural environment. Their questions explore how culture, experience and community values influence decisions about land, water and living things. Students place short recorded answers beside their own respectful commentary and checked background information. A partner group listens and adds one question that the book still needs to answer. Students finish with a narrated digital book containing interviews, images, text and practical stewardship ideas. Book Creator keeps recorded voice, video, images and writing together on each page.

Students program a Micro:bit to count different types of litter found during a marked schoolyard or Camp Mallana survey. They use the two buttons for separate categories and show running totals on the LED grid. This turns a general call to reduce waste into evidence that can guide a specific community response. Groups exchange devices, test the counting instructions and debug any program that records incorrect totals. Students finish with a portable litter-counting device and a tested plan for where it should be used. The buttons, LED grid and battery pack allow the device to collect counts away from a computer.

Students design an environmental campaign for one realistic change at Elsternwick, such as reducing lunch waste, protecting habitat or saving water. They select evidence, name the people whose support is needed and state one action the audience can take. Each campaign is tested with another class, whose response decides which wording or image the designers revise. The strongest campaigns can be shown to campus leaders or included in a real school sustainability drive. Students finish with a campaign poster, infographic or short promotional video. Canva's layouts support clear combinations of evidence, images and short calls to action.

Students will design and build wearable tech accessories—such as wristbands, badges, or hats—using recycled materials, conductive thread, and simple circuits (LEDs, coin cell batteries, sewable microcontrollers). Each wearable will visually represent a chosen environmental issue or Indigenous stewardship practice, lighting up or changing color to communicate key messages. Students prototype their designs, solder or sew in electronic elements, and use digital drawing apps to create stencils or logos. This project challenges students to combine hands-on making with digital design, advocating for conservation and responsible action in a creative, memorable way.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Significant events shape a place
lo: What is a significant event; Why these events occurred; Impact of significant events

s.d: Students interview a teacher-set chatbot portraying a person affected by a significant migration event in Melbourne's history. They ask why the person moved, what changed in the new place and whose experiences might be missing. This opens the central idea through one person's choices before students examine the wider event. Pairs compare the answers they received and write follow-up questions that challenge different points of view. Students finish with a saved written interview and three claims they will check against reliable historical sources. The teacher controls the character, discussion rules and level of support, so the chatbot guides thinking rather than acting as a research source.

Students map migration routes to Victoria and annotate the places where selected significant events began, unfolded and had lasting effects. They switch between population, terrain and climate layers to work out how geography may have influenced why people moved. Each group removes one layer before another group examines the map and identifies what evidence is now missing. Students finish with an annotated map that links routes, causes and changes to communities. They add short notes that clearly separate map evidence from questions needing further research. MapMaker's geographic data layers let students test different explanations rather than simply view a static map.

Students sort and compare Dollar Street photographs of homes, kitchens, bedrooms and valued objects from countries linked to migration stories they are researching. The visual evidence helps them consider what people may preserve, adapt or leave behind when events reshape a place. Students choose two households at similar income levels in different countries so culture is not confused with wealth.
