They exchange comparisons with another pair and check whether their first assumptions are supported by the photographs. Students finish with a captioned set of image observations and careful questions for further inquiry. Dollar Street arranges households by estimated monthly consumption, making fairer visual comparisons possible.

Students build a multimodal case study showing how one significant event changed a Victorian place before, during and after it occurred. They combine written explanations, primary-source images and recorded narration to show causes, different experiences and lasting impacts. A classmate listens without seeing the title and identifies which evidence makes the event seem significant. Students then revise any page where the link between evidence and change is unclear. They finish with a narrated digital book that can form part of the student-led exhibition. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together in one publishable book.

Students write a Kahoot quiz that asks classmates to judge whether events are significant rather than merely recall dates. Each question presents a short event summary and answer choices based on criteria such as scale, duration, change and different community perspectives. Groups swap quizzes and flag any question where more than one answer could be defended. The authors revise those questions or use them to start a class discussion about why historical significance can be contested. Students finish with a playable quiz that checks both historical knowledge and reasoning. Kahoot's immediate answer display gives the teacher a quick view of which significance criteria need more teaching.

Students design and construct a large, interactive 3D board game that traces the journeys of different migrant groups through history. Using recycled cardboard, craft sticks, fabric scraps, and paint, teams build detailed landscapes and landmarks representing significant places and moments along migration routes. They then integrate programmable Ozobots or Sphero Indi robots as 'travellers,' coding them to navigate the maze according to historical challenges, choices, and events. This hands-on project immerses students in the experience of migration, helping them understand how significant events shape communities and places over time.

ci: Personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self.
lo: Physical, social, emotional and intellectual changes that occur throughout life; Influences that shape our identity; Developing a sense of self

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a future-self character describing how their identity, friendships, interests and strengths might change by secondary school. This helps them see that a sense of self keeps growing through new experiences and influences. Each student chooses one current influence that their future character will thank, question or leave behind. Partners watch the characters and suggest one thoughtful question for a second recording. Students finish with a short animated message from their imagined future self. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students paint a layered self-portrait showing physical features, emotions, interests and important influences. The portrait shows that identity has many parts and that some parts are easier to see than others. Students swap portraits without explaining them first, then hear what a partner noticed and decide whether to change one layer. They can hide and reveal layers while discussing how different settings bring out different sides of a person. Students finish with an original digital painting that combines visible and less visible parts of themselves. Brushes Redux layers let students revise one part without changing the whole portrait.

Students arrange six personal or teacher-approved images into a collage showing people, places, activities and ideas that have shaped them. This makes the influences on identity visible without asking students to rank one influence as the most important. Students add a short caption explaining whether each influence has stayed steady, grown stronger or changed over time. A partner identifies one connection between two images that the creator may not have noticed. Students finish with a captioned visual map of the influences around them. PicCollage's grid layouts make it easy to compare the six influences at a glance.

Students film and edit a two-minute interview with a trusted adult about one physical, social, emotional or intellectual change across life. The conversation helps students compare their own expectations of change with a real person's experience. Students choose one answer to place at the beginning as a question-provoking opening, rather than arranging every clip in recording order. Classmates watch selected films and note one similarity and one difference across generations. Students finish with a short interview film containing a title, carefully trimmed clips and a closing reflection. IMovie's editing tools let students reorder clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students design an infographic that traces one personal strength from an early memory to a goal for the next year. This shows how experiences, feedback and deliberate choices can change how someone sees themselves. Students ask a peer to check whether the steps between the memory and goal are clear, then revise the wording or layout. Each student chooses whether the finished piece is private, shared with one trusted person or displayed for the class. Students finish with a visual timeline containing evidence of growth and one realistic next action. Adobe Express templates support clear layouts with short text, icons and images.

Students design and construct a personalised 'totem tower' that visually and interactively represents key aspects of their evolving identity. Using recycled cardboard tubes, fabric, found objects, LEDs, and conductive tape, each section of the tower symbolises a different influence or change in their life (e.g., family, hobbies, beliefs, dreams). Students embed simple circuits or micro:bit-powered elements to bring their stories to life—lighting up or playing sounds when touched. This hands-on project fuses artistic self-expression with digital making, helping students reflect on 'who we are' while learning about circuits and storytelling through physical design.

ci: Emotions influence our wellbeing.
lo: How our feelings and emotions affect us; How feelings and emotions are interpreted; How our emotions and behaviour affect relationships

s.d: Students record short pieces of music that show calm, worry, anger or joy. This helps them hear how emotions can affect the way bodies and minds feel. Partners listen without being told the emotion, choose what they think it is and explain which sounds gave them clues. Students then change one sound to make their emotional message clearer or more open to interpretation. Each child finishes with a short emotional soundscape for a class listening gallery. GarageBand lets them combine and replay instrument sounds before recording their final piece.

Students program two characters to show what happens when one character feels left out during play. They explore how feelings can shape behaviour and change a relationship. Partners swap projects and choose a kind response for the second character to try. Students debug the sequence so the characters move, speak and respond in a clear order. Each pair finishes with a short animated story showing a problem and a caring choice. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young children sequence movement and speech without needing to read instructions.

Students sort teacher-prepared pictures of faces, body positions and everyday situations on a shared Freeform board. They discuss why the same picture might suggest different emotions to different people. Small groups move one picture between emotion groups and record their reasons with a drawing or short teacher-scribed note. The class adds simple calming choices beside situations that may affect wellbeing. Students finish with a connected visual board showing feelings, clues, situations and helpful responses. Freeform's open canvas makes it easy to move, group and connect ideas during discussion.

Students listen to a teacher-selected Epic audiobook in which a character experiences a strong emotion. They pause to name the feeling, point to clues in the words or pictures and copy the character's body position. Pairs choose one moment and act out two possible responses before listening to what happens next. The class compares the author's choice with the children's ideas for protecting wellbeing and relationships. Students finish with a spoken retelling that names the feeling, its cause and a caring response. Epic's read-aloud books allow children to listen while closely studying the illustrations.

Students record brief movements that show emotions such as excitement, disappointment, worry and calm. They replay each action slowly to notice changes in shoulders, hands, face, speed and personal space. Partners view a clip without hearing the emotion named and explain which movement clues shaped their interpretation. Students record the action again after changing one clue, then compare how the message changes. Each pair finishes with two short clips that show how behaviour can be read in different ways. Slow-motion replay makes small body movements visible enough for Prep children to discuss.

Students design and craft their own unique 'Mood Monster' hand puppets using socks, felt, buttons, paper, and recycled materials to represent different emotions. After building their puppets, they use a Sphero Indi robot as a 'Feelings Messenger', coding it with color tiles to travel between puppet stages and deliver emotion cards. Children perform mini puppet shows, expressing how their Mood Monsters feel and react in different situations, while the Indi robot helps connect the stories—blending creative making, technology, and emotional expression in a playful, memorable way.

ci: The products people use go through a process of change.
lo: Where food comes from; How food can be changed for different purposes; An appreciation of food

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles on the carpet to show wheat changing from seed, to crop, to flour, to bread, then send Indi along the sequence. This makes each stage of food production visible, movable and easy to retell. Pairs swap pathways and work out whether the colour instructions take Indi through the stages in the correct order. Each pair chooses one stage where Indi must pause so they can explain who helped or what changed there. Students finish with a working floor pathway that another Prep group can follow and retell. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students arrange teacher-supplied photos of one food before, during and after it changes, such as apples becoming sauce. The image order helps children see that familiar products come from ingredients and a series of actions. Each pair removes one image before showing its collage to another pair, who must work out the missing stage. Students then restore the image and add short captions such as 'grown', 'washed', 'cut' and 'cooked'. They finish with a labelled visual sequence for a classroom food-process display. PicCollage's grid layouts keep the stages clear and easy to compare.

Students code a piece of fruit or grain to move through three scenes showing where it comes from and how people change it. The animation turns a food process into an ordered set of instructions that children can test and fix. Partners exchange projects and check whether the food changes in a sensible order from source to product. Students choose movements, speech and scene changes that make each stage clear without a teacher explaining it. They finish with a short coded story that younger buddies can tap through. ScratchJr's picture-based blocks let Prep students sequence movement and scene changes.

Students record real classroom sounds made while preparing a food, such as washing, chopping with safe utensils, mixing and crunching. Listening closely helps them notice that changing food involves a sequence of actions. Groups rearrange their recordings and ask classmates to identify the correct order using sound alone. They then choose one spoken sentence to add at the end explaining why they appreciate the finished food. Students finish with a short sound sequence that can accompany a class tasting display. GarageBand allows recorded sounds and voices to be arranged on separate tracks.

Students sort teacher-added food pictures into groups showing foods that grow on plants, come from animals or are made by people. This helps them work out where food begins before it reaches a shop or lunchbox. Pairs draw connecting lines from an ingredient to several possible products, such as milk to yoghurt, cheese and butter. Another pair follows the links and moves any picture they think needs more discussion. Students finish with a shared visual web of food origins and changes. Freeform's large canvas allows pictures, words and connecting lines to sit together.

Students design and build a vibrant raceway that traces the adventure of food from farm to table! Using cardboard, craft paper, felt, recycled boxes, and toy vehicles or marbles, children create 3D models of farms, trucks, markets, and kitchens along a winding track. They then use Sphero Indi cars (or similar age-appropriate programmable vehicles) decorated as 'food items' to travel the raceway, stopping at each stage to discuss how food changes and moves through systems. This hands-on journey connects personal meal experiences to bigger food networks, making food origins and transformations come alive through building, storytelling, and play.

ci: The properties of materials influence how objects move and their use.
lo: Properties of materials; How objects move; How we use materials

s.d: Students record balls, blocks and toy wheels moving down ramps covered with foil, felt, cardboard and bubble wrap. They watch each movement slowly to see how the surface and object materials change rolling, sliding, bouncing and stopping. Before replaying each clip, partners predict which object will travel furthest and explain why. Students swap clips with another Prep class and ask them to spot one movement detail. They end with a set of short comparison recordings showing how materials influence movement. Slow-motion replay makes quick changes in speed and direction easier for young children to notice.

Students examine wood, metal, plastic, fabric, rubber and paper with Tablet Magnifiers before touching, bending and sorting the samples. Close observation helps them connect visible features such as fibres, bumps and holes with properties such as rough, smooth, flexible or rigid. Partners choose one mystery sample and give another pair three close-up clues to identify it. Students then sort the real samples by a property they can see and explain any item that could belong in two groups. They end with labelled sorting trays and a spoken bank of useful material words. Magnification reveals details that are difficult to see with the unaided eye.

Students build a small ramp scene and move real objects frame by frame to show rolling, sliding, bouncing and stopping. They use different classroom materials for the ramp and object so the animation shows how material choices can change movement. Pairs exchange unfinished films and suggest one change that would make the science clearer. Students reshoot frames after changing the surface, object or slope. They end with a short stop-motion comparison film that shows a clear before-and-after test. Stop Motion Studio joins individual frames so tiny changes appear as controlled movement.

Students photograph real classroom objects in Seesaw and record themselves naming each material and describing one property. They explain how that property helps the object do its job, such as rubber gripping or fabric bending. Families are invited to add one household example for children to discuss back at school. Students listen to a partner's entry and record a question or a different material choice. They end with a class collection of photographed objects, spoken explanations and responses. Seesaw keeps photos and voice recordings together in each child's portfolio entry.

Students draw two versions of a playground object in Sketchbook using different materials, such as a smooth metal slide and a soft fabric slide. They use arrows and colour to show where an object would slide, roll, bend or stop. Partners swap designs and choose which version would work better for its purpose, giving one reason aloud. Students revise one material choice after hearing the feedback. They end with a detailed digital design showing how material properties affect use and movement. Sketchbook's drawing tools let children change lines, shapes and colours without rebuilding the whole design.

Students design and build their own mini racetracks using cardboard, tubes, recycled containers, and a variety of craft materials, then test different objects (like marbles, toy cars, or balls) made from materials such as wood, plastic, and metal to see how they move. Using simple stop-motion video apps on iPads, students capture their races and observe how different surfaces and materials affect speed and movement. They experiment with adding ramps, barriers, or textured sections, then improve their designs to make the fastest or slowest track. This project encourages hands-on exploration of materials, properties, and motion, linking science concepts with creativity and digital storytelling.

ci: An inquiry into rights and responsibilities in the struggle to share finite resources with other people and with other living things.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students choose an on-screen character and record it explaining one way a family fairly shares food, space or time. This opens a child-friendly conversation about rights, responsibilities and limited resources inside everyday family life. Partners listen to each character and suggest one fair choice the speaker could add. Students then rerecord their message after hearing the new idea. They finish with a short talking-character explanation for a class gallery. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to each child's recorded voice.

Students lay coloured tiles on the carpet to guide Indi between cards showing family members, homes and celebrations. The pathways show that families connect in different ways and sometimes need to share the same spaces. Pairs swap pathways and work out how to reach every destination without removing another family's place. Students change the tile sequence when Indi takes an unexpected turn. They finish with a tested physical pathway that represents respectful family connections. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students build a short puppet conversation between two family members deciding how to share a special object, meal or celebration space. The conversation makes fairness, listening and responsibility visible through a familiar family situation. Another pair watches the first version and chooses a moment where one character could listen more carefully. Students revise the dialogue and record a fairer ending. They finish with a narrated puppet show that can be played to another Prep class. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one app.

Students paint a family symbol using colours, shapes and patterns connected to a tradition, value or celebration. This allows every child to show identity without needing to reveal private family details. Children exchange paintings and ask the artist what one chosen detail means. Students add a new layer that represents a connection their family shares with people, places or living things. They finish with an original layered painting and a short spoken explanation to the class. Brushes Redux lets students build and adjust separate layers while keeping their original artwork.

Students photograph a family-approved object or their own drawing and record why it matters to their family. This shows how objects and stories can carry culture, values and connections across generations. Families can contribute a short response from home, such as a corrected detail, remembered celebration or extra story. Students listen to the response and add a second recording explaining what they learned. They finish with a multimodal journal entry that brings a family voice into the classroom. Seesaw holds the image, voice recordings and family response together in one place.

Students design and craft a banner that represents a special family tradition or celebration using felt, recycled fabric, colored paper, and string. They embed simple LED sticker lights (with coin batteries and adult guidance) to highlight important symbols or words, learning basic circuits as they decorate. The banners can include drawings, collaged photos, or small objects that tell their family's story. This hands-on project combines crafting and basic electronics, helping students share their unique backgrounds while literally shining a light on the diversity within their class community.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Family histories shape who we are and what we value
lo: What makes a family; The people in your family; Your family history; What is important to your family

s.d: Students build a short puppet show in which family characters tell how a tradition began or why an object matters. This shows how family stories can shape what children value today. Children choose which family members appear and may use imagined characters if they prefer privacy. Partners swap shows and notice one similarity and one difference between their families. Each child finishes with a narrated puppet story to play for classmates or families. Puppet Pals lets children move characters across backdrops while recording their voices.

Students photograph a meaningful family object and make it speak about where it came from and why it matters. This helps children connect family history with the things their families value. A family member can help the child choose the object's message before school, giving home voices a place in the classroom. Classmates listen without guessing whose family is better or more typical, then name connections they noticed. Each child finishes with a short talking-object recording for a class gallery. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and the child's recorded voice to the photograph.

Students paint a digital family portrait using colours, shapes and symbols to show people, pets, places or traditions that belong in their family story. This opens up the idea that families can look different while still offering love and belonging. Children choose a symbol that only someone who knows their family would understand, then explain it to a partner. The class places the finished paintings together as a varied picture of belonging at Wesley. Each child finishes with an original digital painting that can be revisited during reflection. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting in separate layers, so children can add or change details without starting again.

Students record one family story at a time in a digital book using drawings, photographs, short text and their own voices. This helps them place people, traditions and past events together as parts of family history. Families can contribute one spoken memory or greeting, while children decide what is safe and comfortable to include. Children read their books with a buddy and find one value that appears in both families. Each child finishes with a narrated family-history book that can grow across the inquiry. Book Creator keeps images, audio, video and text together on simple pages.

Students arrange toys, paper figures or family-object drawings to show how a tradition happens from beginning to end. This makes family customs easier to examine because children must decide which moments matter most. Small groups swap unfinished animations and work out whether the sequence makes sense without an explanation. They then move, add or remove frames so another class can understand the tradition. Each group finishes with a short stop-motion film showing a family practice such as preparing food, welcoming visitors or celebrating together. Stop Motion Studio captures the tiny frame-by-frame changes that make the objects appear to move.

s.t: Time Capsule Treasure Boxes & Talking Tiles
s.d: Students design and build their own 'time capsule treasure box' using cardboard, recycled containers, colored paper, and craft materials, decorating it with symbols and drawings representing their family's unique history, traditions, and values. Each child adds small crafted items (like a mini flag, family pet drawing, or a handmade tradition token) inside the box. Using simple recording buttons (such as Talking Tiles or Talking Photo Frames), students record a short message or story about one special family memory or value and attach it to their box. This hybrid project lets students physically build, decorate, and curate a box of family treasures while integrating technology for sharing personal stories, sparking conversations about diversity and belonging in 'Where We Are in Place and Time'.

ci: Schools are organised to help students learn and work together
lo: The organisation of the Junior School; Routines that allow developing independence; How to make the classroom and playground healthy and safe

s.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a large floor map of the Junior School, stopping at places such as the classroom, toilets, library and playground. They match each route to a familiar routine, showing how school organisation helps everyone know where to go and what to do. Pairs swap destination cards and work out a new route without moving the Bee-Bot by hand. They test, debug and explain why their sequence is safe and efficient. The class ends with a set of tested route cards beside the floor map. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make each planned step visible and easy to change.

Students record a page about a family routine or tradition and a page about a school routine. They compare how routines at home and school help people care for one another, work together and become independent. Families can contribute a short story or greeting for children to add with teacher support. Each child chooses the images, words and voice recording that best represent their identity. The finished class book brings family stories and school routines together in one collection. Book Creator combines images, text and recorded narration on each page.

Students sort teacher-provided photos of Junior School people, places and routines into a PicCollage grid. This helps them see that classrooms, playgrounds and helpers each have a part in keeping school organised. Children compare collages with a partner and move one photo if their partner gives a clear reason. They add short labels such as 'helps us learn', 'keeps us safe' or 'helps us belong'. Each pair finishes with a labelled visual guide for a new Prep student. PicCollage's grid layout keeps the photo sorting clear for young learners.

Students photograph a familiar school object in ChatterPix Kids and record it explaining one helpful routine. A hat might explain sun safety, a drink bottle might explain healthy choices, or a school bag might explain morning organisation. Children play their talking images to another Prep class and listen for any instruction that needs to be clearer. They then re-record using a short sentence and a respectful voice. Each child finishes with a talking image that teaches one safe or independent habit. ChatterPix Kids adds a drawn mouth and a short voice recording to the photo.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a character welcoming a new child and explaining how one part of the Junior School works. Their messages show how routines and shared spaces help children learn, stay safe and work together. Each child chooses the routine they think a new Prep student most needs to know. Partners listen and suggest one missing detail before the message is recorded again. The class finishes with a collection of short animated welcome messages. The Animate from Audio feature automatically moves the character's mouth with the child's recorded voice.

Students design and craft a 3D puppet or figure representing themselves using cardboard tubes, fabric scraps, yarn, and recycled craft bits to showcase features and clothes that reflect their family and culture. Each puppet gets a simple 'home' or scene made from a shoebox or cardboard base, decorated with symbols, drawings, or photos about their family traditions and values. Using a Bee-Bot, students program a short journey between different families' scenes, stopping at each to share a recorded message or story about what makes their family unique (recorded with a talking button or iPad). This collaborative parade celebrates identity and diversity while integrating storytelling, building, and introductory robotics.

ci: People use imagination and materials to express stories, ideas and culture through performance.
lo: Different materials to make puppets; Types and uses of puppets by different cultures; Features and purposes of puppet performances

s.d: Students photograph a puppet one frame at a time as it changes from loose materials into a character and begins a short performance. This shows how imagination can turn ordinary materials into a story. Pairs swap puppets halfway through and continue each other's story without changing the opening frames. They must use movement, position and expression to make the new part understandable without spoken words. Each pair finishes with a short animated puppet performance. Stop Motion Studio joins the individual frames to make the puppet appear to move by itself.

Students build a digital class book that compares puppets from different cultures and records what each puppet is used to express. This helps them notice how materials, movement and performance choices can carry cultural stories. Each pair adds one page, then records a question for the next pair to answer on a following page. Students include a drawing or photograph supplied by the teacher, a short label and their own spoken explanation. The class ends with a narrated puppet guide that families can read and listen to. Book Creator keeps text, images and recorded voices together on each page.

Students record and arrange short sounds for three puppet moments, an entrance, a problem and a celebration. This helps them work out how sound changes the mood and purpose of a performance. Groups exchange one sound sequence and invent a different puppet scene that matches what they hear. They then choose which sounds should be loud, soft, repeated or silent so the audience can follow the action. Each group finishes with a short soundtrack ready to accompany a live puppet show. GarageBand lets students record sounds and arrange them into a simple soundscape.

Students photograph and sort puppet-making items into material groups such as paper, fabric, wood and plastic, then train an image model to recognise the groups. This makes material choice something they can test rather than simply name. Groups challenge the model with crumpled, folded or partly hidden items and add better examples when it makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting systems in recycling facilities learn in a similar way by comparing new objects with many labelled examples. Students finish with a working classifier and a record of which materials were easiest or hardest for it to recognise. Teachable Machine trains a simple image-recognition model from student-provided examples.

Students draw several possible faces for the same puppet character, changing only the eyes, eyebrows and mouth. This helps them see how visual features can express feelings and make a performance easier to understand. Partners view the faces without being told the intended emotion and point to the one they can read most clearly. Students revise one face after hearing the partner's response, then design a matching backdrop for that moment in the story. Each student finishes with a clear puppet-face design sheet and one performance backdrop. Sketchbook's drawing tools let students test, erase and refine small expressive details.

s.t: Shadow Stories: Puppet Theater in a Box
s.d: Students design and build their own shadow puppets using cardboard, paper, fabric scraps, and popsicle sticks, then create a mini puppet theater from a recycled box. Using a simple flashlight or a programmable Bee-Bot with a torch attachment, they experiment with casting shadows and bringing their characters to life. Students work in groups to invent and perform original stories, exploring how movement, shapes, and light can express ideas and emotions. This hands-on project fuses storytelling, cultural exploration, and STEM principles, letting students express themselves creatively while learning about the art of puppetry.

ci: Communities work together by creating systems to help people live and learn.
lo: The roles people play in a community; Systems and routines that help us stay organised; How communities work together to meet needs

s.d: Students train an image-classification model to recognise picture cards showing classroom jobs, places and routines, such as librarian, line leader or lunch-order monitor. They collect and label examples for each category, then test whether the webcam sorts new cards correctly. Incorrect results prompt students to add clearer or more varied training images and retrain the model. The class discusses why an organised system needs accurate information before assigning a card to a group. Students produce a tested classroom-community sorter and explain how they improved its reliability. Teachable Machine's image classes, live preview and confidence scores make the training and testing process visible.

Students program a Bee-Bot to carry messages, supplies and people between places on a floor map of a community. They see that communities need clear routes, ordered steps and different roles to meet people's needs. Groups swap maps and try to follow one another's systems without receiving extra instructions. When a route fails, students change the sequence and test it again. They finish with a working community map and a set of coded routes. Bee-Bot's directional buttons make each planned step visible and easy to debug.

Students photograph an everyday classroom object and record it explaining the job it does within a routine. This helps them notice that systems depend on people, objects and steps working together. A partner listens and asks what would happen if that object or step disappeared. Students revise their explanation so it includes the role, the routine and the need being met. They finish with a collection of short talking images for another Year 1 class. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and a recorded voice to each photograph.

Students build a shared picture map showing how a school need is met, such as borrowing a library book or getting help in the playground. They connect people, places, objects and steps to show that one action often depends on another. Groups remove one part of another group's map and ask them to work out what would stop working. Students reorganise the map until the pathway is clear to someone who has never followed it. They finish with a visual system map that can guide a new student. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes.

Students record themselves carrying out one classroom routine and explain each step as they go. This makes the purpose of routines visible instead of treating them as rules to memorise. Another class watches the entries and identifies any step that needs a clearer explanation. Students record an improved version that includes who is responsible and what need the routine meets. They finish with a student-made collection of practical routine guides. Seesaw keeps the videos, voice and reflections together in each student's journal.

s.t: My Busy Town: Interactive Jobs & Journeys Map
s.d: Students will co-create a large, colorful 3D map of a community using cardboard, felt, recycled boxes, and paper rolls to represent buildings, roads, and parks. Each child crafts a 'community worker' character (like a teacher, baker, or crossing guard) and designs a simple vehicle or tool for their role using craft materials. Using Sphero Indi cars, students program simple routes for their community worker to travel between key locations, demonstrating how different jobs and routines connect and help the town run smoothly. This project immerses students in the systems and roles that organise a community, blending creative building with beginner robotics in a playful, hands-on way.

ci: Movement is dependent on different forces.
lo: Ways objects move; The influence different materials have on movement; How designs can be adapted and improved

s.d: Students record balls, toy cars and blocks moving down ramps, then replay each action in slow motion. They look closely for the moment a push begins, speed changes or friction slows an object. Groups swap ramp surfaces and challenge one another to explain why the same object moves differently. Students pause the footage at key moments and measure the distance travelled during repeated tests. They end with a set of slow-motion clips and spoken explanations comparing force, surface and movement. Slow-motion replay makes changes that happen too quickly for young eyes easy to see and discuss.

Students measure how far a toy car travels from the same ramp across carpet, cardboard, foil and fabric. They add each result to a teacher-prepared Freeform canvas using movable sticky notes, number labels and colour-coded shapes, repeating every test three times. Each group chooses one surface they predict would help a delivery vehicle travel safely rather than simply travel furthest. Students arrange their result cards into rows, compare distances across the class and circle patterns or surprising measurements with the drawing tools. They end with a collaborative visual data board showing how different materials influence movement. Freeform's flexible canvas makes measurements easy for Year 1 students to sort, rearrange and discuss together.

Students photograph examples of rolling, sliding and spinning objects, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images into those three movement groups. This helps them test whether movement types can be recognised from visible clues. Groups exchange unusual examples, such as a rolling cylinder or spinning coin, to find out where the model becomes confused. Similar image recognition helps automated systems sort objects by what a camera can see, including camera-driven sorting machines in recycling facilities. Students end with a working image model and a list of examples it sorted correctly or incorrectly. Teachable Machine lets them add new training images and test whether those examples improve the model.

Students program an object to move after a character gives it a push or pull. They change the number and direction of movement blocks to show a gentle force and a stronger force. Partners swap projects and work out which force each animation represents before hearing the creator's explanation. Students then debug one sequence so the object stops, changes direction or travels a different distance. They end with a short coded animation that shows how changing a force changes movement. ScratchJr's movement blocks make direction and distance visible as a sequence young students can adjust.

Students record a puppet show in which two characters test a moving toy on different surfaces and disagree about which design works best. They explain pushes, pulls and friction through the characters' conversation using evidence from classroom ramp tests. Another pair watches the first version and suggests one design change for the characters to try. Students record a revised ending that explains whether larger wheels, a smoother surface or a changed ramp improved the movement. They end with a narrated puppet show containing a test, evidence and an improved design. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one simple scene-making tool.

Students design and build their own mini racetrack ramps using cardboard, tubes, popsticks, and recycled materials, experimenting with angles, heights, and different surface textures. They craft unique race vehicles from bottle caps, straws, and clay, then use Sphero Indi robots to test and compare how both their handmade cars and the robot move down the tracks. IPads are used to record slow-motion videos of the races, helping students observe the effects of push, pull, and friction. Through playful competition and iteration, students apply the Design Cycle to improve their tracks and vehicles, discovering how forces and materials affect movement in the real world.

ci: Invertebrates are essential to living things and the environment.
lo: The characteristics of invertebrates; The interdependence of invertebrates and their environment; Life cycles of invertebrates

s.d: Students photograph invertebrates in the school grounds and use Seek by iNaturalist to suggest what each one might be. This helps them notice that many small animals support the environment around them. Pairs compare each suggestion with visible features such as wings, legs, body segments and shells before accepting it. Each pair chooses one identification that they can support with the clearest visual evidence. The class ends with a checked list of invertebrates living in different school microhabitats. Seek's camera-based identification gives students an immediate suggestion to question rather than simply accept.

Students sort close-up invertebrate photos into a PicCollage grid and add short labels for features such as six legs, no legs, wings or shell. This makes classification visible and helps children explain why animals belong in different groups. Partners swap collages and move one photograph they think has been placed incorrectly. The original creators then decide whether to keep or change their sorting and explain their choice. Students finish with a labelled visual classification chart for the classroom display. PicCollage's grids, images and captions keep the comparison clear for young readers.

Students watch a short ClickView clip about worms, bees or other invertebrates and pause whenever an animal helps another living thing. This shows how pollination, decomposition and food chains depend on small animals. Groups choose the most important moment and explain what might change if that invertebrate disappeared. Another group listens and checks whether the explanation includes both the animal and its environment. Students finish with a completed set of responses to key moments in the clip. ClickView's curated videos and built-in questions support focused viewing rather than passive watching.

Students use Seesaw's drawing tools to turn class counts of invertebrates found in leaf litter, garden beds and open paths into a picture graph. They duplicate and arrange one insect symbol for each observation, then add labels and a title using the text tool. Pairs compare the columns to identify which microhabitat contained the most and fewest invertebrates. They use the microphone to explain one pattern, such as worms appearing more often in damp leaf litter. Partners listen and leave a teacher-guided response containing one question that can be answered from the graph. The finished Seesaw post combines data, visual evidence and an oral mathematical explanation.

Students build the stages of a butterfly, beetle or snail life cycle from clay and photograph each small change in Stop Motion Studio. This makes growth and change visible instead of showing the stages as separate facts. Groups swap unfinished animations and ask another group to work out which stage should come next. Students revise any unclear movement, add the missing stage and check that the sequence repeats correctly. They finish with a short stop-motion life cycle film for a Prep buddy class. Stop Motion Studio joins frame-by-frame photographs so gradual changes appear to happen on screen.

Students will design and build imaginative 'Bug Hotels' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, paper rolls, natural materials (leaves, twigs, bark), and craft supplies. Using iPads, they will photograph their creations and record short voice tours explaining which invertebrates might live in their hotel and how the habitat supports them. This project combines hands-on construction with digital storytelling, deepening students' understanding of invertebrate needs and how humans can share the planet by providing safe spaces for tiny creatures. The activity encourages empathy, creativity, and real-world connections to environmental stewardship.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: An understanding of history helps us to see how the past shapes the future.
lo: Ways in which children's lives have changed over time; Reasons for changes to children's lives over time

s.d: Students photograph an old toy or childhood object and record it explaining how children once used it. Hearing the object speak makes changes in play, materials and technology easy to understand. Students swap objects and check whether each recording includes a clear reason why life changed. They then play the talking objects to family members and ask what memory each one brings back. Each student ends with a short talking-object recording grounded in historical evidence. ChatterPix Kids makes this possible by adding a moving mouth and recorded voice to one photo.

Students help build a class history wall using Freeform's sticky notes, drawing tools, images and movable connectors. After interviewing parents or grandparents, they add examples of childhood toys, school routines, chores and communication to labelled past and present areas. Before sorting the notes, students predict which experiences will show change and which will show continuity. They cluster similar responses, connect related ideas with lines and discuss reasons for patterns, such as new technology or changing family routines. Each pair adds a drawing or caption that explains one important difference across generations. The completed Freeform board becomes a visual class record of how children's lives have changed over time.

Students arrange coloured tiles to make Indi travel from an old childhood object to its modern version. Changing the tile sequence helps them see that inventions develop through a series of changes rather than one sudden leap. Partners swap routes, follow the visual story and explain why each object may have changed. Students revise any route where the historical sequence is unclear or Indi does not reach the correct object. Each pair ends with a working floor route that shows change over time. Indi responds to the coloured tiles without an iPad or screen.

Students paint the same child's play space in the past and in a possible future. Their choices show how new materials, needs and technologies can change children's lives while some kinds of play continue. Students show their paintings to another class without revealing which details belong to each time and listen to what viewers notice. They then adjust one detail so the reason for change is clearer. Each student ends with a layered digital painting that can reveal past and future versions of the scene. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting on separate layers.

Students capture a 360-degree view of a classroom display arranged with old and new toys, school items and household objects. Looking in every direction helps them notice relationships between objects rather than studying each item alone. Students decide where each object should sit so viewers can move visually from past to present and then towards the future. Another class explores the image and identifies one change, one reason for change and one thing that has continued. The class ends with an immersive 360-degree view of children's lives across time. The Insta360 camera records the whole surrounding space in one spherical image.

Students design and build a mini 'museum exhibit' showcasing toys from the past, present, and their imagined future using shoeboxes, cardboard, fabric scraps, and recycled materials. They create models of old toys (like spinning tops or rag dolls), modern toys, and invent a futuristic toy, then use Bee-Bots or Sphero Indi to 'guide' visitors along a timeline path between exhibits. Students integrate simple craft with programmable robots, exploring how play and technology have changed over time. This hands-on museum helps them connect their own experiences to history, sparking reflection on change and continuity in children's lives.

ci: Emotions, values, and relationships guide how we connect and collaborate
lo: The function of different parts of the brain; Situations that cause pleasant and unpleasant feelings; Actions that support wellbeing

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a brain character explaining how one brain part helps with thoughts, feelings or actions. This shows that feelings and behaviour are guided by processes inside the brain. Partners swap characters and ask each other to add a helpful example from school life. Students choose the character, voice and situation that best explain their idea. They finish with a short talking character that can open a class discussion about emotions. The Animate from Audio feature automatically lip-syncs the character to each student's voice.

Students record short videos showing a pleasant or unpleasant feeling and one action that could help. This connects feelings with practical choices that support wellbeing. A partner watches each clip and suggests a second strategy the speaker could record. Students choose whether to explain breathing, asking for help, taking space or using kind words. They finish with a captioned collection of wellbeing reminders for the class. Apple Clips adds live captions, titles and stickers while students record.

Students film two versions of a playground disagreement, one where the problem grows and one where kind choices repair it. This makes the link between emotions, actions and relationships easy to see. Another pair watches the scenes and chooses which moment should be changed to improve the outcome. Students edit the strongest examples into a short film for a younger class. They finish with a clear before-and-after conflict-resolution film. IMovie lets them arrange clips and add simple titles and transitions.

Students paint the same face twice to show how feelings can change before and after a wellbeing strategy. This helps them notice how colour, line and facial details can communicate pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Partners describe what they notice without guessing the story, then the artist adjusts any unclear details. Students choose a strategy such as movement, breathing, connection or quiet time to inspire the second image. They finish with a paired digital painting that shows an emotional change. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting on separate layers, so details can be refined without starting again.

Students build a personal book with pages for emotion words, body clues, common situations and helpful actions. This brings emotional literacy and self-management together in a resource they can revisit all year. Each student asks a classmate to contribute one kind sentence or calming idea to a page. Students decide which strategies genuinely work for them rather than copying one class answer. They finish with a narrated wellbeing book that can support reflection after real classroom challenges. Book Creator combines text, images, audio and video on each page.

s.t: Mood Monsters: Build Your Own Feelings Friend!
s.d: Students design and craft their very own 'Mood Monster' using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, pipe cleaners, buttons, and colored paper. Each Mood Monster will have features that represent different emotions—like changeable mouths, movable eyebrows, or attachable 'emotion hats'—to help students express how they're feeling. Using a simple digital camera or iPad, students will photograph their Mood Monster showing various emotions, then create a short narrated slideshow or digital story about their Mood Monster's feelings and how they manage them. This project brings emotional literacy to life, blending imaginative making with technology to help students explore and share who they are.

ci: Storytellers use different methods to convey meaning.
lo: Mediums and techniques artists use; Connections between story and illustrations; How ideas and information are communicated

s.d: Students build a frame-by-frame story showing the Moon changing shape across several nights. This shows how movement, sequence and viewpoint can communicate a sky pattern without a narrator. Pairs swap unfinished animations and work out whether the images alone make the meaning clear. They then adjust the timing, camera angle or placement of their paper Moon pieces after hearing the feedback. Each pair finishes with a short stop-motion film that turns scientific observations into a visual story. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame capture makes small changes appear as smooth movement.

Students draw the same night-sky event twice, once as a scientific diagram and once as an imaginative story illustration. Comparing the pictures helps them notice how colour, scale, labels and composition change the meaning. A partner views both images without an explanation and describes the message received from each one. Students revise one detail that caused confusion or made an important idea easy to miss. They finish with two polished digital illustrations and a clear visual connection between science and storytelling. Sketchbook's drawing tools support detailed lines, colour and original illustration.

Students record a short audio story about watching a sunrise, a changing Moon or a seasonal night sky. This lets them explore how voice, word choice, pauses and sound can convey meaning without illustrations. Each student records two different openings, and classmates choose which one makes them want to keep listening. They edit the chosen version so the science is clear and the mood matches the sky event. The class finishes with a collection of short sky stories for another Year 2 class to hear. Podcasting using Canva allows students to record and edit the complete audio story on an iPad.

Students complete a teacher-created Microsoft Forms sky survey each day, selecting daylight conditions, cloud cover and whether the Moon was visible. Forms automatically gathers their responses and displays visual summaries, helping the class identify patterns across the observation period. Small groups compare results from different days and discuss why weather, observation time or viewing direction may affect what they noticed. They use branching questions to add details when they select options such as 'Moon visible' or 'cloudy'. Students then compose a short response explaining one pattern supported by the class results. The completed survey and response summaries become a shared evidence bank about changes in the observable sky.

Students train an image model to sort their physical sky drawings into day, night and changing-Moon groups. This tests whether visual features such as colour, shape and position communicate the intended meaning clearly. Groups exchange drawings and test which images the model sorts correctly, then redraw examples that confuse it. Astronomers use related image-recognition systems to sort large collections of telescope images, although people still check the results. Students finish with a working classifier and a set of revised illustrations with clearer visual clues. Teachable Machine learns from the image examples students show through the camera.

Students design and build their own interactive shadow theaters using large cardboard boxes, colored cellophane, paper cut-outs, and craft sticks to create scenes of the sky—day, night, moon phases, and seasons. Using a simple torch or a Sphero Indi robot with a mounted LED (driven along tracks to mimic the sun or moon's movement), they animate their stories, exploring how light and shadow change with Earth's rotation and lunar cycles. Students work through the Design Cycle to plan, prototype, test, and refine their theaters, expressing their understanding of sky patterns through both engineering and storytelling. This project merges physical making with technology, empowering students to express their place in the universe through light, movement, and creative performance.

ci: A sequence of processes enables a system to function.
lo: The systems in our lives; The purpose of various systems; How systems are made of many interdependent parts

s.d: Students program a Beebot to travel through the steps of a familiar school system, such as borrowing a library book or ordering lunch. Each square on the floor mat represents one part that must happen in the correct order. Groups swap mats, run each other's programs and work out where a missing or misplaced step causes the system to fail. They then change one step and predict what the Beebot will do before pressing go. Students end with a tested floor map and a working sequence of commands. The directional buttons let them enter, clear and debug the route directly on the robot.

Students photograph or draw the parts of a classroom system and arrange them in order on a shared Freeform board. They connect the parts with arrows to show how people, objects and actions depend on one another. Another group removes or moves one part, then the original group explains what would stop working and repairs the sequence. Students can choose systems such as morning arrival, packing a school bag or returning sports equipment. They end with a visual map showing the system working, failing and being fixed. Freeform's open canvas makes it easy to move, group and connect each part.

Students record a sound for every step in a daily system, such as washing hands, preparing for lunch or packing up the classroom. They place the sounds in sequence so a listener can work out the process without seeing it. Pairs exchange recordings, identify any unclear or missing step and suggest one change. Students then reorder or rerecord sounds until another pair can follow the whole process correctly. They end with a short sound sequence that has a clear beginning, middle and end. GarageBand lets them record and arrange each sound on a timeline.

Students build a short class survey about how people complete a familiar process, such as getting ready for school. They ask which step happens first, which parts are sometimes missed and what happens when the order changes. Another Year 2 class completes the survey, giving students real examples that may differ from their own routines. Students read the automatic charts and work out which steps are common and which vary between families. They end with a survey and a set of charts that show how one purpose can be reached through different sequences. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and displays simple response charts.

Students build a tabletop model of a system and photograph one small movement at a time to show its process. They might animate a note travelling through the school office, a book moving through the library system or rubbish reaching the correct bin. Groups deliberately make a second version with one part missing, then ask classmates to spot where the system breaks down. After receiving feedback, they add or reorder frames to repair the process. Students end with two short animations showing a system failing and functioning. Stop Motion Studio joins the individual frames into a clear moving sequence.

Students work in teams to design and build a large, whimsical Rube Goldberg-style machine that represents a typical school day system—like getting ready in the morning or moving from class to class. Using cardboard ramps, dominoes, marbles, recycled tubes, string, and simple levers, they create a chain reaction where each step symbolises a part of the daily routine. Students document each system step using iPads to take photos or record short videos, sequencing the process digitally and physically. This hands-on project helps them see how each part of a system connects, and what happens when one step is missing or out of order.

ci: Changes to materials affect how we use and reuse them in daily life.
lo: Understanding material properties; Reuse and recycling through physical change; Sustainably managing materials

s.d: Students photograph clean samples of paper, foil, plastic and fabric, then train Teachable Machine to sort the images by material. This makes them look closely at properties such as texture, shine, stiffness and transparency before deciding how an item could be reused or recycled. Groups swap unfamiliar objects and test whether each other's model can classify them correctly. They retrain the model when it makes mistakes, showing why a wide range of examples matters. This mirrors the camera-driven sorting arms used in recycling facilities to separate materials moving along conveyor belts. Students finish with a working image classifier and a short demonstration of what it gets right and wrong.

Students record bending, stretching, tearing and crushing tests on everyday materials, then edit the clips into a short comparison film. Seeing each change side by side helps them explain that a material can change shape without becoming a different material. Each group chooses one changed object that could now have a useful second life and adds a spoken explanation. Another class watches the films and votes for the reuse idea they would genuinely try. Students finish with a titled science film showing the tests, observations and reuse choice. IMovie's trimming, titles, transitions and voice recording keep the evidence clear and easy to follow.

Students watch a teacher-selected ClickView clip showing what happens to recyclable materials after they leave a household bin. This helps them connect crushing, shredding and reshaping with the new uses made possible by physical change. Pause at key moments and ask pairs to predict the next machine action before the video continues. Students then answer built-in questions that separate what they observed from what they first expected. The class ends with a completed response set showing where ideas changed. ClickView's curated videos and built-in questions make an unfamiliar industrial process visible and manageable for Year 2.

Students photograph a clean discarded object in ChatterPix Kids and record it explaining its material properties and possible next use. Giving the object a voice makes students justify why bending, cutting, folding or crushing would help rather than simply calling it rubbish. Classmates listen without seeing the original label and decide whether the proposed reuse matches the material's properties. Students revise their spoken message if the audience cannot work out why the choice is suitable. They finish with a short talking-image collection for a classroom recycling display. ChatterPix Kids lets them draw a mouth on the photograph and add a brief voice recording in the same app.

Students record the sounds made when safe materials are tapped, scrunched, torn or shaken, then arrange the recordings into a short composition. Comparing the sounds draws attention to properties such as hardness, thickness and flexibility while keeping the materials themselves at the centre. Groups exchange compositions and try to identify each material from sound alone before hearing the explanation. Students choose whether to repeat, layer or leave space around each sound so the material remains recognisable. They finish with a recorded piece and a spoken ending that names the materials and suggests how each could be reused. GarageBand's audio recorder and track arrangement tools let students capture and organise the sounds in one place.

Students design and build their own mini musical playgrounds using recycled materials like cardboard tubes, tin cans, fabric scraps, plastic lids, and rubber bands. Using Makey Makey kits and iPads, they turn their creations into interactive sound sculptures—tapping, bending, or stretching different parts triggers digital sounds or music. Through hands-on exploration, students investigate how physical changes to materials alter their properties and sounds, linking science, art, and technology. This project encourages creative reuse, teamwork, and reflection on how materials can be transformed for new, joyful purposes.

ci: Patterns in the sky help us understand our place in the universe.
lo: Earth's place in the solar system; Observable patterns in the sky; Tools and methods we use to observe the sky

s.d: Students build a 3D model showing Earth, the Sun and the Moon, then program each object to move in a repeating path. This helps them see how movement in space creates patterns such as day, night and changing Moon views. Pairs swap models and check whether the movement matches the explanation. They revise any confusing sizes, paths or labels after the test. Each pair finishes with an interactive solar system scene that classmates can explore. Delightex's block coding lets students make objects move and repeat actions.

Students submit regular Moon-shape or playground-shadow observations through a teacher-created Microsoft Forms survey, selecting a picture choice and entering a short description. The response summary builds automatically, revealing how the Moon's appearance or a shadow's position changes over time. Before each observation, students predict which response will become more common and explain why. Groups examine the live charts, compare patterns and identify any surprising entries that may need checking. They finish with a labelled screenshot of one response chart and a sentence predicting the next observation. Microsoft Forms' choice questions and automatic response charts make class evidence easy to collect and interpret.

Students program an animation in which Earth turns while the Sun stays in one place, changing one side of Earth from day to night. This makes the repeating day-and-night pattern visible and links it to Earth's movement. Students exchange projects and follow each other's code to find any movement that does not make scientific sense. They debug the sequence and add a character who explains what the sky would look like from Earth. Each student finishes with a working animated explanation of one complete day. ScratchJr's motion and repeat blocks make the cycle run again and again.

Students record regular sky observations in a digital book using drawings, short text and spoken explanations. This brings together evidence about Moon phases, daylight and the tools people use to observe the sky. Each student chooses one page to rewrite for a younger class, replacing difficult space words with a clear comparison. Partners listen to the narration and point out any claim that needs stronger evidence. Students finish with a narrated sky-pattern book that can be read across the term. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page.

Students stretch virtual bands between pegs to recreate familiar star patterns and invent a constellation that can be recognised when rotated. This shows that people notice, name and communicate patterns in the night sky even though the stars are far apart in space. Students swap designs and test whether a partner can rebuild the constellation from spoken directions alone. They revise the pattern or directions when the result does not match. Each student finishes with a clear constellation design made from points and connecting lines. Geoboard lets students move the bands quickly while exploring position, shape and symmetry.

Students will work in small teams to design and build a large, circular 'solar system racetrack' using cardboard, paper plates, bottle caps, and craft materials to represent the Sun and planets. Each group will craft a push-powered planet vehicle (using straws, balloons, or wind-up mechanisms) and program a simple Sphero Indi robot to follow their planet's orbital path around the Sun. Along the way, students decorate their orbits with facts and patterns about day/night and moon phases, connecting physical movement to celestial cycles. The project fuses engineering, art, and basic robotics to help students visualize and experience how planets move in our solar system.

ci: Water is a limited resource that is essential to life.
lo: Unequal access to water; Communities affected by water access; Transferral of water from source to use; Responsibility as global citizens

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles to make a route that carries water from a reservoir to homes, farms and a hospital. They work out how distance, blocked paths and limited supply can affect who receives water. Each group chooses whether its route is fastest, shortest or fairest, then another group tests that choice. Students change the tiles when Indi stops, turns the wrong way or misses a community. They finish with a working floor model of water moving from source to use. Indi's coloured tiles let students change the route without using a screen.

Students build a digital book comparing two children's daily access to water using teacher-provided case information. This shows how the same essential resource can be safe and nearby for one community but scarce or distant for another. Students record questions for a partner class, which adds spoken answers or suggestions to the book. Each pair decides on one realistic water-saving action to include on the final page. They finish with an illustrated, narrated book about water access and responsibility. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration on each page.

Students photograph and identify plants, insects and animals found near the school garden or a local waterway. They discuss what each living thing might need from water and what could happen during drought or pollution. Pairs compare identifications and check uncertain matches against visible features before accepting them. Students choose one species whose water needs they want the class to protect. They finish with a set of local species records and a specific watering or habitat-care suggestion. Seek uses the camera to suggest an identification, so each result should be treated as a guide to check.

Students record a puppet-show meeting in which families, farmers and wildlife must share a limited water supply. This makes unequal access and competing community needs easier for young learners to discuss. Another group watches the scene, pauses before the decision and suggests a fair solution. The creators then record a revised ending that shows the consequences of that choice. Students finish with a short narrated story showing a water problem and a possible response. Puppet Pals lets them move characters across backdrops while recording their voices.

Students draw and connect the stages that move water from a catchment through storage and treatment to a household tap. This helps them see that clean water depends on many connected places and processes. Groups exchange boards and place a warning beside one stage where water could be wasted, polluted or delayed. The original group adds a practical change that could protect the supply at that point. Students finish with a clear flow diagram showing the water system, a risk and a response. Freeform's large canvas allows drawings, labels and arrows to remain connected on one board.

Students will work in teams to design and build mini villages using recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, sponges, and foil, then engineer clever water-collection and distribution systems for their community. They'll use droppers or spray bottles to simulate rain, testing how well their creations capture, store, and share water between 'houses' and 'gardens'. Incorporating simple circuits with LED 'water alert' lights (using coin batteries and conductive tape), students explore how technology and teamwork can help manage water fairly. This hands-on project immerses children in the challenges of water access, encouraging empathy, problem-solving, and creative solutions for a sustainable planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploring the past helps us to understand the present.
lo: Evidence and its significance in a place; Connections between the past and present within a place; Personal history shapes the present

s.d: Students capture 360-degree views of several Wesley College spaces where old photographs show clear changes. This helps them look closely at evidence and work out how the past still shapes the campus today. Pairs choose the camera position that best matches each historical photograph, then invite another class to search the view for what has stayed and what has changed. They produce an immersive virtual tour of the campus in the present. The spherical view lets viewers turn around and inspect the whole setting rather than seeing one carefully framed angle. Students finish by naming which visible detail gives the strongest evidence of change.

Students sort teacher-provided photographs of Wesley College buildings, clothing, classrooms and objects into past-and-present pairs. They see that photographs can provide evidence about how a place and its people have changed. Each pair removes one caption and asks classmates to work out which clues reveal the older image. They produce a clear comparison grid with short captions naming what changed, what stayed and why it matters. PicCollage makes it easy to arrange images side by side and add brief labels. Students revise any caption that states a guess without pointing to visible evidence.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short explanation spoken by an on-screen character representing a carefully studied object from Wesley College's past. Giving the object a voice helps them explain what it can tell us about school life at the time. Students swap recordings and check whether each explanation separates visible evidence from an imagined detail. They produce a short lip-synced character video for a class history display. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically matches the character's mouth to the recorded voice. Students end with the sentence, 'This matters today because...', linking the object to present-day school life.

Students interview a family or Wesley community member about one object, place or routine they remember from childhood. Personal stories show how earlier experiences can shape choices, traditions and routines today. Students choose one follow-up question after hearing an unexpected detail rather than reading every question from a fixed list. They produce a short, clearly recorded oral-history interview that can be played for families or another Year 2 class. The physical microphones and recorders help capture the speaker's voice clearly in a quiet space. Students introduce the speaker and explain which part of the recording counts as historical evidence.

Students build a simple 3D scene showing one Wesley College space in the past and another version of it in the present. Rebuilding the same place twice makes changes in buildings, objects and daily routines easy to compare. Partners exchange scenes and suggest one missing detail that could be added only if evidence supports it. They produce an interactive virtual comparison with objects that respond when selected. Delightex lets students build 3D worlds and use CoBlocks to control how objects move or respond. Students include one unchanged feature so the scene shows continuity as well as change.

Students design and build miniature 'time capsule' boxes using recycled materials, decorating them with symbols and artefacts representing important moments from Wesley College's history and their own lives. They then create a collaborative treasure trail map of the campus, marking where each capsule could be 'hidden', and use Sphero Indi cars to navigate a large, hand-crafted floor map, stopping at each time capsule location to share stories. This project blends physical crafting, storytelling, and basic coding, encouraging students to connect past and present through hands-on exploration and teamwork. It brings the unit to life by making history tangible, personal, and interactive.

ci: Humans have a responsibility in their relationships to value the rights of others
lo: The difference between needs and wants; Everybody has rights and responsibilities; What is a respectful relationship

s.d: Students photograph classroom places where a right is being valued, then record a short voice explanation. They show how everyday actions such as taking turns, listening and including others carry responsibilities. Partners compare entries and suggest one small change that would make each place fairer. Students revise their explanation after trying the change in the classroom. They end with a class collection of photographed rights and responsibilities. Seesaw keeps the photos, voice recordings and reflections together in each student's journal.

Students paint a digital quilt square showing what respect looks like between two people. They include colours, shapes and small details that show listening, fairness or inclusion. Each student first asks a partner which respectful action matters most to them, then uses that answer in the painting. The finished squares can be displayed together as a digital kindness quilt. Students explain which part of their image represents a right and which part represents a responsibility. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with layers.

Students build a short class survey that asks whether familiar items are needs, wants or sometimes both. They include examples such as water, a home, friendship, toys and internet access. Another Year 2 class completes the survey, giving students an audience beyond their own discussion group. Students read the automatic charts and discuss why people may answer some questions differently. They end with real class data and a list of examples that need further discussion. Microsoft Forms collects responses and turns them into charts automatically.

Students record a puppet scene in which two characters disagree over space, belongings or joining a game. They show the characters naming their rights, accepting responsibilities and working towards a respectful solution. Groups swap planned scenarios so they must solve a problem written by someone else. Students replay the shows and check whether both characters were heard and treated fairly. They end with a short narrated puppet show that can prompt a class discussion. Puppet Pals combines characters, backdrops, movement and recorded voices in one app.
