Students code an animated story where a character must choose how to respond when someone is excluded or treated unfairly. They create two possible responses and show what happens after each choice. A partner tests the story without being told which response is respectful, then explains what the code helped them notice. Students debug the sequence so actions and speech happen in a clear order. They end with an interactive story that shows how choices affect relationships. ScratchJr uses simple blocks to control characters, movement and speech.

Students design and build their own 'Identity Island'—a 3D pop-up park that represents who they are and what makes a respectful community. Using cardboard bases, recycled materials, fabric scraps, markers, and craft supplies, each child creates miniature features (like bridges of kindness, sharing swings, or fairness fountains) that symbolize rights, responsibilities, and values important to them. Then, using Bee-Bots, students program simple routes for their bots to 'visit' each island, sharing stories about their choices as the Bee-Bot explores. This project celebrates individuality and respectful relationships through hands-on making and storytelling, reinforcing empathy and inclusion.

ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Students paint the same familiar Melbourne scene twice, using colour, pattern and scale to show two different ways of understanding it. This makes it clear that technology can expand the choices artists make when expressing a point of view. They swap untitled paintings and ask a partner what each image seems to say. Students then revise one layer after hearing an interpretation they did not expect. They end with two detailed digital paintings that show how creative choices can change meaning. The layered painting tools let students alter parts of an image without starting again.

Students record a short audio story describing the world through the eyes of an overlooked object, such as a lost button, playground gate or paintbrush. This shows how voice, words and sound can turn an ordinary object into an expression of a person's understanding. Another class listens without seeing the object and sketches what it imagines from the description. Students use that response to edit unclear language or add a more effective sound. They finish with a polished audio story ready for families to hear. Canva supports recording and editing the whole podcast on an iPad.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students draw or select a character and record it explaining why two people might understand the same image differently. This brings together voice and image while showing that meaning depends on perspective. Students exchange animations and respond in character with a different interpretation of the image. They then rerecord one line so the character's words and appearance communicate more clearly together. The result is a short talking-character exchange that can open a class discussion about visual meaning. Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs the character to each student's recording.

Students compose two contrasting soundscapes for the same imagined place, such as a city at dawn or a garden after dark. This helps them notice how technology can shape mood and influence what an audience pictures. Classmates listen with their eyes closed and describe the place they imagined from each version. Students adjust the order, volume and choice of sounds after comparing those responses with their intention. They finish with two recordings that express different understandings of one setting. GarageBand's music-creation and recording tools allow sounds to be arranged and edited in one place.

Students hold a teacher-guided Project Ideation conversation about how text and images could express an idea such as belonging, wonder or change. This lets them examine how an AI suggestion can influence creativity without treating it as the author. Halfway through, students reject one suggestion, change another and add an idea drawn only from their own experience. They compare their conversation with a partner's and point out where human choices made each plan different. Each student ends with a written conversation and a clear plan for an original text-and-image piece. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support in Schoolbox.

s.t: Mood Machine: Build Your Expressive Robot Buddy
s.d: Students design and build their own expressive 'robot buddy' using recycled materials, cardboard, fabric scraps, and craft supplies for features like eyes, mouths, and arms. Using simple robotics kits (e.g., micro:bit with servo motors or Sphero Indi), they program their robot to display different 'emotions' or messages—such as changing colors, moving in unique ways, or playing sounds—based on how they want to express themselves. Each robot's appearance and programmed behaviors reflect its creator's personality or feelings, connecting to the theme of expressing our unique perspectives. The project encourages students to combine physical making with digital coding, exploring how technology and art can work together to communicate ideas and emotions.

ci: Needs and wants drive innovation.
lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

s.d: Students build a short survey that asks classmates which classroom items they need, which they want, and what problem each item solves. The responses help them see that inventions often begin when many people have the same problem. They choose one surprising result from the auto-charts and ask another Year 3 class whether they agree. Students use the answers to write a clear claim about a need that could lead to a new invention. Their finished survey and response charts give the class real evidence to discuss. Microsoft Forms collects responses and makes simple charts automatically.

Students make a six-page digital book about one everyday invention, such as a lunchbox, bicycle light or hearing aid. They explain the need that came first, the problem the inventor tried to solve, and whether the invention also became something people wanted. Each student records a short narration for one page so a younger reader can hear the explanation. Students swap books with a partner and check whether the need and want are easy to tell apart. Their finished book has labelled pages, drawings or images, text and recorded voice. Book Creator lets students combine text, images, audio and video in one book.

Students rotate digital device models on Merge Cubes and sort each one by the need it meets, such as communicating, finding information or keeping people safe. They see that inventions begin when someone wants to solve a real problem. Pairs choose a phone, router and laptop, then explain how a message can travel between them on a network. Another pair listens and checks whether the explanation includes the device, the connection and safe behaviour online. Students make a labelled paper pathway showing their chosen message travelling through the devices. Merge Cubes lets children turn and inspect 3D models from every angle while they talk through how the network works.

Students train a simple image model to sort classroom rubbish into recycling and rubbish using teacher-provided examples. They see how a digital system can help meet the need to reduce waste, while also learning that a computer can make mistakes when its training examples are limited. Students test the model with new objects and keep a tally of wrong guesses before deciding which images should be added. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities use a similar kind of image recognition to sort materials. Students finish with a tested model and a short list of examples that confused it. Teachable Machine lets students train and test a basic image-recognition model.

Students design a Canva infographic for an invention that solves a real Glen Waverley school need, such as finding a lost drink bottle or reminding families about a changed pickup time. Each panel separates the need from the want, then explains why the invention would be useful. Students draw the path a message takes from a person's device through a network to another person's screen, and add one rule that keeps names, photos or locations safe. Pairs swap infographics and use the arrows to check whether the message route and safety choice make sense. Canva's shapes, arrows and text boxes let students build the explanation on one clear page. Each student finishes with a revised infographic ready for a classroom display of responsible inventions.

s.t: Spin & Share: The Smart Supply Carousel
s.d: Students invent a hand-cranked classroom supply carousel from recycled cardboard, popsticks, paper cups and split pins, with compartments for shared pencils, erasers and other essentials, exploring how needs and wants inspire inventions that help us organise ourselves. Using teacher-supported micro:bit MakeCode, they program a separate cardboard request console to send radio messages to a micro:bit on the carousel, which displays a matching compartment symbol so a classmate can turn the wheel and share the requested item. They follow the Design Cycle: investigate classroom sharing challenges, sketch ideas, build and code prototypes, test with classmates, then improve confusing signals or tricky mechanisms. Teams use anonymous item requests rather than names, practise respectful messaging and explain how their sending and receiving devices form a small wireless network.

ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
lo: Observable properties of solids and liquids; How heating and cooling change state; Scientific thinking helps solve everyday problems

s.d: Students measure ice, chocolate and butter at regular intervals as they warm or cool, then enter the observations and times into Microsoft Excel. This helps them see that careful observations can reveal patterns in how materials change state. Groups compare which material changes first and decide whether the evidence supports their original prediction. They swap tables with another group and check whether the same pattern can be found without an explanation. Each group finishes with a labelled table and graph showing change over time. Excel turns the class measurements into charts that make patterns easier to spot.

Students train Teachable Machine with images of familiar solids and liquids, then test it with ice, water, butter and melted butter. This shows that observable properties help us classify materials, but materials that change state can confuse simple categories. Students choose the clearest training images and swap models with another group to find out which examples are misclassified. Camera-driven sorting systems in recycling facilities work in a similar way by learning visual differences between materials. Each group finishes with a trained image model and a record of the examples it classified well or poorly. The live image classifier gives immediate feedback when students show each sample to the camera.

Students program a Micro:bit to show an LED warning when its rough temperature reading rises above a chosen limit for protecting chocolate. This connects heating and cooling with an everyday problem, keeping a material solid long enough to carry or store it. Groups test several thresholds in different classroom locations and adjust their code when the warning appears too early or too late. Another group receives the device without instructions and checks whether its display clearly communicates the warning. Students finish with a coded temperature-alert device and a short test record. The Micro:bit's LED grid, buttons and rough temperature sensing let the device collect an input and respond straight away.

Students record and edit a short film showing ice, chocolate or butter before, during and after heating or cooling. This makes cause and effect visible while students explain which changes are reversible. Each group leaves a pause before the result so a younger class can predict what will happen next. Students add spoken explanations that separate what they observed from what they think caused it. They finish with a short science film containing evidence, a prediction pause and a clear conclusion. IMovie combines recorded clips, titles, narration and transitions in one project.

Students post labelled observations of solids and liquids to a shared Padlet wall, including shape, flow, texture and response to heating or cooling. This builds a class evidence bank that shows how scientific descriptions differ from everyday guesses. Groups find two posts that seem to disagree and add a question asking what test could settle the difference. The class then sorts the strongest posts into evidence for solids, liquids and changes of state. Students finish with a collaborative display of observations, questions and proposed tests. Padlet's shared wall keeps every group's notes, images and responses visible together.

Students will design and build imaginative 'mansions' or rooms using cardboard, foil, clay, and recycled materials, then select and place objects made from chocolate, ice, and butter inside. Using iPads and thermal cameras or temperature sensors, they will digitally document and analyse how heating and cooling (by moving their mansions to sunny, shady, or icy spots) change the states of these materials. The challenge: invent creative insulation or cooling features to protect their treasures from melting or solidifying, iterating their designs with the Design Cycle. This hands-on investigation brings the science of materials and change of state to life, blending physical crafting with digital observation and problem-solving.

ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
lo: Observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals; Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly; First Nations knowledge of soils and rocks

s.d: Students build a cutaway landscape that shows soil layers, rock, minerals, plant roots and water below the surface. They then copy the landscape and change one version to show mining, farming or construction that uses resources carelessly. This makes the link between Earth's hidden materials, people's choices and changes above ground easy to see. Teams visit one another's worlds and suggest one realistic way to repair or protect the altered land. Each team finishes with two contrasting landscapes and signs explaining the evidence behind its design choices. Minecraft's blocks let students show underground layers and land use in the same three-dimensional world.

Students design an infographic that compares how one soil, rock or mineral is observed, used and cared for. This shows that the same Earth material can have scientific, practical and cultural value. Students select information from teacher-approved First Nations sources and clearly name the relevant Nation or community rather than treating knowledge as one shared story. A partner checks whether every image and claim is respectful, clear and supported before publication. Students finish with an exhibition-ready infographic for families or another Year 3 class. Adobe Express makes it easy to combine short text, labelled diagrams and photographs in one clear layout.

Students sort classroom soil and rock samples by observable properties, then write Kahoot questions using their own observations. Their questions focus on evidence such as colour, grain size, texture, layers and visible crystals rather than guessing a specimen's name. Groups exchange quizzes and challenge any answer that cannot be justified from what a person can actually observe. The class then improves unclear questions and discusses why scientists need agreed classification rules. Each group finishes with a playable quiz that teaches others how to examine Earth materials carefully. Kahoot's game-based questions give the teacher an immediate check of which properties students can use confidently.

Students build an interactive 3D soil profile with topsoil, subsoil, weathered rock, bedrock, roots and small organisms. This helps them show how living things and Earth's materials depend on one another below our feet. Each group codes one change, such as vegetation removal, so objects move or respond and reveal a possible effect on the soil. Groups swap scenes and work out which clues show healthy soil and which show damage. Students finish with a virtual model that classmates can explore and discuss. Delightex's CoBlocks let students code movement and responses inside the three-dimensional scene.

Students photograph soil and rock samples in Seesaw, record close observations and add a short voice explanation for each classification choice. This keeps attention on evidence while showing that specimens with similar colours can still have different textures, grains or layers. Partners listen without seeing the specimen first, then test whether the description is precise enough to identify the correct sample. Students revise vague words such as 'rough' or 'brown' by adding comparisons, measurements or visible details. Each student finishes with a multimodal field journal containing photographs, labels, observations and corrected explanations. Seesaw combines photographs, voice and text in one student portfolio entry.

s.t: Soil Safari: Build Your Living Landform
s.d: Students team up to design and construct a vibrant 3D landform diorama using cardboard, clay, fabric scraps, pebbles, and natural materials, representing different soil types, rocks, and native plants from Australia and a neighbouring country. They embed Sphero Indi robots programmed to 'explore' these terrains, using coloured code cards to simulate resource collection and highlight responsible land use. Along the way, students integrate elements of First Nations knowledge—such as traditional uses of soils and rocks—by crafting miniature artefacts and signage. This hands-on project brings together science, culture, and technology, emphasizing the importance of caring for Earth's resources and celebrating our shared responsibility.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
lo: How Australia and neighbouring regions define places; Australia's states/territories have unique identities; First Nations connections to Country

s.d: Students layer and annotate maps of Australia to compare state borders, terrain, climate and nearby countries. They work out how one place can be divided politically while its landforms continue across borders. Pairs hide one layer and ask another pair to predict what the missing information might show. They finish with an annotated map that explains three different ways Australia can be represented. MapMaker's data layers let students move beyond a single outline map. Students add a short conclusion about which representation best answers a chosen geographic question.

Students photograph 360-degree views of school places that different people use and value. This shows that a place is more than its location because people notice, use and care for it differently. Each group chooses a camera position that includes details an ordinary photograph might leave out. They finish with a collection of immersive views that classmates can turn around and examine. The camera captures the whole surrounding space in one spherical image. Students compare two views and explain how camera position changes the story told about a place.

Students draw a layered digital portrait of an Australian state or territory using its outline, landforms, symbols and important places. The layers show that political boundaries, physical features and regional identity can represent the same land differently. Students swap drawings and reveal one layer at a time while a partner works out what each layer adds. They finish with an original place portrait that combines geographic information with artistic choices. Sketchbook's layers allow parts of the representation to be hidden, shown and revised. Students label which parts are mapped facts and which parts express how people value the place.

Students build a walk-through model showing the distinct identity of one Australian state or territory. They represent carefully researched landforms, settlements, state symbols and places people value rather than trying to copy an entire region. Groups exchange worlds and identify what the builders chose to include, enlarge or leave out. They finish with a navigable model that shows how design choices shape a viewer's understanding of place. Minecraft's blocks make scale, boundaries and spatial relationships visible and easy to revise. Students place signs explaining that First Nations connections to Country extend beyond state and territory borders.

Students record a short poem and compose a soundscape about a local place they know and value. Their words and sounds show that maps are not the only way people can represent a place. Students play their draft to a partner who describes the place they imagined, then revise any unclear section. They finish with a recorded poem layered with original voice, body percussion and classroom-made sounds. GarageBand allows students to record and arrange several audio tracks. Students explain one sound choice that shows their personal connection to the place.

s.t: Story Stones: Mapping Our Place & Time
s.d: Students will craft a large, tactile 3D map of Australia and its neighbouring countries using cardboard, fabric scraps, clay, and recycled materials. Each student creates a set of 'story stones'—painted or decorated pebbles—that represent important places, landmarks, or cultural stories, including First Nations perspectives. Using an Ozobot or Sphero Indi, students program simple routes that connect their story stones across the map, physically and digitally sharing how places are valued and interconnected. This immersive project blends mapping skills, creative storytelling, and robotics to deepen understanding of identity, land, and connection.

ci: The choices and actions we make contribute to our health and wellbeing.
lo: What it means to be healthy; Choices and their impact on health; Actions to maintain a healthy mind and body

s.d: Students build a branching map of everyday choices about food, movement, sleep and calming down. This shows how one small decision can affect both body and mind later in the day. Groups swap maps and add a different healthy choice wherever they think the outcome could improve. Each group then explains which change had the strongest effect and why. Students finish with a connected visual map showing several possible paths through one day. Freeform's shared infinite canvas lets them place, move and link every choice and consequence.

Students collect class data before and after a short movement or mindfulness break, using a simple one-to-five focus rating. This helps them test whether a healthy action can change how ready they feel to learn. Pairs choose the clearest graph type and compare patterns across several days rather than trusting one result. They discuss unusual results and avoid claiming that one strategy works for everyone. Students finish with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based conclusion. Excel turns their table of numbers into charts that make patterns easier to notice.

Students draw and label a body outline while recording an explanation of how sleep, food, exercise and mindfulness can affect it. This makes them connect daily choices with signs such as energy, mood, concentration and muscle tiredness. After watching a partner's explanation, they revise one unclear link and record that section again. A guest speaker or another Year 3 class can view the strongest explanations and leave questions for discussion. Students finish with a narrated screencast that shows their thinking developing on screen. Explain Everything records their voice together with each drawing, label and annotation.

Students build a paper-cutout sequence showing one daily choice and its effect on health or wellbeing. This helps them show cause and effect rather than simply listing healthy habits. They pause the animation before the key decision so classmates can predict what the character should do next. Students then add alternative frames to show how a different choice changes the ending. They finish with a short stop-motion film containing two possible outcomes. Stop Motion Studio captures the scene frame by frame so small physical changes appear as movement.

Students compare photos of food, beds, play spaces and hygiene items in homes at different income levels around the world. This helps them see that health is shaped by personal choices as well as what families can access. Pairs choose two homes that challenge an assumption they held and explain what the photographs actually show. They also identify questions that cannot be answered fairly from a photograph alone. Students finish with a carefully selected on-screen comparison of homes and an evidence-based oral explanation. Dollar Street arranges homes by estimated monthly consumption, making differences and similarities visible without ranking cultures as better or worse.

s.t: Healthy Habits Arcade: Build-Your-Own Wellness Game
s.d: Students design and construct their own tabletop arcade game that teaches a healthy habit, such as balanced eating, exercise, mindfulness, or sleep routines. Using cardboard, bottle caps, rubber bands, fabric scraps, and recycled materials, they create interactive elements like spinning wheels, flippers, or pop-up targets. With Makey Makey kits and Scratch Jr on iPads, students add simple digital feedback—lights, sounds, or scorekeeping—to enhance the physical game. This creative fusion lets students explore how daily choices impact wellbeing while inventing a fun, memorable way to inspire healthy living in others.

ci: Responding to different artistic expressions can promote thinking.
lo: Ways forms of expression convey messages; Creative and critical thinking skills; The language used to respond to The Arts

s.d: Students study a Yayoi Kusama artwork and write their first response to a teacher-set Socratic Tutor. The chatbot asks open questions that help them explain how colour, repetition and scale carry a message. Students then swap artworks and compare how the questions lead to different interpretations. They choose one response to revise after considering an idea they had not noticed themselves. Each student ends with a written conversation and a stronger paragraph about the artwork. The teacher controls the questions, timing and level of support.

Students paint an original digital response to a poem, musical excerpt or gallery artwork using colour, line and texture. This helps them show how one artistic expression can spark another kind of thinking. Students exchange paintings without explaining them, and their partners write what message or feeling they see. The artists then decide whether to strengthen, soften or deliberately leave that reading open. Each student finishes with a layered digital painting that can be displayed in the student-led art show. Brushes Redux lets students build and revise the painting in layers.

Students compose a short soundscape that responds to a visual artwork, using rhythm, silence and changes in sound to show what they notice. This makes them work out how music can carry a message without using an image or written explanation. Another class listens without seeing the original artwork and describes the colours, movement or mood they imagine. Students use those responses to revise one section of their composition. Each pair finishes with a recorded soundscape and a short spoken introduction explaining one musical choice. GarageBand provides the recording and music-making tools in one place.

Students record and edit a short film comparing two different responses to the same artwork, poem or performance. This gives them practice using precise Arts language while showing that thoughtful viewers can disagree. They interview classmates who noticed different details, then choose clips that fairly represent both viewpoints. The finished film includes close analysis rather than a single correct interpretation. Each group produces a two-minute response film for screening beside the chosen work at the art show. IMovie lets students combine recorded footage, titles and transitions in one project.

Students collect images of class artworks on a shared canvas and add short notes about message, mood, technique and questions. This makes the language used to respond to The Arts visible and open to revision. Students draw connections between works that use very different forms but prompt similar thoughts or feelings. Each artist chooses one unexpected connection and replies with evidence from both works. The class ends with a large visual web of interpretations that can guide labels and conversations at the art show. Freeform's infinite canvas allows ideas and evidence to be moved, grouped and connected.

Students design and build their own 'emotion machine' automata—moving sculptures that visually express a chosen feeling or message. Using recycled cardboard, wooden skewers, cams, levers, paper, fabric scraps, and hot glue, students craft imaginative characters or scenes. They embed a simple programmable micro:bit or Makey Makey to trigger lights, sounds, or movements (like spinning eyes or waving arms) that amplify their artwork's emotional impact. This hands-on project lets students explore how movement, color, and interactive elements can communicate feelings and stories, culminating in a parade of expressive automata for the art show.

ci: Communities create rules, laws and services to help people live together fairly and safely.
lo: Effective and influential leadership; Strengths that help leaders guide others; How leadership impacts communities

s.d: Students map a community decision, such as where to place a new pedestrian crossing, and record themselves drawing who is affected at each step. This shows how leaders use rules, evidence and community needs to make fair and safe choices. Groups swap scenarios, watch each other's reasoning and add a different decision path that protects someone who was overlooked. They then compare the likely impact of both choices before choosing the fairest response. Each group finishes with a narrated decision map that can be played to the class. Explain Everything records students' voices and on-screen drawing together.

Students train an image model to sort pictures of community services, such as emergency, transport and recreation services. They test whether the computer can reliably recognise each group and discuss who could be affected when a classification is wrong. Groups deliberately change backgrounds, angles or picture choices to find out whether their model has learned the right clues. This mirrors image-recognition systems that can help council CCTV or emergency-dispatch systems identify vehicles and services, where careful training matters for fair and safe decisions. Students finish with a working model and a set of examples that reveal its successes and mistakes. Teachable Machine lets them retrain the model immediately after each test.

Students design a persuasive campaign for one new rule or service that would make the school community fairer or safer. This asks them to explain a need, propose a clear action and show how responsible leadership could improve daily life. Each campaign is designed for a real audience, such as the Junior School leadership team or another Year 4 class. Peers check whether the message explains who benefits, who might disagree and how the decision could be made fairly. Students finish with a campaign poster or short explainer carousel supported by reasons and evidence. Canva provides layouts for combining concise text, images and simple diagrams.

Students write quiz questions built around difficult leadership choices, such as applying a rule to a friend or dividing limited community resources. This helps the class examine how honesty, courage, empathy and clear communication guide leaders. Groups exchange questions and revise any option that makes the fair choice too obvious. The class plays the finished quizzes, then pauses after divided responses to hear different reasons. Students finish with a student-made scenario quiz that can be replayed at the end of the inquiry. Kahoot displays response patterns straight away, making disagreement visible for discussion.

Students record a short interview with a guest speaker or school leader about a rule, service or decision they have helped shape. This gives students first-hand examples of how leaders listen, communicate and take responsibility for community outcomes. Each group includes one respectful follow-up question based on something unexpected in the guest's answer. They edit the interview into a focused episode and choose one quotation that best shows effective leadership. Students finish with a class podcast series that can be played to families or another year level. Podcasting using Canva supports recording and editing on iPads in one place.

s.t: Council of Critters: Animal Town Governance Game
s.d: Students design and build a bustling animal-themed town using cardboard, recycled containers, fabric scraps, and craft supplies, assigning each area a specific function (e.g., school, park, market). They then create and program simple rules and scenarios using Ozobot robots, which act as the 'mayor' or 'council members', navigating pathways to make decisions and solve community problems. Throughout the process, students must collaborate to establish leadership roles, set rules, and adapt their town's organisation to new challenges. This project brings the unit's themes to life by letting students physically construct, govern, and experience the interconnectedness of systems and leadership in a playful, memorable way.

ci: The design and use of products can have an impact on the natural world.
lo: How material properties determine their use; Material solutions for a sustainable future; How research solves problems in the natural world

s.d: Students photograph and sort everyday packaging by material, then train an image model to recognise categories such as cardboard, metal and plastic. They test whether the model can tell materials apart when colour, shape and lighting change. Groups swap mystery items and work out which examples confuse each other's model. They then improve the training set so the model makes more reliable sorting decisions. Students finish with a working classifier and a short demonstration of where each item should go. This mirrors the camera-driven sorting systems that guide robotic arms in recycling facilities.

Students program a Micro:bit conductivity tester and connect classroom materials with crocodile clips. They test foil, cardboard, fabric, wood, plastic and other safe samples to find out which allow electricity to flow. Each pair chooses one surprising result for another pair to check with the same testing method. They use the evidence to explain why conductive and insulating materials suit different products. Students finish with a working tester that shows a symbol on the LED grid when a circuit is completed. The Micro:bit's pins and LED grid make the material test immediate and easy to repeat.

Students measure the strength, water resistance or flexibility of packaging samples and enter their results into an Excel table. They compare performance with the amount of material used and whether each sample can be reused or recycled. Groups exchange data so they can check whether repeated tests produce a similar pattern. Each group uses the combined evidence to recommend a material for a lunch container, delivery package or animal enrichment device. Students finish with a labelled graph and an evidence-based material recommendation. Excel's chart tools make differences between materials easier to see.

Students build a virtual animal enclosure and add an enrichment device designed for one chosen animal's needs. They select shapes and layouts that reduce waste while still making the device safe, usable and interesting for the animal. Partners explore each scene and identify one design choice that helps the animal and one that could use less material. Students revise the scene, then code an object to move or respond so the enrichment idea can be demonstrated. They finish with an interactive 3D model showing the animal, enclosure and proposed device. Delightex's CoBlocks let students test movement and interaction inside the virtual scene.

Students make a digital case-study book about a product redesigned to reduce harm to the natural world. They explain the original material choice, the environmental problem, the research that informed the redesign and the benefits and limits of the new solution. Each group writes for a different audience, such as families, product designers or the school canteen. Classmates listen to one another's pages and suggest where a claim needs clearer evidence. Students finish with a multimodal book containing text, labelled images and recorded narration. Book Creator keeps the written, visual and spoken explanation together in one publication.

Students work in teams to design and build imaginative animal shelters using recycled materials like cardboard, fabric scraps, and plastic containers, integrating simple circuits (LEDs, battery packs) or Sphero Indi sensors to create interactive features—such as 'rain sensors' or light-up entrances. They'll research the needs of different animals and the properties of chosen materials to ensure their shelters offer comfort, enrichment, and sustainability. Teams test their prototypes with mini animal figures, reflecting on how material choices affect the environment and animal wellbeing. This hands-on project fuses scientific inquiry, design thinking, and digital tech to explore how innovation shapes our world.

ci: Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people.
lo: Diversity of First Nations people; Importance of community, family and traditions; Importance of Country to First Nations people

s.d: Students map the many First Nations language groups across Australia and annotate several regions with their researched language names. This shows that First Nations Australians are diverse peoples, not one single culture or community. Each group compares a coastal, desert, river or urban region and works out how Country may shape community life and traditions. Groups then swap maps and add one respectful question prompted by the geographic patterns they notice. Students finish with an annotated map that shows diversity while avoiding fixed state and territory boundaries as the main story. MapMaker's terrain and other data layers help students examine how language regions connect with real landscapes.

Students record a 360-degree view of a carefully chosen place on campus and explain the natural and human features they notice around them. This helps them consider that Country includes relationships, stories, responsibilities and living things, not simply a location. Before recording, students listen to locally approved guidance about caring for Country and choose what should and should not be filmed. Another class views each recording and identifies evidence of care, change or connection in every direction. Students finish with a short immersive tour that asks viewers to look closely at one place. The spherical recording matters because the whole surrounding environment stays visible rather than being cropped into a single viewpoint.

Students animate a physical diorama to show how family, community, traditions and Country connect across several moments. This makes relationships visible without copying sacred stories, restricted symbols or cultural practices. Students base their sequence on an approved First Nations source, then ask a partner to check whether the animation avoids stereotypes and unsupported claims. They move one element at a time so that a waterway, gathering place, seasonal change or community action gradually alters the scene. Students finish with a short stop-motion explanation containing a clear beginning, change and ending. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame capture lets students show connections developing through movement.

Students watch and pause a teacher-selected First Nations-authored or First Nations-led video about Country, language or community. This places living voices and contemporary experiences alongside historical knowledge. Pairs compare two speakers or communities and note both differences and shared ideas without treating either example as representative of everyone. Students answer teacher-selected questions that ask whose voice is heard, what evidence is offered and what remains unanswered. They finish with a set of responses and one careful question for further inquiry. ClickView's curated video library and built-in questions keep the viewing focused and manageable.

Students build a Minecraft place that shows how a community could care for land, water, meeting spaces and living things. This helps them explore Country as a network of relationships and responsibilities rather than empty land to own or decorate. Each build must be based on teacher-approved local knowledge, and students avoid recreating sacred places, restricted designs or imagined First Nations ceremonies. Groups exchange worlds, follow the routes through each place and suggest one change that would make care or community connection clearer. Students finish with a walkable model containing visible evidence of responsibility, access and environmental care. Minecraft's shared building space lets groups test how the placement of paths, water, plants and community areas changes the whole design.

s.t: Sacred Sites Soundscapes: Interactive Country Dioramas
s.d: Students work in teams to design and build a vibrant 3D diorama of a significant First Nations Australian landscape, using recycled cardboard, natural materials, clay, and fabric scraps to represent features such as rivers, rock formations, and bushland. They embed simple Makey Makey circuits and conductive materials to create interactive 'sound spots'—touching these triggers recorded Indigenous stories, place names, or nature sounds via a connected laptop or tablet. This project weaves hands-on making with digital storytelling, deepening understanding of connection to Country, language, and respectful sharing of knowledge. Students reflect on the rights and responsibilities involved in preserving both land and cultural heritage.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration leads to discoveries, opportunities and new understandings.
lo: Reasons for exploration; How people have explored over time; Consequences of exploration

s.d: Students program Sphero BOLT to travel across a floor map that represents an explorer's journey through unknown territory. They work out how distance, direction, obstacles and limited supplies can change an expedition. Groups exchange routes and try to navigate each other's maps without seeing the original code. They then revise the route after every wrong turn, collision or missed stopping point. Each group finishes with a working coded journey and a short explanation of the decisions that helped or hindered exploration. Sphero BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid let students show travel, pauses and discoveries along the route.

Students map a historical voyage and add notes showing its starting point, route, destination and major discoveries. They manipulate terrain, climate and population layers to work out why explorers chose particular paths. Pairs compare two journeys from different periods and decide which environmental challenge shaped each route most strongly. They annotate places where exploration created opportunities or harmful consequences for communities and environments. Each pair finishes with a labelled map that tells a clear geographic story. MapMaker's data layers help students test ideas rather than simply look at a static map.

Students build two versions of a place, one before explorers arrive and one after contact, settlement or resource use. They include homes, transport, natural features and evidence of changes affecting local communities or environments. Another group visits the world and leaves questions about whose lives improved, whose lives changed and what may have been lost. Students revise their builds so both opportunities and consequences can be seen without a long written explanation. Each team finishes with a walk-through world that compares the same place across time. Minecraft Education makes large-scale change visible through blocks, space and movement.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short first-person account from an explorer, navigator, local community member or scientist connected to a historical journey. They explain one reason for exploration, one challenge and one consequence from that person's point of view. Classmates watch two accounts describing the same event and identify where the perspectives agree or conflict. Students then rewrite and rerecord one sentence so the account separates known evidence from personal opinion. Each student finishes with a brief talking-character video suitable for a class history gallery. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs the chosen character to the student's recorded voice.

Students build a survey asking which reasons for exploration people consider most worthwhile, such as trade, knowledge, resources, safety or adventure. They collect responses from classmates or another Year 4 class and compare choices across the group. Before viewing the results, each student predicts the most common answer and explains why. Students then use the auto-generated charts to identify patterns and write a follow-up question that probes an unexpected response. The class finishes with a set of survey results showing how opinions about exploration differ. Microsoft Forms collects responses automatically and turns them into charts for quick discussion.

Students will design and build a 'time capsule terrain' from recycled materials—complete with mountains, rivers, and hidden landmarks—representing a landscape from a famous era of exploration. Using Sphero Indi cars, students will craft and decorate physical 'explorer robots' that must navigate their handmade world to discover and collect miniature artifacts or messages placed throughout. They'll use coloured coding tiles to program their Indi explorers' journeys, reflecting on the challenges and discoveries real explorers faced. This immersive project brings together creative crafting, robotics, and historical inquiry, letting students experience the excitement and obstacles of exploration across time.

ci: People's beliefs contribute to the diversity of human life.
lo: Spiritual or religious beliefs; Similarities and differences of spiritual beliefs; Contributions of different religions to human diversity

s.d: Students post one carefully sourced image, fact or question about a spiritual or religious belief to a shared Padlet wall. This shows how beliefs shape identity, traditions and communities while making room for similarities and differences. Students respond to two classmates by naming a connection and asking a respectful question rather than judging the belief. The class invites another Year 4 group to add what they notice and what they still wonder. Students finish with a collaborative gallery of evidence, questions and connections that can grow across the inquiry. Padlet keeps notes, images, links and peer responses together on one shared wall.

Students design an infographic comparing how two spiritual or religious traditions express one shared idea, such as gratitude, belonging, care or remembrance. This keeps the comparison focused on a human idea rather than ranking entire belief systems. Each student chooses the traditions and checks that images, symbols and words are used respectfully. Partners swap drafts and identify one similarity that is easy to miss at first glance. Students finish with a clear exhibition panel for a classroom gallery walk. Adobe Express combines short text, images and graphic layout in one place.

Students write respectful survey questions about everyday values, belonging and practices that are safe for classmates to answer. The responses show that people can share values while expressing them through different beliefs, traditions or personal choices. Students include a 'prefer not to say' option and decide which questions should remain anonymous. They study the automatic charts and discuss what the data does not tell them about a person's identity. Students finish with a class survey and a set of charts showing patterns without naming individuals. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and displays summary charts.

Students record a short interview with a willing family or community member about a tradition, value or belief that contributes to their sense of belonging. This gives students a real voice to listen to instead of treating religions and spiritual beliefs as lists of facts. Students send questions in advance and let the guest choose anything they do not wish to discuss. Pairs listen back and select a respectful section that challenges a stereotype or reveals a shared value. Students finish with a collection of short recorded interviews for a supervised listening station. The physical microphones and recorders capture clear voices during face-to-face conversations.

Students build an interactive 3D gallery showing how several belief communities contribute to human diversity through celebrations, service, art, architecture or care for others. This helps them show both distinct practices and ideas that communities may share. Each group gives another group a virtual space to check for missing context, stereotypes or unclear labels. Students then code selected objects to reveal a short explanation or question when a visitor interacts with them. Students finish with a virtual gallery that classmates can explore and discuss. Delightex supports 3D scene building and block coding for object responses.

s.t: Belief Boxes: Interactive Identity Treasure Chests
s.d: Students design and build personalised 'Belief Boxes'—mini treasure chests crafted from cardboard, recycled materials, and decorative supplies. Inside, they create physical artefacts (symbols, objects, or tiny models) that represent aspects of their identity, beliefs, and cultural backgrounds, using clay, fabric, and natural materials. Using Makey Makey kits and conductive materials (foil, copper tape), students wire their boxes so that opening compartments triggers recorded audio reflections or stories about each artefact, played through a connected laptop or tablet. This hands-on project lets students celebrate diversity and share their unique stories, making identity and belief tangible, creative, and interactive.

ci: People design for purpose.
lo: How design thinking creates in various ways; Design thinking meets community needs; Effective ways to engage an audience

s.d: Students design a small 3D classroom aid for a person who finds an everyday task difficult, such as holding cards, organising pencils or turning book pages. They work from a short user brief so every choice has a clear purpose. Students swap models and check whether the size, shape and openings would suit the intended user. They revise one feature after receiving specific feedback. Each student ends with a measured 3D model ready for a plastic test print. Tinkercad lets students reshape and resize solid objects as their ideas improve.

Students collect and connect notes about small problems experienced by people around the school. They sort the needs by user, place and purpose before choosing one worth solving. Another class adds questions and marks the ideas that would make the greatest difference. Students then map several possible solutions and show why one best matches the need. Each group ends with a clear design brief and a visual trail from problem to chosen idea. Freeform's shared infinite canvas keeps notes, sketches and feedback together.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a designed character delivering a 30-second message that asks the school community to support a useful change. They choose the character, words and tone to suit a specific audience such as younger students, families or teachers. Partners listen without seeing the planning notes and explain what action they think the message requests. Students rewrite and record the message until the purpose is immediately clear. Each student ends with a short animated appeal that can be played to its intended audience. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the on-screen character to the student's recorded voice.

Students explore and build in Revamp Melbourne to create a solution for the city's future needs: https://education.minecraft.net/en-us/lessons/revamp-melbourne. They make design choices that respond to what people need now and may need later. Teams exchange builds and test whether visitors can work out each solution's purpose without an explanation. Students revise confusing spaces, signs or structures after the visit. Each team ends with a working Minecraft model of a purposeful Melbourne improvement. Minecraft's shared building world allows students to walk through and experience one another's designs at human scale.

Students build a short Kahoot that teaches an audience how to use a newly designed school service, space or object. They write questions that reveal whether their instructions and visual choices are clear. A different group plays the quiz without receiving any extra explanation. Students study the incorrect responses and rewrite the questions or information that caused confusion. Each group ends with a tested interactive quiz that teaches its intended audience. Kahoot displays player responses immediately, giving designers quick evidence about what worked.

Students use the Design Cycle to create an interactive cardboard and recycled-material sculpture that expresses a message, story, or need from the Glen Waverley community, such as welcoming new students, caring for shared spaces, or celebrating cultural identity. They build with cardboard, foil tape, fabric scraps, popsticks, clay, bottle caps, and hot glue, then connect hidden conductive touch points to a Makey Makey so the sculpture plays student-recorded voices, sound effects, or music when an audience touches different parts. Each prototype is tested with classmates to see whether the design clearly communicates its purpose and invites people to interact. The final gallery becomes a hands-on expression exhibition where students show how design choices can engage an audience and give ideas a memorable voice.

ci: Economic systems are an integral part of human society.
lo: Wealth is more than money; Responsibilities when managing income; Income is earned and managed in many ways

s.d: Students compare photos of beds, kitchens, toys and transport across different income levels on Dollar Street. They look for signs of wealth that money alone cannot explain, such as safety, time, health, skills and family support. Each pair chooses one everyday object and swaps its photo trail with another pair to check whether their conclusions are fair. Students discuss why two homes with similar incomes may still offer very different choices and opportunities. They finish with a paper evidence board showing the photos they examined, what they noticed and one question they still have. Dollar Street's homes are arranged by purchasing-power-adjusted consumption, making visual comparison across countries possible.

Students build a survey that asks classmates how they would manage a fixed weekly income across needs, wants, saving, giving and unexpected costs. This makes the responsibilities of managing income visible through real choices rather than a single correct budget. Another Year 5 class completes the survey, then the creators compare the responses with their own predictions. Students revise one question if its wording pushed people towards a particular answer. They finish with an auto-generated chart and a short written conclusion about the choices people valued most. Microsoft Forms collects responses and creates charts automatically.

Students draw and record a narrated money-flow diagram showing how income moves through a household, business or community organisation. They explain where money is earned, spent, saved, taxed or donated and what happens when one part changes. Partners exchange diagrams and ask the creator to add one unexpected event, such as a broken appliance, fewer customers or a rise in costs. Students then update their explanation to show how the whole economic system responds. They finish with a narrated screencast that makes each decision and consequence easy to follow. Explain Everything records students' voices while they draw, move and annotate items on the whiteboard.

Students layer population and terrain data, then annotate places where people might earn income through farming, manufacturing, tourism, trade or services. This shows that income is earned in different ways because places have different resources, environments and connections. Small groups exchange maps and challenge one claim that does not yet have enough geographic evidence. Students adjust their annotations and add a possible responsibility, such as protecting land or paying workers fairly. They finish with an annotated map showing how geography can shape economic choices and opportunities. MapMaker's data layers let students compare patterns rather than simply view a static map.

Students design a short campaign video arguing that a community should measure wealth with more than money. They choose three indicators, such as health, education, clean spaces, free time, belonging or access to services, and explain why each matters. The videos are shown to another class, whose students choose the indicators they would use when judging whether a community is doing well. Creators revise one scene after hearing which message was least clear. They finish with a polished video that proposes a broader way to describe community wealth. Adobe Express provides simple layouts, text, images and short-video editing in one app.

s.t: Mini Marketplace Mayhem: Build, Trade & Thrive!
s.d: Students work in teams to design and construct their own miniature market stalls using cardboard, fabric scraps, recycled packaging, and craft materials. Each group invents a unique product or service (e.g., tiny crafts, handmade tokens, or simple games) and sets up their stall in a classroom 'market'. Using Sphero Indi robots coded as delivery carts, students simulate trading, earning income, and managing resources—navigating their robots between stalls to buy, sell, and barter. This hands-on project lets students experience the complexities of economic systems, understand wealth beyond money, and reflect on the responsibilities of managing income in a vibrant, creative marketplace they build themselves.

ci: The interactions between living things, materials, and light enable us to make decisions about the world
lo: How structural features and adaptations help living things survive; How weathering and erosion cause change to Earth's surface; How light is used in science and technology

s.d: Students program a micro:bit to measure light levels in sunny, shaded and covered places around the classroom or school grounds. They test how leaves, feathers, paper, plastic and other materials change the reading when placed between the board and a light source. This shows how living things and technologies can use or respond to different amounts of light. Groups swap their mystery materials and use only the readings to work out which ones block, scatter or let through the most light. Each group ends with a coded light meter, a table of readings and a decision about the best material for shade. The micro:bit's built-in light sensing and 5x5 LED grid make the testing visible straight away.

Students build three versions of the same coastline to show its shape before erosion, after gentle weathering and after a major storm. They change blocks in measured layers so viewers can see how moving water and loosened material reshape Earth's surface. Another group inspects the sequence and suggests where plants, rocks or barriers might reduce further erosion. Students then revise the final coastline and add signs explaining which evidence guided their decisions. Each group ends with a walk-through model that shows change over time and a tested protection idea. Minecraft's block-based world makes removed, moved and deposited material easy to compare.

Students photograph and sort examples of leaves into visible feature groups such as broad, narrow, waxy, hairy or spiny, then train an image model to recognise the groups. This helps them test whether structural features can be identified reliably and how those features may support survival. Groups exchange unfamiliar leaf images and check when the model makes a strong match, a weak match or a mistake. Wildlife-monitoring cameras and identification apps use a similar process, learning patterns from many labelled images before classifying a new one. Students end with a working classifier and a record of the extra examples they added to improve it. Teachable Machine displays confidence scores that make uncertain classifications easy to discuss.

Students move sand, pebbles and paper landforms one small step at a time to record weathering, erosion, transport and deposition. The animation makes slow changes to Earth's surface visible within a short viewing time. Groups swap films without titles and check whether viewers can identify each process from the movement of material alone. Students reshoot unclear sections so the cause and effect can be seen rather than merely stated. Each group ends with a short stop-motion sequence showing where material starts, how it moves and where it settles. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame capture lets students control each stage precisely.

Students collect repeated measurements of how far light travels through clear, translucent and opaque materials, then enter the results in Microsoft Excel. They use tables and graphs to compare how material type and thickness affect the amount of light that passes through. Each group receives another group's graph without its material labels and uses the pattern to predict which sample was tested. The original group reveals the samples and checks which conclusions were supported by the data. Students end with a labelled graph and a short evidence-based recommendation for a window, shade cover or scientific instrument. Excel's chart tools turn repeated measurements into patterns that are easier to compare.

s.t: Camouflage Coastlines: Build, Erode & Light-Test Survival Creatures
s.d: Students use the Design Cycle to invent a fictional shoreline creature, then prototype its body adaptations with clay, cardboard, fabric scraps, foil, cellophane, popsticks, pipe cleaners, recycled packaging and hot glue. They build a mini coastal habitat in a tray with sand, gravel, rocks and water channels, then simulate weathering and erosion using spray bottles, droppers and gentle water flow to see how the habitat changes. Using LED torches and a simple Arduino or light-sensor meter, teams test how well their creature's colours, textures and reflective features help it hide, signal or survive under different light conditions. After collecting evidence, students redesign both creature and habitat to explain how living things, materials, erosion and light interact to help us make decisions about the world.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways.
lo: The need for conservation; Community values inform management of the natural environment; Ways environmental stewardship can drive change

s.d: Students photograph a local creek, reserve or school habitat in 360 degrees, making sure the whole environment can be seen. This shows how paths, bins, plants, water and buildings reveal what a community values and protects. Groups choose one place where better management could help wildlife or reduce human impact, then capture a second view from that decision point. Another class explores the images and identifies evidence of conservation, neglect or competing needs. Students end with an immersive before-action tour that can open discussion about environmental stewardship. The spherical view lets viewers look in every direction rather than seeing only what the photographer framed.

Students collect counts of litter, native plants, introduced plants, shade, foot traffic or visible wildlife across several school locations and enter them into Microsoft Excel. Comparing the results helps them work out where conservation action is most needed. Each group must use its data to recommend one realistic change, then swap spreadsheets with another group to see whether the evidence supports the same decision. Students end with organised tables, charts and a short evidence-based recommendation written in the spreadsheet. The class can combine its results to compare how different uses of the grounds affect environmental health. Excel's chart tools make patterns and differences easier to see.

Students hold a structured written discussion about whether a local natural area should prioritise habitat protection, recreation, cultural care or new community facilities. This helps them examine how different community values can shape management of the same environment. The teacher sets the chatbot as a Socratic Tutor that asks students to explain trade-offs, question assumptions and improve weak reasoning without supplying research facts. Students then revisit one answer after reading a class case study and show how stronger evidence changed their view. They end with a discussion transcript and a carefully justified management decision. The teacher-controlled prompts and support level keep the conversation focused and suitable for Year 5.

Students program a Micro:bit to record light-level readings at several points around a garden, habitat corridor or proposed planting area. This gives them real evidence for deciding where shade-loving or sun-loving plants might be placed as part of a conservation plan. Groups exchange devices and test whether another group's instructions produce consistent readings in the same locations. They then debug their code or measurement method when results vary unexpectedly. Students end with a working light data logger and a site recommendation based on repeated measurements. The built-in light sensing and battery pack allow the Micro:bit to gather readings away from the computer.

Students design a public campaign that asks the Wesley community to support one achievable conservation action, such as protecting habitat, reducing litter or planting local species. This turns environmental stewardship into a clear request for change rather than a general message to care for nature. Each group creates two versions for different audiences, such as students and the local council, changing the evidence, wording and images to match what each audience values. Peers compare both versions and identify which choices make the action more convincing. Students end with a pair of campaign posters or exhibition panels ready for a sustainability pitch. Canva's layout and infographic tools help students combine short persuasive text, evidence and visuals.

Students will design and construct interactive model habitats for endangered local species using recycled materials, cardboard, fabric scraps, clay, and natural found objects. They will embed simple sensors (e.g., with Makey Makey or micro:bit) to create dynamic features—like warning lights for pollution or sound alarms for habitat disturbance—that activate when parts of the habitat are touched or disturbed. The project encourages students to research the needs of their chosen species, incorporate First Nations land management insights, and demonstrate conservation challenges and solutions through their builds. This hands-on, tech-enhanced maker challenge brings environmental stewardship to life, inviting creative problem-solving while fostering empathy for the planet's vulnerable inhabitants.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: The discovery of resources has impacted the growth and development of nations.
lo: Significance of resource discovery in development of societies; Impact of migration on cultural, social and economic growth; Exploration and settlement effects on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students map gold discoveries, shipping routes and migration paths that changed Australia during the Gold Rush. They add terrain and population layers to work out why some settlements grew while others did not. Groups swap maps and challenge each other to explain one pattern using geographic and historical evidence. They also mark areas where mining and settlement disrupted Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Country. Each group ends with an annotated map showing links between resources, movement, settlement and change. MapMaker's data layers let students test different explanations rather than simply viewing a finished map.

Students build a multimodal book that follows one Victorian goldfields location before, during and after the Gold Rush. They combine short historical accounts with maps, images and recorded narration to show how resource discovery changed people and places. Each group includes contrasting pages voiced from colonial, migrant and Indigenous perspectives, while clearly separating evidence from imagined details. Groups exchange books and identify whose perspective is strongest, missing or supported by the best evidence. Students finish with a narrated digital history that shows change over time rather than listing disconnected facts. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together in one readable book.

Students compose a short soundscape tracing a journey from an overseas port to the crowded Victorian goldfields. They arrange sounds to show migration, difficult travel, mining work, rapid settlement and environmental change. Another group listens without an explanation and places markers where they think the journey, mood or setting changes. The composers then revise any section that did not communicate their intended historical moment clearly. Students finish with an original audio timeline that can open a class exhibition. GarageBand's tracks and sound library allow sounds to overlap, repeat and change in volume.

Students post evidence cards showing one social, cultural, economic or environmental change caused by the Gold Rush. They sort posts around questions such as who benefited, who was harmed, what changed quickly and what effects remain. Students must respond to a classmate by adding supporting evidence, a respectful challenge or a missing perspective. A partner class reads the wall and votes for the three links between resources and national growth that are most convincingly explained. The class ends with a collaborative evidence wall containing sources, claims and peer responses. Padlet's shared wall keeps the discussion visible so students can trace how an explanation improves.

Students record and edit a short interview that compares two perspectives on migration, mining or settlement during the Australian Gold Rush. Their questions explore why people moved, what opportunities they expected and how rapid development affected different communities. Partners listen for claims that need stronger evidence and record a revised section after receiving feedback. Selected episodes are played to families beside a question inviting listeners to decide whether the Gold Rush brought progress, harm or both. Students finish with a polished podcast episode containing an introduction, interview and evidence-based conclusion. Podcasting using Canva lets students record and edit the whole episode on an iPad.

s.t: Goldfields Quest: Design Your Migration Adventure Map
s.d: Students will design and construct an immersive, 3D board game that traces the journeys of diverse groups during the Australian Gold Rush. Using cardboard, clay, fabric, recycled materials, and craft supplies, they'll build landscapes (bush, goldfields, towns), create custom game pieces representing migrants and Indigenous peoples, and engineer interactive elements like bridges or 'chance' wheels. Incorporating a programmable Sphero Indi or similar robot as the 'traveller,' students will code it to navigate the map, encountering historical challenges and decisions based on real events and perspectives. This hands-on project fuses design thinking, storytelling, and empathy, helping students understand how movement, resources, and choices shaped Australia's past.

ci: Managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies.
lo: Establishing, managing and maintaining relationships; Managing behaviours in digital situations; Managing changes associated with puberty

s.d: Students paint a three-layer self-portrait showing who they were, who they are now and who they hope to become as they manage change. This makes identity and puberty visible without asking anyone to reveal private details. Students choose colours, symbols and brush marks that show strategies, trusted relationships and growing confidence. They swap portraits with a partner, who responds only to the strengths and changes they notice. Each student finishes with an original digital portrait that can anchor a private reflection or class gallery. Separate painting layers let students reveal each stage one at a time.

Students hold a teacher-guided written conversation about a realistic digital dilemma, such as being excluded from a group chat or receiving an unkind message. They work out how acceptance, knowledge and practical strategies can change what happens next. The teacher sets the chatbot as a Socratic Tutor so it asks questions rather than supplying answers. Students compare two possible responses and choose the one most likely to protect both safety and relationships. Each student ends with a written conversation and a short personal action plan. Teacher controls for rules, timing and support keep the discussion focused and age-appropriate.

Students record and edit two versions of a short scene about friendship, disagreement or respectful online communication. One version shows a rushed reaction, while the other shows a strategy such as pausing, checking meaning, setting a boundary or asking for help. Another class watches both endings and explains which choices helped the relationship recover. Students revise unclear dialogue after hearing that feedback. Each group produces a short comparison film with titles naming the strategies used. IMovie's editing tools let students trim scenes and arrange the two outcomes clearly.

Students build an anonymous class survey about helpful ways to manage friendship changes, strong emotions and difficult digital situations. This gives them real evidence about which strategies peers understand and which need more teaching. They avoid questions about bodies, personal experiences or named people and test every question for safety before publishing it. Groups study the automatic charts and choose one class strategy that deserves more attention. Each group finishes with a survey, a set of response charts and an evidence-based recommendation. Microsoft Forms collects responses automatically without requiring students to sort answers by hand.

Students build a 3D scene showing a digital situation where a character must decide how to respond to pressure, exclusion or an unwanted message. They code two choices so objects move or respond and each decision leads to a different outcome. Classmates explore the scene and explain which response protects wellbeing and relationships most effectively. The creator then changes one choice or consequence after listening to that feedback. Each student finishes with an interactive 3D decision scene that can be explored on an iPad. CoBlocks make it possible to code how objects respond inside the virtual world.

s.t: Emotion Motion Robots: Build Your Feelings Friend
s.d: Students design and construct a physical 'Feelings Friend' robot that visually expresses different emotions and personal traits using craft materials like cardboard, LEDs, motors, fabric, and recycled items. Working through the Design Cycle, they prototype faces, accessories, and moving features that symbolize aspects of their identity and wellbeing (e.g., a spinning heart for kindness, light-up eyes for curiosity). Using micro:bit or Hummingbird kits, students program their robots to display emotion animations or simple movements in response to buttons or sensors. This hands-on project links self-reflection with digital citizenship by inviting students to share and celebrate diversity, empathy, and self-management in a creative, memorable way.

ci: The media engages its audience and invites a response
lo: How media targets audiences; Techniques used to engage and persuade; Critical evaluation of media messages

s.d: Students question a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about how a tempting advertisement targets a Year 6 audience. This helps them notice how colour, popularity, urgency and selective facts invite a response. The chatbot keeps asking for evidence when a student makes a claim too quickly. Students then swap advertisements and test whether a partner reaches the same conclusion. Each student ends with a written conversation showing how their thinking changed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support in Schoolbox.

Students watch and pause selected advertising clips to record the exact moment each one tries to influence its audience. This makes persuasive techniques easier to spot than discussing advertising in general. Groups compare whether the same clip influences them differently and explain why. Students then answer built-in questions that separate facts, feelings, assumptions and missing information. Each group ends with an evidence-based evaluation of one media message. Clickview's curated clips and built-in questions keep the viewing focused and manageable.

Students build a survey that asks peers what influences their choices between similar products. This shows whether price, packaging, friends, social media, sustainability claims or brand names have the strongest pull. Each group predicts the result before sending its survey to another Year 6 class. Students compare their prediction with the automatically collected responses and look for surprising differences between groups. They end with a survey and a set of charts that reveal real audience patterns. Microsoft Forms automatically gathers responses and displays clear summary charts.

Students compose two short jingles for the same product, one designed to create excitement and one designed to build trust.
