This lets them test how sound can engage an audience before any factual claim is made. Another class listens without seeing the product and records which version makes it seem more appealing. Students revise the less effective jingle after hearing the audience's reasons. Each group ends with two contrasting recordings and a refined final jingle. GarageBand provides instruments, loops and recording tools in one music-making space.

Students photograph and sort clean packaging into recyclable and non-recyclable groups, then train an image model to recognise the two categories. This opens a sharp discussion about whether green colours and nature images persuade people even when the packaging itself is difficult to recycle. Groups test each other's models with misleading packages and record where the computer makes mistakes. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, using images to direct materials into different streams. Students end with a working classifier and a test record showing which visual clues helped or confused it. Teachable Machine trains a simple image-recognition model from student-provided examples.

s.t: Brand New Me: The Ethical Sneaker Hackathon
s.d: Students team up to design and prototype their own 'ethical sneakers' using recycled materials (cardboard, fabric scraps, plastic bottles) and basic electronics (LEDs, simple circuits) to integrate interactive features like light-up logos or pressure sensors. Using tablets and the Makey Makey kit, they program a digital 'ad campaign' that activates when their sneaker is stepped on or touched, linking the physical prototype to a creative digital message about fair trade, sustainability, or consumer choices. Throughout, students apply the Design Cycle to research real sneaker brands, brainstorm features that reflect responsible consumerism, and iteratively build and test their hybrid creations. The project culminates in a 'Sneaker Expo' where teams showcase both their wearable prototypes and their persuasive tech-powered campaigns, reflecting on how products and advertising express values and influence choices.

ci: An inquiry into the interconnectedness of human-made systems and communities; the structure and function of organisations.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students collect advertising examples and build a shared map showing how price, packaging, influencers, friends and values shape consumer choices. This shows how organisations connect people, messages and purchasing systems. Groups draw arrows between examples and label who benefits, who pays and what happens after the product is discarded. Another class adds comments showing which messages would influence them and why. Students then reorganise the board to separate strong evidence from assumptions. They finish with a visual map of the forces behind everyday purchases.

Students enter class ratings for several product advertisements and graph which messages most affect willingness to buy. This makes peer pressure, price, sustainability claims and emotional appeals visible in real data. Groups compare results by changing one advertising feature at a time and recording any shift in ratings. They use the patterns to advise a fictional company which strategy is persuasive and which could mislead buyers. Students finish with a spreadsheet containing organised data, charts and evidence-based recommendations. Excel's tables and charts make patterns easier to spot and question.

Students hold a structured written discussion about whether a company should sell a cheap product when its production harms workers or the environment. This helps them examine how business decisions affect consumers, communities and a sustainable future. The teacher sets up a Socratic Tutor that asks students to explain evidence, consider another viewpoint and revise weak claims. Students swap one key argument with a partner, then return to the discussion and test whether their position still holds. They finish with a written conversation showing how their thinking changed. The teacher-controlled prompts keep the discussion focused without treating the chatbot as a research source.

Students build a virtual shop where each product choice leads to a different social, financial or environmental consequence. This makes the links between advertising, purchasing, organisations and waste easier to see. Groups exchange shops and test whether the clues provided are enough to support a fair choice. They then revise prices, signs and consequences so the choice is difficult rather than obviously right or wrong. Students finish with an interactive 3D scene that invites visitors to make and explain a consumer decision. CoBlocks let students code how objects respond when a visitor selects them.

Students design a short advertisement for a familiar product, then remake it as an honest version that includes its environmental and ethical costs. This shows how organisations can frame information to influence what people notice and buy. Groups show both versions to another class and ask which words, images and omissions changed their response. They revise the honest advertisement so it stays persuasive without hiding important information. Students finish with a matched pair of social-style graphics or short promotional videos. Adobe Express provides quick layouts for combining clear text, images and simple video.

s.t: Future Market Makers: The Ethical Pop-Up Shop Challenge
s.d: Students design and build miniature pop-up shop stalls from recycled cardboard, fabric scraps, and craft supplies, representing businesses that prioritise ethical and sustainable consumer choices. Using micro:bit or Makey Makey kits, they integrate interactive digital elements—like simple LED displays or touch sensors—to showcase advertising strategies, product info, and eco-impact stats. Teams prototype their stall layout, signage, and product packaging, then pitch their business model to classmates, reflecting on how organisation, ethical decisions, and advertising shape consumer behaviour. The hands-on project empowers students to creatively visualise and test real-world sustainable commerce in a collaborative, memorable Makerspace experience.

ci: Scientists undertake experimentation to confirm, contest and create new theories.
lo:
The transfer and transformation of energy in electrical circuits (physical science)
Reversible and irreversible changes (chemical science)
The movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the sun
How scientists conduct experiments using inquiry methods

s.d: Students build two geared winches, code each motor to lift the same small load, and test which design lifts it fastest. They see that scientists need a fair test before they can support or challenge a claim about energy transfer. Each team chooses one variable to change, such as gear size or load, while keeping the other parts the same. Another team repeats the test with the written method and checks whether the result holds up. Students finish with a working coded winch and a clear claim backed by repeated trials. LEGO SPIKE Prime motors let students change their code, run the model, and improve it straight away.

Students build a Sun, Earth, Moon and a marked orbit path in Minecraft Education, then move through the model to show changing positions over time. The build helps them work out that Earth's movement relative to the Sun is a pattern that can be modelled and checked. Pairs swap worlds and test whether they can use the signs and paths to explain day, year and seasons. Students revise any part that gives a misleading explanation, rather than simply keeping their first build. They finish with a walk-through Minecraft model that explains relative movement using labelled places and routes. Code Builder and the Agent can help students place repeated orbit markers accurately.

Students plan and film a short stop-motion sequence showing one reversible change and one irreversible chemical change. They must show what is changed, what evidence they would look for, and whether the original material can be recovered. Groups choose everyday examples that are safe to model with classroom materials, such as melting and refreezing water or cooking a batter substitute with paper props. A partner watches the film without explanation and identifies the evidence for each type of change. Students finish with a short labelled animation that can be replayed during a science discussion. Stop Motion Studio captures one frame at a time, so students can make gradual changes easy to see.

Students draw an electrical circuit investigation in Explain Everything and record their voice while they explain the method, variables and results. This makes the inquiry method visible, including why one result is not enough to prove a scientific idea. They pause at a planned point to state a prediction, then add the evidence that made them keep or change it. Another pair listens to the recording and leaves a question for any step that is unclear or unfair. Students finish with a narrated screencast that shows their experiment from question to conclusion. Explain Everything records their drawing and voice together as they explain.

Students enter repeated results from electrical circuit tests into Microsoft Excel and make a graph for each variable they changed. The graphs help them spot patterns, odd results and cases where more testing is needed. Groups compare graphs from the same investigation and decide whether their evidence supports the same claim. They add a short chart title that states exactly what was tested, rather than a broad science topic. Students finish with labelled tables and graphs that support or contest a claim about energy in a circuit. Microsoft Excel turns their class data into charts that are easy to compare.

s.t: Cosmic Clue Lab: Build a Meteorite Mystery Machine
s.d: Design and build an interactive meteorite-testing machine from recycled cardboard, popsticks, foil, clear sample pots and copper tape, with a micro:bit controlling LED evidence signals and a servo-powered sample hatch. Follow the Design Cycle to investigate, sketch, prototype, test and improve the machine, creating safe mystery samples using ice, clay and teacher-prepared bicarbonate mixtures to compare reversible melting with irreversible chemical reactions. Conduct fair tests by changing one variable at a time, collecting temperature readings and observations, and programming the machine to reveal evidence rather than declare an automatic answer. Connect the investigation to 'How the World Works' by tracing electrical energy transformations and using a physical solar-system map to explain how orbiting debris can encounter Earth, then invite classmates to challenge their meteorite theories using experimental evidence.

ci: The influences on our consumer choices reveal the interdependence between human and natural systems and call for responsible action toward just and sustainable futures.
lo: Influences on consumer choices (function); How consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats (causation); Alternative models of consumerism that honour a fair and sustainable future (perspective)

s.d: Students design two advertisements for the same everyday product, with one selling status or convenience and the other selling fairness and sustainability. This helps them see how images, slogans and selected facts can steer consumer choices. Students swap the advertisements with another class, which votes on the more convincing message and explains why. They then revise the less convincing advertisement using the audience feedback. Each student finishes with a paired set of campaign posters that exposes how advertising changes what people value. Canva's poster templates and Remove Background feature make it easy to control which product details attract attention.

Students map the possible journey of a familiar product such as chocolate, a cotton shirt or a mobile phone. They add and compare layers for climate, population and terrain to work out where natural and human systems meet along the supply chain. Groups exchange maps and question any route or claim that lacks clear evidence. They then annotate places where workers, wildlife, habitats or consumers may carry the hidden cost of the product. Each group finishes with a labelled supply-chain map showing where a fairer choice could change the journey. MapMaker's data layers let students test ideas against real geographic patterns rather than relying on a static map.

Students record a short podcast interview that compares the views of a consumer, producer, worker and environmental advocate on one product. This shows why a decision that feels simple at the checkout can affect people and habitats far away. Pairs exchange unfinished episodes and identify whose voice or evidence is still missing. Students then edit their questions and ending so listeners must choose between realistic alternatives rather than an obvious right answer. Each pair finishes with a focused podcast episode that recommends a fairer model of buying, borrowing, repairing or sharing. Canva supports recording and editing the whole audio episode on an iPad.

Students photograph and sort examples of packaging into clear visual groups such as reusable, recyclable and difficult to recycle, then train an image model to recognise them. This helps them question how packaging design influences what consumers buy and what later enters habitats. Teams test one another's models with unfamiliar items and record which shapes, colours or labels cause mistakes. They adjust their training examples so the model relies less on misleading features such as brand colour. Each team finishes with a working classifier and a short demonstration of its successes and limits. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, using trained image systems to direct different materials into separate streams.

Students program a Micro:bit to tally choices during a rapid series of shopping dilemmas, using button A for the cheaper option and button B for the fairer or lower-impact option. This makes the pull between price, convenience and responsibility visible as decisions accumulate. Groups change one piece of information in each dilemma, such as adding a habitat warning or fair-work label, and repeat the test. They compare how strongly each new message changes the pattern of button presses. Each group finishes with a portable choice counter that displays totals on the LED grid. The two buttons, variables and LED display allow the whole decision test to run on one small device.

s.t: Ad-Busters Arcade: The Sustainable Choice Showdown
s.d: Students design and build interactive arcade-style games using recycled materials (cardboard, bottle caps, rubber bands, LEDs, switches) that challenge players to spot greenwashing, make ethical consumer choices, or navigate the consequences of fast fashion and food waste. Incorporating Makey Makey kits or micro:bit controllers, teams wire up their games so choices trigger real-time feedback—lights, buzzers, or scoreboards—teaching critical thinking about advertising and sustainability. Each game includes persuasive elements and hidden ads crafted by students, connecting to their research on how media influences purchasing decisions. The arcade culminates in a class expo where peers and staff play, reflect, and vote for the most impactful, creative, and thought-provoking builds.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human needs drive the development of nations.
lo: How human needs drive national development; Role of migration in nation building; Impacts of development on Indigenous and colonial populations

s.d: Students map Australian migration routes and layer them with population, terrain and climate data. This helps them work out how needs such as safety, work, water and transport shaped where communities grew. Groups compare one migration route with the Country it crossed and add notes about effects on First Nations peoples. They swap maps and challenge another group to explain which need had the greatest influence on development. Each group ends with an annotated evidence map showing routes, needs, settlement patterns and impacts. MapMaker's data layers let students test whether their first explanation still holds when new information appears.

Students compare photographs of homes, food, transport and everyday objects from families in countries linked to Australian migration. The comparisons show how access to safety, income, education and services can influence decisions to move. Each group chooses one family they must describe without stereotypes, using only details visible on Dollar Street. Groups then compare how the same human need can look different across places and income levels. Students end with a carefully selected set of visual evidence and short written observations. Dollar Street's income-ordered photographs make everyday differences easier to see and question.

Students edit a short documentary that connects one personal or community migration story with a wider event in Australian history. This shows how individual needs and national policies can shape one another over time. They ask a family or community member to check whether the story is accurate and respectfully represented before the final edit. Classmates then watch the films and identify repeated patterns such as seeking safety, work, family or opportunity. Each student ends with a titled documentary containing narration, evidence and a clear historical explanation. IMovie's editing, titles and transitions let students join several pieces of evidence into one coherent film.

Students build a multimodal book that places an Indigenous account, a colonial account and a migrant account beside the same Australian place. This helps them examine how development can benefit one population while disrupting another. Students exchange drafts and flag any page where one voice is missing, simplified or treated as less important. They then record a final reflection explaining whose needs shaped decisions and whose needs were ignored. Each group ends with a digital book containing text, images and recorded narration. Book Creator keeps these different forms of evidence together in one page-by-page publication.

Students build an interactive 3D scene showing one Australian place before colonisation, during colonial development and after later migration. This makes changes to land, movement, services and cultural life visible across time. Another group explores the scene and chooses objects to question, prompting the builders to strengthen weak or one-sided explanations. Students code selected objects to reveal short information points or move when a visitor interacts with them. Each group ends with a virtual historical scene that visitors can explore rather than simply watch. Delightex's 3D building tools and CoBlocks make the changes and interactions part of the explanation.

Students design and build interactive 'time capsules' that tell layered migration stories using both physical craftsmanship and simple electronics. Using recycled boxes, craft materials, and conductive tape or basic circuitry kits (e.g., Makey Makey or Chibitronics), students create dioramas or sculptural capsules representing a chosen era or migration journey in Australia. Each capsule features touch-activated elements—like opening a door or pressing a symbol—to trigger audio snippets, LED highlights, or digital slideshows on a connected tablet, revealing personal, Indigenous, and national migration narratives. This immersive project invites students to weave together place, time, and identity through hands-on making, storytelling, and basic coding, culminating in a class 'museum' of interactive capsules.

ci: An inquiry into the nature of the self; beliefs and values; personal, physical, mental, social and spiritual health; human relationships.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students paint a layered self-portrait showing influences on identity, wellbeing and learning. Each layer represents something different, such as relationships, values, experiences, emotions or brain function. Students choose which parts remain clear, overlap or sit beneath the surface, so they control what the portrait reveals. Partners view the paintings and describe the connections they notice before the artist explains their choices. Students finish with an original digital painting that shows identity as complex and changing. The app's layers let students build, hide and reorder parts of the portrait.

Students animate a short brain response to a challenging learning moment using paper shapes, clay or labelled cards. They show how a trigger, emotion, body response, thought and regulation strategy can form a sequence. Groups swap animations and check whether the brain process and chosen strategy are easy to follow. Students then adjust unclear frames or timing after receiving this feedback. Each group finishes with a stop-motion explanation of how managing wellbeing can support learning. Frame-by-frame capture makes processes that happen inside the body visible and discussable.

Students post realistic school scenarios involving stress, friendship, sensory needs, setbacks or learning pressure. They respond to classmates' scenarios with possible regulation strategies and explain why each one might help. Students can add more than one response because wellbeing strategies do not work equally for every person. Another Year 6 class can read the wall and contribute different approaches, widening the range of experiences considered. The class finishes with a searchable wall of situations, strategies and respectful peer advice. Padlet keeps notes and replies together so students can compare choices in one place.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record an avatar explaining how their brain and body respond during a difficult learning experience. They describe one sign they notice, one possible cause and one strategy that helps them regulate. Students choose whether the speaker represents themselves or a fictional learner, allowing safe discussion of personal topics. Peers listen and suggest one respectful question the speaker could answer in a revised recording. Each student finishes with a short animated explanation that could open a class conversation about neurodiversity. The Animate from Audio feature automatically lip-syncs the character to the student's recorded voice.

Students write scenario-based questions about growth mindset, relationships, brain function, safety and self-management. Each question asks players to choose a helpful response rather than simply recall a definition. Small groups test one another's quizzes and challenge answers that treat wellbeing as the same for everyone. Authors revise the options so more than one perspective can be discussed after each vote. Students finish with a playable class quiz bank for reviewing wellbeing choices. Kahoot's live question-and-answer format gives the teacher an immediate view of ideas that need further discussion.

s.t: Brainwaves Balance Board: Build Your Mindful Maze
s.d: Students will design and construct a tabletop 'balance board' maze that symbolises the journey of self-regulation and wellbeing. Using cardboard, marbles, recycled materials, and art supplies, each group creates a unique maze representing different brain regions, emotions, and mindset challenges. With a Makey Makey kit and Scratch, students embed interactive digital checkpoints—such as sound effects or animations triggered as the marble passes milestones—blending physical engineering with coding. This creative build challenges students to reflect on their own identities, experiences, and strategies for maintaining balance in learning and life.

ci: People recognise important events through celebrations and traditions.
lo: The traditions of our families and communities; How and why people celebrate; The similarities and differences between celebrations

s.d: Students photograph a family celebration object or their own drawing, add a mouth and record it telling why the event matters. This shows how objects, foods, clothing and decorations can carry family traditions. Children ask a family member for one detail to include, so every talking image brings a real voice from home into the classroom. They swap recordings with a partner and listen for something familiar and something new. Each child ends with a short talking image for a class celebration gallery. ChatterPix Kids makes the photograph talk through a drawn mouth and a recorded voice clip.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a teacher-made floor mat showing steps from a celebration, such as preparing food, dressing, gathering, giving and dancing. Sequencing the route helps children notice how and why traditions happen in a particular order. Pairs exchange route cards and work out which celebration sequence another pair has planned. They debug their button presses whenever the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong picture. Each pair ends with a working route they can demonstrate and explain to the class. Bee-Bot's directional buttons let children enter and test the whole sequence without a screen.

Students record a spoken sentence about a family celebration and build a short piece of music around it. This helps them hear how voices, rhythms and instruments can express joy, remembrance, welcome or togetherness. Children play their recordings to another Prep class, whose listeners guess the feeling before hearing the explanation. They make respectful choices about whether their music should sound lively, gentle, steady or quiet. Each child ends with a short celebration sound recording containing voice and original music. GarageBand allows children to record and arrange sounds in one music project.

Students sort teacher-provided celebration pictures on a shared Freeform canvas and draw lines between pictures that show similar traditions. This makes common features such as special food, light, music, clothing and gathering easy to see. Small groups choose one surprising connection and explain it to a visiting family member or another class. They can move a picture when discussion changes their thinking rather than treating the first answer as final. The class ends with a large visual web showing similarities and differences across celebrations. Freeform's open canvas allows pictures, drawings and connections to sit together in one shared space.

Students arrange paper figures and loose parts to animate two different celebrations from preparation to gathering. This lets them compare what people do while avoiding the idea that every family celebrates in exactly the same way. Partners swap storyboards and check whether each film shows both a similarity and a difference respectfully. They retake frames when an action is unclear and invite a family member to suggest one accurate detail. Each pair ends with a short stop-motion comparison film. Stop Motion Studio captures one frame at a time so children can make physical materials appear to move.

Students design and craft their own unique musical shakers inspired by a family or cultural celebration, using recycled containers, rice, beads, and colourful decorations like fabric, stickers, and metallic paper. After decorating, students use a simple recording tool on iPads (such as the camera or voice memos app) to capture the sound of their shaker and share a short story about its meaning. The class then assembles all the shakers and recordings into a 'Celebration Soundscape', building a multisensory display that celebrates the diversity of traditions in their community. This project helps students express themselves through both hands-on making and digital storytelling, connecting sound, art, and culture.

ci: We all have roles and responsibilities in the community
lo: Roles people play; Responsibilities in the community; How working together helps everyone

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles to program Indi along a path between picture cards showing classroom roles. Each stop shows a responsibility, such as carrying the lunch tub, tidying blocks or welcoming a visitor. Small groups build one section, then join their sections to make a route that only works when everyone contributes. Another group follows the route, checks the order and moves any tile that causes a problem. Students end with a working floor pathway that shows how several roles help the classroom run smoothly. The coloured tiles control how Indi moves without an app or screen.

Students code a character to complete a familiar classroom routine, such as arriving, unpacking, listening and joining the group. The ordered blocks show that responsibilities often need to happen in the right sequence. Partners swap projects and test whether they can understand each routine without an explanation. They then change one step to show what happens when someone forgets a responsibility and how others can help. Students end with a short coded animation that shows a routine working well. ScratchJr's picture blocks let young children sequence movement, speech and scene changes.

Students draw a school helper doing a real job, then add a second layer showing the people, places or objects helped by that work. This makes the effect of a responsibility visible rather than showing only a uniform or job title. Students ask the chosen helper one simple question, then adjust their drawing to include a detail they had missed. Partners hide and reveal the layers and explain how one person's work supports others. Students end with a layered illustration of a role and its impact on the school community. Sketchbook's layers allow different parts of the explanation to be viewed separately.

Students plan and record a puppet scene in which two characters must work together during a classroom or playground routine. The story shows why listening, following instructions and noticing other people matter. Each pair chooses a small problem, such as equipment left out or someone missing an instruction, and records a fair way to solve it. Another pair watches the scene and suggests one clearer or kinder response before it is recorded again. Students end with a short narrated puppet show that models shared responsibility. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one app.

Students interview a real school helper and record one answer about what they do and who depends on them. Hearing directly from staff shows that every school role includes responsibilities to other people. Children choose the most important part of the answer and add a short title that names the role. The finished clips are screened for another Prep class, which matches each helper to the way they support the school. Students end with a collection of brief video interviews about the St Kilda campus community. Apple Clips can record video and add live captions, stickers and titles in the same app.

Students design and build their own 'Command Centre' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, paper plates, and colourful craft materials to represent different classroom jobs and routines (like Line Leader, Librarian, or Gardener). Each role gets its own interactive station with moving parts (spinners, flaps, sliders) that students engineer themselves. Using an Osmo iPad base with the 'Monster' app, students animate their Command Centre: drawing or photographing their built stations, then bringing them to life with digital characters who 'perform' the jobs. This hands-on project helps students understand how roles and routines help organise their classroom community, blending creative making with playful technology.

ci: An inquiry into the natural world and its laws; the interaction between the natural world and human societies.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students photograph plants, insects and fungi in the school grounds and use Seek to suggest what each living thing might be. This helps them notice that even a built environment contains living things with particular needs. Pairs revisit one small area after rain or on a warmer day to see whether different species appear. They choose one discovery to show another Prep class and explain how people could protect it. Each pair finishes with a recorded set of local species observations. Seek's camera-based identification gives children an immediate suggestion that the class can check together rather than treating it as always correct.

Students magnify leaves, bark, feathers, soil and human-made materials, then describe the tiny details they can see. Close observation helps them work out differences between natural materials, living things and things people have built. Children swap mystery specimens and use visible clues to decide what they are examining. They arrange the specimens in a physical display with drawings of the patterns, edges and textures they noticed. The class compares which details were visible with their eyes and which only appeared under magnification. The magnifier keeps screen use brief while making real objects the centre of the investigation.

Students photograph a real plant or classroom animal habitat and record a short voice explanation of what the living thing needs. This makes food, water, shelter, air and light visible in places children know. Families can add a response describing how they care for a plant or animal at home. Each child finishes with a narrated journal entry that combines a photograph and their own voice. The teacher can replay entries during discussion and listen for changes in children's ideas about living and non-living things. Seesaw keeps the recording process simple and stores each child's entry in their portfolio.

Students draw an animal found around Melbourne, photograph the drawing in ChatterPix Kids and record it explaining what it needs to live. Speaking through the animal helps children connect habitat features with food, water, shelter and safety. Partners exchange recordings and suggest one change people could make to care for that animal's environment. Each child finishes with a short talking picture ready to show peers or families. The class can group the recordings by garden, tree, pond or coastal habitat and compare the animals' needs. ChatterPix Kids makes the drawing talk by adding a mouth and a brief recorded voice clip.

Students record seeds with different shapes being dropped, rolled or blown, then watch the movement in slow motion. This helps them see how natural shapes affect where seeds may travel and where new plants might grow. Groups choose one variable to change, such as release height or wind direction, and repeat the test. They compare clips and point to the moment a seed spins, glides, bounces or stops. Each group finishes with two slow-motion clips that show a fair before-and-after comparison. Slow playback reveals movements that happen too quickly to study clearly with the eye alone.

Students design and construct their own mini 'Bug Hotels' using recycled boxes, cardboard tubes, sticks, leaves, and natural materials to create cozy habitats for imaginary or real mini-beasts. After building, they use a simple tablet camera app (e.g., iPad Camera) to document their creations, narrating what creatures might live there and why each habitat feature is important. Students reflect on what living things need to survive and how humans can help care for tiny creatures in the environment. This project blends hands-on building, digital storytelling, and inquiry into how the world works for insects and animals.

ci: Human actions change the environment.
lo: How people interact with different environments; The effect people have on the environment; Ways in which people can take action and care for the environment

s.d: Students capture a 360-degree view of one small school environment, then photograph it again after rubbish, shade or safe animal shelter has changed. They look around each image to spot how one human action can affect the whole space. Pairs choose which change helped the environment and explain their choice to another Prep class. They end with two immersive views that can be turned and compared from every direction. The whole-surroundings view helps children notice details that an ordinary forward-facing photograph may miss. The class can revisit the images later to check whether caring actions have lasted.

Students search the school grounds for signs of local animals, then use Book Creator to identify animals that may live nearby. This shows that even a garden, tree or patch of soil can be an important environment. Each pair chooses one animal and works out what people should keep, add or stop doing near its habitat. They show their chosen animal profile and care idea to a buddy pair. The class ends with a checked set of local Victorian animals connected to real places around the school. The app's Victorian species information keeps the inquiry local and age-appropriate.

Students photograph clean, damaged and cared-for places around the school, then arrange the pictures in PicCollage. Comparing the images helps them see that everyday human actions cause visible changes. Children swap collages and add a short spoken explanation to their partner before choosing the clearest example for a class display. They end with a three-picture collage labelled 'helping', 'hurting' and 'changing'. The grid layout makes differences easy for young children to see side by side. Short captions let students name a practical action such as using a bin, saving water or protecting plants.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record the voice of a forest, ocean or desert animal explaining one human action that changes its home. Speaking from an animal's point of view makes cause and responsibility easier to understand. Each child chooses whether the animal asks people to stop something or start something, then plays the message for a buddy class. They end with a short animated character message that can open a class discussion. The Animate from Audio feature automatically lip-syncs the on-screen character to the child's recording. Re-recording gives students an easy way to make their care message clearer.

Students answer a teacher-made picture survey about actions such as dropping rubbish, turning off taps, planting flowers and walking on garden beds. The responses reveal what the class already does and which caring action needs more attention. Children study the automatic charts together and vote for one realistic class action to try for a week. They end with a class chart and a chosen environmental promise based on real responses. The same survey can be repeated after the action week to show whether behaviour changed. IMovie collects the answers and produces charts automatically.

Students will design and build miniature environments (desert, ocean, or forest) using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, paper, and natural materials. They'll craft native animals from modeling clay and create simple obstacles or shelters within each habitat. Using Sphero Indi cars, students will program simple color-coded paths for their 'animal' to explore, demonstrating how different habitats provide for living things and how human changes (like adding or removing elements) impact the journey. This playful, hands-on project helps students see their actions' effects on the planet while combining imaginative making with beginner robotics.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: An inquiry into orientation in place and time; personal histories; the relationship between and the interconnectedness of individuals and civilisations.
lo: Lines of inquiry to be confirmed once planner is uploaded

s.d: Students program a Bee-Bot across a floor mat showing places where family and community celebrations happen, such as home, school, a park and a place of worship. This makes orientation meaningful because each journey follows a real celebration story through place and time. Pairs swap mats and work out another family's route from picture clues placed on the squares. Children test the sequence, notice where the Bee-Bot goes wrong and change their button presses. Each pair ends with a working route that they can explain aloud to the class. The Bee-Bot's directional buttons keep the coding physical, visible and manageable for Prep learners.

Students photograph drawings or family objects linked to a celebration and record a short explanation on each page. Their pages show how traditions carry personal and family histories from one generation to another. Families can contribute a sentence in a home language, which the child records alongside an English explanation. The class combines the pages into a narrated book showing both shared practices and important differences. Children listen to a partner's page and add one respectful question for the next class conversation. Book Creator holds images, text and recorded voices together in one child-friendly book.

Students record a puppet conversation between two children whose families celebrate in different ways. The conversation explains what happens, where it happens, who joins in and how each child feels. Partners choose one similarity and one difference that the puppets must discuss respectfully rather than simply listing facts. They rehearse with paper puppets first, then move the characters across simple celebration backdrops while recording their voices. Each pair ends with a short puppet show that can open a class discussion about culture and belonging. Puppet Pals lets young children move characters and record dialogue in the same activity.

Students paint a digital picture of one moment before, during or after a celebration that matters to their family. The picture helps them show how a tradition is remembered through colours, symbols, clothing, food or movement. Children exchange paintings without explanations and describe what they notice before hearing the artist's real story. The artist then adds or changes one visual detail so the meaning is clearer while avoiding symbols that do not belong to their tradition. Each child ends with an original painting and a short spoken explanation given beside the display. Brushes Redux supports layered painting, so students can revise details without starting again.

Students code a short animated story showing the order of events in a familiar celebration or tradition. Sequencing what happens first, next and last connects personal history with the passage of time. Partners trade projects and try to work out the celebration from the characters' movements and setting. The creator then changes one block sequence or adds a recorded explanation where the meaning is unclear. Each child ends with a playable animation that shows a celebration unfolding in order. ScratchJr's picture blocks let Prep students move characters and record voices without needing to read complex instructions.

Students build giant cardboard flowers whose folded petals open with a gentle pull on a ribbon, revealing paper pictures and fabric textures representing a celebration meaningful to their family or community. Using recycled cardboard, split pins secured by an adult, ribbon, fabric scraps, tape and child-safe glue, they follow the Design Cycle: ask what makes their celebration special, imagine and plan their surprise, then build a working prototype. With adult support, students use an iPad's camera and a simple stop-motion app to animate their physical flower opening, testing for stuck petals and improving the mechanism before filming again. Sharing the flowers and animations connects 'Where We Are in Place and Time' to family memories, changing traditions and respectful discussion of how different celebrations bring people together.

ci: To be healthy, people's basic needs must be met.
lo: How our brain is growing and changing; How our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships; How we care for our bodies

s.d: Students record a short balance, hop or ball-catching action, practise it, then record it again in slow motion. They look closely for small changes that show how the brain and body learn through practice. Partners watch each other's clips and choose one helpful action, such as bending knees or watching the ball. Each child explains one change they can now see but could not notice at normal speed. They finish with a before-and-after movement comparison and a spoken reflection. Slow-motion playback makes brief body movements easier for young children to observe.

Students record voices, claps, taps and classroom instruments to show how calm, worried, excited and angry feelings might sound. This helps children notice emotions and consider how their actions affect relationships. Partners listen without seeing the chosen emotion and explain which sounds helped them recognise it. Children then change one sound so the recording moves from a strong feeling towards calm. They finish with a short emotion soundscape that can support a class discussion about calming choices. GarageBand lets students layer and replay recorded sounds as they refine their ideas.

Students photograph drawings of food, water, sleep, movement, shelter and caring relationships, then record why people need each one. This shows that health depends on both physical needs and feeling safe and connected. Each child invites a family member or trusted adult to add a brief recorded example of how they meet one need at home. Children listen to different examples and notice that families may care for health in different ways. They finish with a narrated class book called What People Need to Be Healthy. Book Creator keeps images, text and recorded voices together on each page.

Students watch short teacher-selected clips about sleep, food, exercise, emotions and growing brains, pausing to copy a movement or discuss a choice. The clips give children visible examples of how daily care helps bodies and brains grow. Small groups choose one moment to replay and explain whether it shows a need, a feeling or a healthy action. The class compares answers and talks through moments that could fit more than one group. Students finish with a teacher-recorded list of evidence gathered from the clips. Seesaw provides curated educational videos that can be paused and revisited closely.

Students paint a self-portrait and add separate layers showing things that help them feel healthy, safe and connected. This brings body care, emotions and relationships together in one personal image. Partners temporarily hide one layer, work out what is missing, and explain why that need matters. Each child then adds a colour, shape or symbol inspired by a healthy tradition or celebration from home. They finish with a layered portrait showing that wellbeing has many connected parts. Brushes Redux allows layers to be shown, hidden and changed without covering the original painting.

s.t: My Celebration Self: Wearable Story Hats
s.d: Students design and craft vibrant, wearable hats that tell the story of their unique identity, family, and favourite celebration. Using cardboard headbands, coloured paper, fabric scraps, recycled materials, and decorative bits, each child builds a hat featuring symbols, drawings, and 3D elements representing their traditions, foods, and special moments. With iPads, students use a simple AR (augmented reality) app to record a short video introducing their hat and its meaning, then add a QR code tag to their creation for friends to scan and watch. This hands-on project celebrates diversity, creativity, and community, making identity visible and shareable in a joyful, playful way.

ci: People express their emotions through the way they communicate.
lo: Different ways to communicate emotions; How art, music and movement express feelings; Understanding others' expressions through body language and facial cues

s.d: Students train Teachable Machine to recognise three body poses that they choose to show emotions such as excitement, worry and calm. They test whether a computer can understand feelings when it cannot hear any words. Pairs swap models and try poses that are clear, subtle or deliberately confusing. They record which poses the model recognises reliably and discuss why people can also misread body language. This works like pose-recognition systems used in accessibility tools, physiotherapy and sports-coaching apps. Each pair ends with a working pose model and a short demonstration of what it can and cannot understand.

Students paint a Frida Kahlo-inspired self-portrait using colours, lines and symbols to express a chosen emotion. This helps them show that a face is only one part of emotional communication. Each student hides the emotion word and asks classmates to work it out from the artistic choices. They then adjust one layer to make the feeling clearer or more complex. The finished work is a class gallery of expressive digital self-portraits. Brushes Redux allows students to build and revise their paintings with separate layers.

Students record a short puppet scene in which one character misunderstands another character's facial expression, movement or tone of voice. The scene shows how emotions can be communicated and misread in everyday situations. Students pause before the ending and ask another pair to suggest an empathetic response. They then record a resolution in which the characters ask a question instead of making an assumption. Each pair finishes with a narrated puppet show that can prompt a class discussion. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one app.

Students compose two short pieces of music that express contrasting emotions without using spoken words. They choose sounds, tempo and volume to communicate feelings such as joy, loneliness, anger or calm. Another group listens without seeing the emotion labels and explains what the music makes them feel. Composers then change one musical choice after hearing the listeners' responses. Each student finishes with a pair of contrasting emotion soundscapes. GarageBand lets students arrange and record musical parts in one project.

Students record a short movement that expresses an emotion through posture, pace and gesture, then watch it in slow motion. They look closely at when the feeling first becomes understandable without words. Partners identify one body cue, such as lowered shoulders, quick steps or open arms, and explain what it might communicate. Students repeat the movement with one cue changed and test whether a partner reads it differently. Each pair ends with two slow-motion recordings that show how a small movement can change meaning. Slow playback makes brief gestures easier for Year 1 students to notice and discuss.

Students design and build creative 'wearable machines' that show different emotions using moving parts and colour-changing features. Using cardboard, felt, ribbons, recycled bits, paper plates, and simple mechanisms (like spinning emotion dials, pop-up eyebrows, or flapping wings powered by split pins and string), they craft hats, masks, or badges that physically change to express feelings. Students then use a simple coding robot (like Sphero Indi) to 'activate' their wearable by driving it onto colour-coded tiles that trigger the wearer to show a specific emotion. This hands-on project lets students explore how we express ourselves through movement, colour, and design, blending art, technology, and self-awareness in a joyful, memorable way.

ci: Systems are involved in preparing products for consumers.
lo: Where products come from; The systems products go through; How people choose their products

s.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to carry a picture of bread across a floor mat from farm to factory, transport, shop and consumer. This makes each stage of a product system visible and shows why the order matters. Pairs swap route cards, test each other's instructions and fix any step that delivers the bread to the wrong place. They then add a blocked road or closed factory and program a new route through the system. Each pair finishes with a working route they can explain to another class. The Bee-Bot's directional buttons let students enter, test and debug the sequence one move at a time.

Students sort teacher-added pictures of food and clothing on a shared Freeform canvas, then draw arrows from each product's origin to the consumer. This helps them work out where products come from and what happens between making and buying. Groups exchange canvases and move one misplaced stage, leaving a short label to explain their choice. They also circle packaging or transport steps that could create waste. The class finishes with a large connected map of several product systems. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and connect pictures without squeezing their thinking onto one page.

Students train a teacher-guided Teachable Machine image model to recognise products with minimal packaging, reusable packaging or multiple layers of packaging. They collect examples such as loose fruit, a reusable lunch container and individually wrapped snacks, then place each example into the correct training class. After training the model, pairs test unfamiliar products and notice when the classification is accurate or confused. They improve its decisions by adding more varied examples, changing angles and removing distracting backgrounds. The finished image classifier becomes an interactive sorting station that reveals how packaging changes before products reach consumers. Students explain which examples helped the model learn and identify one packaging choice that could reduce waste.

Students record a 360-degree view of a classroom arranged as a farm, factory, transport depot, shop and home. Each group stands at one station and briefly explains what happens to the same product there. Because the whole room is captured, viewers can turn around and see that all parts of the system are connected. Another class watches the recording and tries to identify the correct order of the stages. Students finish with an immersive recording of a complete product journey. The 360-degree view makes every station visible from one recording rather than showing the process as separate scenes.

Students build a narrated digital book that follows one everyday product from its source to the person who buys it. Each page shows one stage, with a picture, a short label and the student's recorded explanation using words such as farm, factory, process and transportation. Partners swap books and listen for a missing stage or a step that is out of order. Students then add a final page comparing two packaging choices and explain which one they would buy. Each child finishes with a sequenced product-journey book for the class library. Book Creator combines pages, images, text and recorded narration in one place.

s.t: From Farm to Table: Supply Chain Train Adventure
s.d: Students design and build a giant tabletop 'train track' system using cardboard, tubes, recycled boxes, and craft materials to represent the journey of a product (like bread or a t-shirt) from its origin to the consumer. Along the track, they create and decorate stations for each stage—farm, factory, transport, shop, and home—using found materials, drawings, and labels. A Sphero Indi or push-along train serves as the 'product,' traveling through each stop as students narrate and sequence its journey. This playful project helps students physically map out and understand how products move through organised systems, connecting vocabulary and concepts to a hands-on, collaborative creation.

ci: Weather affects our lives in different ways.
lo: Types of weather conditions; How weather impacts our lives (clothing, activities, food, feelings); Why weather changes (seasons, patterns)

s.d: Students become weather-advice trainers by sorting teacher-provided images into sunny, rainy, windy and cold categories, then adding them to a teacher-guided Teachable Machine image-classification model. They test the model by holding up new weather scenes and noticing which category it predicts. Pairs investigate mistakes, such as a dark beach image being classified as rain, and improve the training set with clearer examples. They then test pictures of raincoats, sunhats and kites to discuss whether visual clues always reveal suitable choices. The class produces a tested weather classifier and a pictorial chart of accurate and inaccurate predictions. Teachable Machine's live confidence scores make patterns, uncertainty and improvement visible to young scientists.

Students photograph paper weather symbols one frame at a time to animate a week changing from sunny to windy, rainy and cool. This shows that weather can follow patterns while still changing from day to day. Partners swap animations and choose suitable clothing, food and activities for each animated day. They then revise any sequence that changes too quickly for the audience to follow. Each pair finishes with a short weather-pattern animation and a spoken explanation. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame playback makes slow changes and repeating patterns visible.

Students photograph a hand-drawn Chinese weather character, add a mouth and record it saying the weather word in Chinese and English. This links weather conditions with Chinese vocabulary and the pictographic shapes used to represent ideas. Each talking character gives another Year 1 class one useful choice, such as wearing a raincoat or playing indoors. Students listen to a partner's recording and check whether the advice matches the named weather. They finish with a set of short talking weather-character clips for a class language display. ChatterPix Kids lets students draw a mouth on one image and add a brief voice recording.

Students record and arrange sounds that suggest sunshine, wind, rain or a storm in GarageBand. This helps them explore how weather can affect feelings, movement and daily choices. Another group listens without being told the weather, names what they think is happening and chooses suitable clothing or an activity. The composers adjust sounds that gave the wrong clue and test the piece again. Each group finishes with a short weather soundscape that classmates can interpret. GarageBand allows students to layer, record and rearrange sounds in one project.

Students code a character to move through two different weather scenes and make a different choice in each one. This shows how rain, heat, cold or wind can change clothing and activities. Partners exchange projects and check whether each coded choice makes sense for the weather shown. Students debug the sequence when a character wears the wrong item, speaks at the wrong time or enters the scenes out of order. They finish with an interactive animation showing one person adapting to changing weather. ScratchJr's picture blocks make movement, speech and scene changes manageable for Year 1 coders.

s.t: Weather Wonder Wheels: Rolling Forecast Dioramas
s.d: Students design and build a rolling diorama that shows different weather scenes using large recycled cardboard tubes as the base. They craft interchangeable weather panels (sunny, rainy, windy, snowy) with collage materials, cotton balls, fabric scraps, and tissue paper, attaching them around the tube. Using simple axles and wheels, students create a handle to rotate their diorama and reveal changing weather. With the help of an iPad, they record short videos narrating their diorama's story, explaining how people and places adapt to each weather type—blending creative making, storytelling, and weather science.

ci: Living things have structures that allow them to survive in different environments.
lo: The physical structure of plants and bees; How features support survival in different environments; Human impact on living things

s.d: Students magnify fallen flowers, leaves and a safely preserved bee specimen to inspect petals, pollen, veins, hairs and body parts. Close observation shows how small structures help plants and bees collect resources and survive. Each pair chooses one feature they think is especially useful and shows it to another pair through the magnifier. They compare the same feature at different magnifications before drawing only what they can truly see. Students end with a labelled scientific drawing and a spoken explanation of how one structure supports survival. The magnification makes details visible that young eyes would usually miss.

Students scan plants and safe-to-approach insects in the school grounds to identify local living things. They notice which plants grow in sunny, shady, dry or damp places and consider how their features suit those conditions. Pairs choose one identification to check again from a different angle rather than accepting the first result. They compare their records to find plants that may provide shelter or food for pollinators. Students end with a class record of local species and suggested places where bee-friendly planting could help. Seek uses the camera to suggest an identification, which students treat as a guide to check.

Students create a Seesaw growth journal by photographing the same plant at regular intervals and adding its height, leaf count and growing conditions as labels. They use the drawing tools to circle new leaves, mark changes in stem height and identify signs that the plant needs more light or water. A sequence of dated posts reveals how plant structures develop when their needs are met. Students compare two entries, then use Seesaw's voice-recording feature to explain one change they can see. They select their clearest evidence and place it in a final post with a labelled before-and-after image. The journal becomes an observable growth record showing how environmental conditions affect a living thing.

Students investigate Victorian insects and other small animals in Field Guide to Victoria, paying close attention to body coverings, legs, wings and habitats. Comparing local fauna helps them see how physical features support survival in different environments. Each pair selects two animals with noticeably different structures and asks another pair to match each animal to its habitat. They then explain which visible clues made the match possible. Students end with a comparison card showing two local animals, their habitats and one useful feature each. The guide provides identification information about fauna found in Victoria.

Students watch a teacher-selected ClickView clip about flower structures, bees and pollination, pausing to notice each contact between bee and flower. The sequence shows how the structures of two living things work together for survival. Before the ending, groups predict what could happen if flowers, nesting places or bees disappeared from the environment. They revisit key moments and answer questions using evidence from what they saw. Students end with an ordered explanation of pollination and one action people can take to reduce harm. ClickView provides curated educational video that can be paused and replayed for close analysis.

Students will design and build a large, 3D collaborative garden using recycled boxes, paper tubes, and craft materials to create flowers, plants, and a variety of habitats. They'll craft simple bee robots using Sphero Indi cars decorated as bees, then code the Indis to 'pollinate' their handmade flowers by following colour-coded paths they design with tape and paper. As they test and refine their gardens, students observe how bees interact with plants and discuss ways to make their garden more bee-friendly. This hands-on quest helps them understand the vital relationship between plants, pollinators, and the shared responsibility of caring for our planet.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Stories and artefacts help us to understand connections between the past, present and future.
lo:
How we learn about the past
Why people preserve stories and artefacts
How stories and artefacts can be shared into the future

s.d: Students photograph a family or classroom artefact in ChatterPix Kids and record it telling a short story about the past. Giving the object a voice shows how stories can help us understand why it was used and kept. Pairs swap clips and listen for clues that place each object in the past, present or future. Each student ends with a talking artefact clip that can be played beside the real object. ChatterPix Kids lets students draw a mouth on the photograph and add a short voice recording. Families can watch the clips and send back another detail about why the object matters.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students select an on-screen character and record it retelling a story that an older family or community member has preserved. They work out which people, places and objects in the story reveal something about the past. Another Year 1 class watches the character and identifies the clues that should be remembered in the future. Students produce a short animated retelling with clear words and one important message. The Animate from Audio feature automatically matches the character's mouth to the student's recorded voice. Re-recording encourages students to make the story accurate, clear and respectful.

Students draw the same treasured object as it may have looked in the past, as it looks now and as it might look in the future. Comparing the three views makes change over time easy to see and discuss. Students exchange drawings and add one visual clue that could help a future viewer understand why the object mattered. Each student finishes with a detailed three-part illustration for a class timeline display. Sketchbook's drawing tools allow students to add colour, texture and small details carefully. The class can compare which details were preserved and which changed across the three time periods.

Students record a short museum-style report showing an old classroom or household object and explaining what has changed since it was used. This helps them connect physical evidence with stories about everyday life in the past. A partner asks one question on camera about what a child in the future might misunderstand about the object. Students finish with a brief captioned video containing the object, an explanation and a future question. Apple Clips provides live captions, stickers and titles within the same recording process. The completed reports can play beside the objects during a classroom exhibition.

Students plan and record a puppet conversation between a child from the past and a child from the future about one preserved story or object. The conversation shows that the same object can carry different meanings across time. Partners swap scripts before recording and suggest one question the future child should ask. Each pair produces a narrated puppet show with a clear beginning, problem and explanation. Puppet Pals lets students move characters across backdrops while recording their voices. Younger students can watch the shows and point out what was preserved for them to understand.

s.t: Future Finders: Build a Story-Saving Treasure Capsule
s.d: Students investigate how artefacts tell us about the past, then design a treasure capsule to carry a present-day story into the future, using a handmade clay keepsake or paper replica rather than a precious original. Following the Design Cycle, they ask what needs protecting, sketch ideas, and build protective compartments from recycled cardboard tubes, popsticks, fabric scraps and paper cushioning, using tape and child-safe glue. With adult support, students record a short audio message on an iPad explaining their keepsake, then attach a teacher-created QR code to a lift-up cardboard story tag so future finders can scan and hear its story. Partners gently shake-test the capsules and check that the tags scan, then improve their designs and share how preserving both objects and voices connects the past, present and future.

ci: We learn about ourselves through the games we play.
lo: How to identify and manage emotions; How players' choices affect relationships; Our responsibilities when playing games

s.d: Students record a short video before, during and after playing the same class game, naming how they feel each time. This shows that games can teach us how our feelings change when we win, wait, disagree or try again. Students choose one difficult moment and record a second response showing a calm-down or conflict-solving strategy. They finish with a three-part video reflection that families can watch and discuss. Seesaw keeps each recording together in the student's journal. Voice and video let Year 1 students explain ideas without needing long written answers.

Students photograph examples of fair and unfair choices during carefully staged playground games. They sort the photographs into a collage and add short captions such as 'invited someone', 'changed the rule' or 'waited for a turn'. Partners swap collages and choose one unfair moment that could be repaired. Students finish with a visual guide showing how players' choices can help or hurt relationships. PicCollage makes it easy to arrange photographs in clear groups. The finished guides can be displayed beside the class game equipment.

Students record two versions of a short game disagreement, one where the problem grows and one where players repair it. This helps them notice how words, facial expressions and choices affect relationships. Small groups choose their own conflict, such as skipping a turn, changing a rule or refusing to include someone. They finish with a short comparison film that pauses for classmates to suggest a better choice. IMovie allows students to join scenes and add simple titles. Watching both endings side by side makes cause and effect easy to discuss.

Students paint two digital self-portraits showing how their face and body might look during different moments in a game. This builds precise feelings vocabulary beyond simply happy, sad or angry. Partners view each painting without its emotion being named and explain which visual clues helped them work it out. Students finish with paired portraits that show how emotions can change during play. Brushes Redux supports expressive colour, line and layered painting. Students can revise a layer after peer feedback without starting their artwork again.

Students lay coloured tiles to create a game path where Indi's journey changes after each player choice. This makes rules, turn-taking and consequences visible as the car follows the path the group has agreed on. Groups exchange paths and must ask permission before moving another group's tiles or changing its rules. Students finish with a working floor game and a spoken explanation of each player's responsibilities. Indi drives according to the sequence of coloured tiles placed on the floor. Moving one tile gives students an immediate way to test how a choice changes the whole game.

s.t: Friendship Forts: Build & Code Your Team Hideout
s.d: Students work in small teams to design and construct colourful cardboard 'forts' or cozy hideouts using large boxes, fabric scraps, paper, and markers. Each team personalises their fort to reflect their unique group identity, decorating with symbols, drawings, and words that represent fairness, respect, and teamwork. Using Sphero Indi cars, students collaboratively create a simple coded pathway leading friends to their fort, reinforcing the importance of clear rules and cooperation. This project celebrates classroom community and gives students a tangible, playful space to discuss and role-play positive social behaviours.

ci: Artefacts provide a window into the beliefs and values of cultures.
lo: Beliefs and values contribute to a culture; The importance of rituals and traditions; How artefacts capture history and cultural expression

s.d: Students photograph a family object frame by frame as it moves through three moments in its imagined or known history. This shows how an object can carry beliefs, memories and values across time. Students ask a family member which details must stay truthful, then choose how movement can show the object's changing use. They swap unfinished animations and work out what cultural meaning a viewer can understand without words. Each student finishes with a short stop-motion film that treats the object with care and keeps its story clear. Stop Motion Studio joins the photographs into a frame-by-frame animation.

Students interview a family member about a ritual, celebration, food, song or treasured object and record the conversation. Listening to a real voice helps them hear why traditions matter to people, not just what happens during them. Each student selects one answer that challenged an assumption and adds a respectful follow-up question. A partner listens before publication and checks that names, pronunciations and private details have been handled carefully. Students finish with a short edited podcast episode for a class listening library. Podcasting using Canva lets them record and edit the episode on an iPad.

Students code an animated story showing how an object is used during a family or cultural tradition. The characters' actions reveal the beliefs and values connected with the object. Students exchange projects, then add one question a viewer can tap to explore before the story continues. They revise any scene that makes a culture look like one fixed experience shared by everyone. Each student finishes with an interactive story containing sequenced actions, recorded speech and a clear ending. ScratchJr's blocks let young learners program movement, speech and scene changes.

Students build a small 3D exhibition scene around one carefully researched cultural object. The surrounding people, setting and actions show that an object's meaning comes from the culture and history around it. Students invite another class to explore the scenes and identify which details helped them understand the object's importance. They then change one object, label or action that visitors found confusing. Each group finishes with an interactive virtual exhibition scene that can be explored on screen. Delightex provides 3D objects and block coding for simple movement and responses.

Students record and edit a short film comparing two traditions through music, dance, food, storytelling or meaningful objects. The comparison helps them notice shared purposes while respecting important differences. Students choose whether to include their own narration, a family interview or a filmed demonstration, with permission from everyone shown. A partner checks the draft for sweeping claims such as 'everyone does this' and suggests more accurate words. Each pair finishes with a titled mini-documentary for a class screening. IMovie allows them to arrange clips and add titles and transitions in one place.

Students will design and build miniature parade floats that represent a cultural celebration or tradition from their own background or one they've researched. Using recycled boxes, fabric scraps, coloured paper, and craft materials, they'll craft 3D floats and then integrate simple LED circuits (battery packs, LEDs, copper tape) to illuminate their creations. Students will document their design choices and the story behind their float using iPads to record a short video explanation, which is displayed alongside their float. This project encourages creative expression, hands-on making, and respectful sharing of diverse cultures through both physical building and basic tech integration.

ci: Technology can influence the way ecosystems can survive.
lo: An ecosystem has animals, plants and microorganisms; Technology can cause ecosystems to adapt and evolve; Technology can help or hinder ecosystems

s.d: Students train an image model to recognise two types of local leaves by showing each leaf to the camera many times. This shows how technology can help people notice patterns in ecosystems, while mistakes reveal that computer decisions depend on the examples people provide. Students choose whether their model will sort leaves by species, shape or visible damage. Another class tests the model with unfamiliar leaves and records where it succeeds or gets confused. Students finish with a working classifier and a clear example of how technology can help or hinder environmental decisions. Similar image recognition is used by wildlife-monitoring cameras and plant-identification apps to sort large numbers of nature images.

Students identify and research three Victorian animals that could live in or near St Kilda. They trace what each animal needs from plants, other animals and its habitat, then check how roads, lighting or nesting boxes might affect its survival. Pairs swap one animal and challenge each other to find a helpful technology and a harmful technology. Students choose the species they think most needs human help and explain their reason to the class. They finish with an on-screen shortlist of local species, their needs and the technologies that may change their ecosystem. The app's Victorian species information keeps the inquiry local and manageable for Year 2.

Students build a digital book showing one ecosystem before and after a new technology arrives. This makes the chain of change visible as plants, animals and microorganisms respond to inventions such as roads, irrigation, lights or wildlife crossings. Each pair chooses whether the technology mostly helps, mostly harms or creates both results, then another pair adds a question to test that claim. Students record short animal and plant viewpoints so different needs can be heard. They finish with a narrated ecosystem story that can be read by another Year 2 class. Book Creator keeps text, pictures and recorded voices together on each page.

Students build a survey asking which technologies should be allowed near a wetland, park or beach ecosystem. Their questions compare choices such as bright night lighting, nesting boxes, rubbish bins, drones and wildlife tunnels. Students send the survey to classmates, then predict which choice will divide opinions before responses arrive. They read the automatic charts and discuss why a technology might help one living thing but hinder another. Students finish with a real set of class opinions and a decision supported by the survey results. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and turns the answers into charts automatically.

Students build two interactive 3D versions of the same ecosystem, one before technology arrives and one after. They add plants, animals and human-made objects, then code simple movements to show changes such as animals avoiding a road or reaching a new water source. Students exchange scenes and look for one effect the builder did not intend. Each group then changes one part of its world to improve the balance between human needs and ecosystem survival. Students finish with a virtual ecosystem comparison that visitors can explore from different viewpoints. Delightex's 3D building tools and block coding let students show both the parts of a system and how they respond.

Students design and build their own imaginative 'techno-bugs' using recycled materials like egg cartons, pipe cleaners, cardboard, and bottle caps, combined with simple motors or battery-powered movement kits. Each student invents a bug that could help an ecosystem (like cleaning up litter or watering plants), decorating it to show its function and role in the community.
