They then test and refine their bugs' movement through a collaborative, student-made habitat, reflecting on how technology and nature can work together. This project links directly to the unit's exploration of systems, change, and the impact of technology on living things.

ci: People and the planet are reliant on different energy sources.
lo: Energy types (electricity, fossil fuels, solar); Energy helps us in daily life; Energy transformation; Responsibility to conserve energy and find sustainable sources

s.d: Students programme Sphero Indi to travel through a floor-sized ecosystem where coloured tiles represent solar energy, fossil fuels, habitats and environmental hazards. Teams design two routes—one that keeps the ecosystem balanced and another that reveals consequences such as pollution or habitat loss. They arrange Indi's colour cards to control movement, speed and direction, then test whether the robot can deliver energy to homes without entering sensitive habitats. When Indi takes an unintended path, students debug the sequence and explain what went wrong. Each team produces a tested energy route and a labelled floor model showing its environmental effects. A final robot demonstration supports discussion about how technology can help or harm ecosystems.

Students draw the same local ecosystem twice, once beside a fossil-fuel power source and once beside a solar energy source. They include plants, animals, water, shelter and signs of human technology in each scene. Students swap drawings and look for changes that might disturb or restore the ecosystem's balance. Each artist then adjusts one detail after hearing a partner's question or suggestion. They finish with two detailed illustrations that support persuasive writing about responsible energy choices. Sketchbook's layers let students separate the ecosystem, energy source and environmental effects while they revise.

Students record a short puppet conversation between the Sun, a lump of coal and an electrical appliance. Each character explains where its energy comes from, how people use it and what effect it may have on the planet. Groups exchange scripts first so another group can check whether the energy ideas are clear and accurate. Students must include one disagreement about convenience, pollution or conserving energy. They finish with a narrated puppet show that can open a class discussion about sustainable choices. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one simple production.

Students watch a teacher-selected ClickView clip about electricity generation and pause whenever energy changes form. They say what the energy was before the change and what it became, such as sunlight changing to electrical energy. Small groups are each given one viewing question about homes, power stations or environmental effects. After replaying key sections, groups compare answers and decide which claim the video supports best. The class ends with an agreed sequence of energy transformations and a list of questions that still need investigation. ClickView's pause and replay controls make fast or hidden changes easier for young learners to notice.

Students photograph a classroom appliance in ChatterPix Kids and make it explain how it depends on energy. The talking object names its energy source, its useful job and one way people could avoid wasting its energy. Students play their clips to a partner who checks for the words electricity, transformation or conserve. They then rerecord one sentence so the advice is clear enough for a Year 1 audience. Each student finishes with a short talking-appliance message for an energy-saving display. ChatterPix Kids adds a drawn mouth and a recorded voice directly to the photo.

Students work in teams to design and build mini playground models using cardboard, paper rolls, fabric scraps, and recycled materials, then wire up simple solar-powered circuits (with teacher support) to add moving features like spinning merry-go-rounds or seesaws. They'll test how their playgrounds work under sunlight or a lamp, exploring how solar energy powers movement. This project links energy sources and technology to real-world fun, encouraging students to consider eco-friendly designs that minimize harm to local ecosystems. The Design Cycle guides them from sketching ideas to hands-on building, testing, and sharing their solar-powered creations with classmates.

ci: Choices about how we use and care for resources can shape shared environments.
lo:
An inquiry into the interdependence of human and natural worlds through rights, responsibilities and dignity of all
An inquiry into the interdependence of human and natural worlds through pathways to just, peaceful and reimaged futures
An inquiry into the interdependence of human and natural worlds through nature, complexity, coexistence and wisdom

s.d: Students program Bee-Bots to travel across a floor map of a shared beach, choosing refill, reuse and rubbish-collection squares instead of squares that harm birds. Each route helps children see that a small choice changes what people and animals can use in the same place. Pairs swap route cards and debug each other's instructions when a Bee-Bot lands on a harmful square. They end with a tested route card and a working Bee-Bot pathway that shows one caring choice. Bee-Bot's directional buttons keep the focus on putting clear steps in order.

Students photograph plants, insects and birds around the school with Seek, then check each suggested identification by looking closely at the living thing and its habitat. Seeing which species use a busy patch of garden helps them talk about why shared places need care. Each pair chooses one practical change, such as leaving leaf litter, protecting flowering plants or keeping paths clear of habitat. They end with a paper observation card showing the species, where it was found and the care action they recommend. Seek gives students a suggested identification from the image they take.

Students plan and record a short Puppet Pals scene in which a child, an animal and a park worker disagree about litter, water or damaged habitat. The conversation helps them practise rights and responsibilities when humans and natural worlds need the same resources. Another pair watches each scene and asks whether the ending is fair to every character, then the creators revise one line if needed. They end with a recorded puppet show that explains a peaceful, workable choice. Puppet Pals lets students use characters, backdrops and recorded voices to build the scene.

Students paint two versions of the same local place in Brushes Redux, one where resources are wasted and one where people care for water, plants and animals. Painting the change side by side makes cause and effect visible without needing a long written explanation. Students place their iPads together in a gallery walk and explain which details show a fairer shared environment. They end with a layered digital painting that compares the consequences of two choices. Brushes Redux lets students build an original painting in layers.

Students photograph one shared classroom resource they use during the week, such as paper, water, lights or art materials, and record a short voice reflection in Seesaw. Their reflections turn everyday routines into evidence about how choices shape a place everyone uses. Students listen to a partner's entry and add one kind, practical suggestion for reducing waste or caring for the resource. They end with a Seesaw journal entry containing a photo, spoken explanation and one next-step promise. Seesaw captures photos, voice and student reflections in one journal.

Students build a working, hand-operated swap machine that turns clean leftover craft materials into treasures for someone else's next creation, using recycled cardboard, paper tubes, popsticks, fabric scraps, tape and child-safe glue. An iPad running ScratchJr becomes the machine's interactive control panel: children tap a material picture to reveal which numbered cardboard drawer to open and hear a student-recorded idea for reusing its contents. Following the Design Cycle, teams investigate classroom waste, imagine fair ways to share, plan and build their machines, then test whether classmates can find and exchange materials before improving confusing labels or jammed drawers. Their invention brings Sharing the Planet to life by conserving resources and helping everyone access useful materials without always buying something new.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Journeys can lead to challenges and new understandings.
lo: Types of journeys (physical, learning, cultural); Challenges encountered on journeys; New understandings gained through journeys

s.d: Students walk a short route around the St Kilda campus and capture places where a journey changes, pauses or becomes difficult. Seeing the whole space helps them notice how surroundings can shape a physical journey and what someone learns along the way. Pairs choose one important stopping point and explain why a younger student should look closely there. They arrange their captures in route order and invite another class to explore the journey by turning to look in every direction. The finished work is an immersive tour showing the route, its challenges and the students' new observations. The Insta360 camera records the complete surroundings rather than just what is directly ahead.

Students photograph or select pictures of family objects that have travelled, such as a recipe, toy, letter, suitcase or piece of clothing. They add short captions explaining where each object came from, what challenge it connects to and what it helps the family remember. Students ask a family member which object best shows change or growth, then give that object the most important place in the layout. Classmates view the collages and look for similarities between journeys from different families and cultures. Each student finishes with a labelled visual family-journey display. PicCollage makes it easy to arrange photographs in a grid and place short captions beside them.

Students interview a family or community member about a journey that brought a challenge and a new understanding. This lets them hear how physical, cultural and learning journeys can shape a person's identity. Students choose one follow-up question after listening carefully, rather than reading every question from a prepared list. They play selected interviews to another Year 2 class, whose students identify the challenge and the change they heard. Each pair produces a clear short audio interview with an introduction and closing sentence. The physical microphones and recorders help students capture voices closely during the conversation.

Students record and arrange sounds that show the beginning, challenge and ending of an imagined journey. Changing pace, volume and sound choice helps them show how feelings and understandings shift along the way. Partners swap unfinished soundscapes and guess what happened before the creator explains the journey. Students then change one section if the intended challenge was not clear to the listener. Each student finishes with a short three-part journey soundscape. GarageBand lets them record sounds and arrange them into a layered piece of music.

Students program a character to travel across several scenes and face a challenge such as getting lost, meeting someone new or learning an unfamiliar skill. The sequence shows that journeys can change direction and lead to new understanding. Students exchange projects and choose what the travelling character should do at one decision point. The creator then adds or changes code so the character's actions match that choice. Each pair finishes with an animated journey story that has a clear beginning, challenge and learning moment. ScratchJr's blocks let young students sequence movement, scene changes and character actions.

s.t: Journey Map Movers: Rolling Story Trails
s.d: Students design and build a 3D rolling map that traces a personal or family journey using large sheets of cardboard, recycled tubes, craft paper, and found materials to create mountains, rivers, and landmarks from their stories. They craft a 'journey cart' or small vehicle from bottle caps and boxes, then use simple push-and-go Sphero Indi robots to help their carts travel along the map's path. As they build, students decorate key stops with artefacts and story prompts, connecting physical movement with narrative milestones. This hands-on adventure helps students reflect on how journeys shape identity and place through collaborative making and imaginative storytelling.

ci: The way we interact with others is influenced by who we are
lo: Personal identity and strengths; How self-regulation supports learning; Building resilience through knowledge of ourselves

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a character explaining one personal strength, one calming strategy and how these affect the way they treat others. This makes the link between identity, self-regulation and everyday interactions easy to hear. A partner listens and asks one question that helps the speaker add a more specific example. Students then record a polished character clip for a class gallery of different voices and strengths. The automatic lip-sync turns each voice recording into an animated performance. Students finish by choosing one classmate's strategy they would like to try.

Students sort notes showing common classroom moments, feelings and calming strategies on a shared Freeform board. They work out that different people may need different ways to become ready to learn. Each pair connects one challenging moment to several possible responses, then another pair adds a response they had not considered. The class ends with a visual map of choices students can use when learning feels difficult. Freeform's open canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their thinking changes. Students place a star beside a strategy they can practise independently this week.

Students compose a short piece of music that moves from unsettled to calm and ready to learn. They choose changes in sound, speed and volume that match how self-regulation can feel. Classmates listen with closed eyes and point to the moment when they think the music begins to feel calm. Each composer adjusts that moment after hearing the listeners' responses. Students end with a recorded musical sequence that can support a real classroom reset. GarageBand's tracks and loops make it possible to layer and refine the changing mood.

Students photograph a frame-by-frame story in which a small figure faces a setback, pauses, chooses a strategy and tries again. The sequence shows resilience as a set of actions rather than simply a positive slogan. Pairs swap unfinished animations and predict what helpful choice the character could make next. The creators then add an ending that responds to their partner's suggestion. Students produce a short stop-motion film with a clear problem, pause, choice and outcome. Stop Motion Studio joins the individual frames so small physical changes become visible steps in the story.

Students build a personal digital book with pages for their strengths, needs, calming choices and the person they hope to become. This helps them see how knowing themselves can shape their choices with other people. Each student invites a trusted classmate to suggest one strength they may not have noticed in themselves. Students add that new perspective and record a short response explaining whether they agree. The finished book is a multimodal self-portrait with words, images and recorded narration. Book Creator keeps these different forms of expression together in one readable book.

Students design and build a personalised 'Me-Bot'—a simple moving creature that represents their unique feelings, strengths, and calming strategies—using recycled boxes, craft materials, coloured paper, and markers. Each Me-Bot features a 'mood meter' dial and interchangeable face plates or accessories that students create to show different emotions or resilience strategies. Using Sphero Indi cars as the 'engines,' students test and refine how their Me-Bots move along a path they design, symbolising their personal journey and self-regulation choices. This hands-on project weaves together creative crafting and basic robotics, helping students explore and express 'Who We Are' in a playful, memorable way.

ci: Methods of communication have different features which impact their effectiveness
lo: The forms of verbal, non-verbal and visual communication; How the correct form enhances the effectiveness of a message; How people interpret messages and bring their own meaning to interactions

s.d: Students record body poses for messages such as stop, welcome, unsure and help, then train a model to recognise them. They test whether posture alone communicates clearly when facial expression and voice are missing. Groups swap models and try the same poses, revealing how different people can read one gesture differently. Pose recognition works in a similar way in accessibility tools that turn body movements into computer commands. Students improve unclear training examples after checking which gestures the model confuses. They finish with a working pose classifier and a list of changes that made each message easier to recognise.

Students compose three short pieces that communicate the same idea as joyful, threatening or calm. They change tempo, instrument sounds, volume and silence to find out which features shape the listener's interpretation. Another class listens without being told the intended emotion and records what each piece seems to say. Students revise one piece when the audience's response does not match their intention. They finish with three contrasting recordings that communicate without words. GarageBand lets students arrange, layer and edit their music in one place.

Students record and edit a silent film in which a simple message must be understood through gesture, framing and title cards. This shows how body language and visual choices can make a message clear, confusing or persuasive. Pairs exchange unfinished films and write what they think happened before seeing the planned storyline. Students then change one shot, gesture or title card to close the gap between intention and interpretation. They finish with a one-minute silent film and a short end title explaining the most effective communication choice. IMovie provides the titles, transitions and editing needed to complete the film.

Students hold a teacher-guided written conversation about ambiguous messages such as 'Fine.', an emoji by itself or a reply written in capital letters. They consider how tone, context and personal experience can change the meaning a reader brings to digital communication. The teacher sets the chatbot as a Socratic Tutor so it asks students to explain and reconsider their interpretations rather than giving them answers. Students compare selected responses with a partner and decide which extra words would make each message safer and clearer. They finish with a written conversation and three revised messages that reduce misunderstanding. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support in Schoolbox.

Students build a survey showing symbols, short phrases and visual signs, then ask another Year 3 class what each message means. The responses reveal which communication forms are widely understood and which depend on culture, experience or context. Students include one symbol they predict everyone will read alike and one they expect will divide opinion. They compare the live response charts with their predictions and discuss surprising differences. They finish with a survey, a set of response charts and an evidence-based recommendation for improving one unclear message. Microsoft Forms automatically collects answers and turns them into charts.

s.t: Secret Message Quest: Build & Break the Code Trail
s.d: Students design and construct a hands-on 'communication obstacle course' by creating physical stations—each featuring clues or challenges using different forms of coded expression, such as Morse code, Braille, pictograms, and gesture symbols. Using recycled boxes, cardboard, string, craft sticks, clay, and markers, they craft tactile puzzles or interactive props (e.g., a Braille message hidden in clay dots, a string-and-bead Morse code bracelet, or a pictogram decoder wheel). Incorporating simple robotics like Bee-Bots or Sphero Indi, students program paths that reveal or unlock hidden messages as bots travel between stations. This project immerses students in the evolution and diversity of communication, making them code-makers and code-breakers while emphasizing creativity, teamwork, and the power of expression.

ci: Ethical decision making supports online choices.
lo: How choice of action and reaction affects others online; How informed choices can make a positive difference; Our right to feel safe online and the responsibility to make ethical decisions

s.d: Students build a 3D online chat scene and code two possible reactions to an unkind message. This shows how one online choice can change what another person experiences. Classmates explore each scene, choose a response and explain which action is safer and kinder. Students revise any choice whose consequence is unclear after watching their classmates test it. They finish with an interactive 3D scene that shows two different chains of action and reaction. CoBlocks make objects and characters respond when a viewer selects an option.

Students hold a teacher-guided written conversation about what to do when a game chat, message or request feels unsafe. The chatbot asks open questions that help them work out their rights, responsibilities and possible choices. Students compare their reasoning with a partner, then return to the conversation and strengthen one answer. The teacher can include a genuine class dilemma, such as whether to forward an embarrassing screenshot. Students finish with a written conversation that explains a safe choice and why it protects others. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support.

Students record a short advice podcast answering a Year 2 student's question about an online choice. They explain how to pause, check facts, protect private information and ask a trusted adult for help. Another pair listens before publication and identifies any advice that could blame, embarrass or confuse the person asking. Students rerecord unclear sections so their words are safe as well as helpful. They finish with a polished audio episode that younger students can hear during a digital citizenship lesson. Canva supports recording and editing the whole podcast on an iPad.

Students sort short online scenarios across a shared board from safe and respectful to risky or harmful. They connect each possible action to the effect it could have on the sender, receiver and wider group. Groups then swap sections and add a safer response where they disagree with a choice. The class uses the board to agree on practical actions for blocking, reporting, saving evidence and seeking adult help. Students finish with a connected decision map that remains visible during the unit. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move, group and link ideas as their thinking changes.

Students make a choose-your-own-path digital book about a child facing online messages, rumours and requests for personal information. Each choice leads to a page showing how that action affects the child and other people. Students give the unfinished book to another pair, who follows one path and marks where the safest action is not obvious. Writers then improve the wording and add a clear point for getting help from a trusted adult. They finish with a narrated digital story that can be read by families together. Book Creator combines text, images and recorded narration in one book.

Students design and build a vibrant, walkable 'park' using cardboard, recycled materials, and craft supplies, where each pathway represents different online choices and their outcomes. Along the paths, students place interactive QR codes (created on iPads) that link to short, student-made videos or comics about safe and ethical online behaviour. Sphero Indi cars are programmed to follow chosen routes through the park, visually demonstrating how each decision can lead to positive or negative scenarios for digital citizens. This hands-on project helps students physically map out the impact of online actions, reinforcing their responsibility to make ethical choices and keep themselves and others safe online.

ci: Materials behave and interact in certain ways, which poses challenges and solutions
lo: The three states of matter and their properties; How matter changes states depending on particles, temperature and energy; Responsible and ethical use of materials like glass and plastic

s.d: Students build two versions of a Melbourne neighbourhood, one before a natural disaster and one redesigned with safer, more responsible material choices. They use what they know about glass, plastic, water and building materials to explain why each block represents a suitable material. Teams visit one another's worlds and test whether roads, shelters and recycling areas would still work after a flood or earthquake. They leave signs beside key structures to explain choices such as raised floors, protected glass and places to collect reusable plastic. Students then rebuild one weak part after receiving a practical suggestion from another team. The finished world is a walk-through model showing how material choices can create challenges or solutions.

Students photograph small balls or counters frame by frame to show particles in a solid, liquid and gas. Moving the pieces closer together, faster or further apart helps them show how temperature and energy change matter. Pairs swap unfinished animations and work out which state or change is being shown before the title appears. They revise any movement that gives the viewer the wrong scientific idea. The finished short film shows melting, freezing or evaporation through a clear particle model. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame playback makes changes that cannot normally be seen visible and easy to discuss.

Students record a narrated explanation while drawing what happens inside an ice cube as it melts and later evaporates. They connect particle movement, temperature and energy instead of only naming the three states of matter. Each student pauses halfway through and asks a question for a partner to answer in the next part of the recording. They replay their explanation and correct diagrams or words that suggest particles disappear. The finished screencast combines moving drawings, labels and the student's own scientific explanation. Explain Everything records the screen and voice together, so the teacher can hear how each idea develops.

Students explore terrain and population layers to locate communities that may face greater challenges during floods or other natural disasters. They consider how roads, buildings, glass, plastic and waste systems can affect a community's safety and recovery. Groups compare two places and choose where stronger structures, safer material storage or recycling services may matter most. They annotate the map with short evidence-based recommendations rather than guessing from a single view. The finished labelled map links real geographic conditions with practical material choices. MapMaker's adjustable data layers let students check whether their first idea still makes sense when new information is shown.

Students design an infographic that follows one glass jar or plastic bottle from manufacture to use, disposal and possible reuse. They explain how the material's properties make it useful while also creating environmental challenges. Each student chooses a real audience, families, the canteen or another Year 3 class, and writes one action that audience could genuinely take. Partners check whether each claim separates reducing, reusing and recycling clearly. The finished infographic combines a material life cycle, a balanced judgement and a practical recommendation. Adobe Express provides a clear poster layout for arranging short text, icons and images.

s.t: Matter Morphers: Transforming Transport Rescue Bots
s.d: Students design and build their own rescue vehicle using recycled materials (boxes, bottle caps, straws, fabric scraps), exploring how different states of matter (solids, liquids, gases) could affect its function during a simulated natural disaster. They'll integrate simple robotics by attaching a Sphero Indi or similar programmable base, coding it to navigate a handmade disaster obstacle course (e.g., 'flooded' zones with blue cellophane, 'earthquake' rubble from foam blocks). This hands-on project connects science concepts of matter and responsible material use with practical engineering and digital skills, challenging students to iterate their designs for real-world resilience. The result is a creative, memorable blend of physical making and tech that brings disaster adaptation to life!

ci: People can respond to natural disasters with resilience
lo: The causes and types of natural disasters (tectonic events, weather events); How natural disasters impact the environment and people; How humans respond with resilience and connection

s.d: Students build paper models of an earthquake, cyclone or flood and photograph each small change in Stop Motion Studio. This shows both how a natural disaster develops and how people can respond with resilience. Groups swap unfinished animations and work out which response should happen next. They add an ending that shows people reconnecting, rebuilding or reducing future harm. Each group produces a short frame-by-frame explanation of cause, impact and response. Onion-skin guides help students move each model in small, consistent steps.

Students enter teacher-provided data about the number of homes, roads, habitats or people affected by several natural disasters. Comparing the data helps them see that different hazards can affect communities and environments in very different ways. Each pair chooses the graph type that makes one important pattern easiest for another Year 3 class to notice. Partners then swap graphs and check whether the visual evidence supports the written claim. Students finish with a labelled table, graph and one evidence-based statement. Excel turns the same class data into charts that can be compared and revised.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short explanation spoken by an animated emergency radio, rescue vehicle or disaster-prepared home. Giving a useful object a voice helps them explain how preparation and connection support resilience. Students choose a specific audience, such as younger children, pet owners or families living near the coast, and adjust the advice for them. Classmates listen and identify one action that could reduce harm before, during or after a disaster. Each student finishes with a brief animated public-safety message. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the chosen character to the student's recorded voice.

Students code Sphero BOLT to carry a small paper supply symbol through a floor route blocked by model floodwater, fallen trees and damaged roads. The route shows why reaching people after a natural disaster can require careful planning and repeated problem-solving. Groups exchange courses, then debug their programs without moving the obstacles. They compare which routes are safe, short and able to reach the most isolated location. Each group finishes with a working coded route and a brief live demonstration. BOLT's programmable movement and 8x8 light grid can show travel and a simple arrival signal.

Students watch selected natural-disaster clips and pause to record evidence of causes, impacts and human responses. Looking closely at real examples helps them separate the hazard itself from the choices people make before and after it. Small groups receive different clips, so the class can compare tectonic events with weather events rather than all seeing the same example. Students identify one moment that shows resilience and explain what made the response effective. The class finishes with a teacher-led comparison chart based on students' spoken observations. ClickView provides curated educational video that can be paused and replayed for close analysis.

s.t: Rescue Rally: Rapid Response Robot Race
s.d: Students will design and craft a model landscape featuring a community struck by a natural disaster (such as flood, earthquake, or cyclone) using recycled materials, cardboard, and craft supplies. They will then build and decorate 'rescue vehicles' (using Sphero Indi or similar simple robots) to navigate the terrain, delivering tiny relief packages to marked 'safe zones'. The project challenges students to prototype both resilient structures and clever pathways, applying their understanding of disaster impacts and community response. Through testing and refining their creations, students explore teamwork, empathy, and how innovative design helps people share and protect our planet in times of need.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Many factors shape the development of cities.
lo: The essential features of a city; The function of a city; The development of cities through time

s.d: Students record 360-degree views of selected St Kilda streets, capturing buildings, transport, shops, parks and public spaces. The complete view helps them notice how many essential city features work together in one place. Groups choose one location they believe best shows why St Kilda developed as it did and explain their choice during a class viewing. They swap recordings and look for features their classmates noticed but they missed. Each group ends with an immersive street record and a labelled list of visible city functions. The spherical recording lets viewers turn in every direction and examine the whole setting.

Students build three versions of the same city block, past, present and possible future, in one Minecraft world. Comparing the builds shows how transport, housing, work, recreation and population needs can change a city through time. Another group visits the world and requests one change that would make the future block work better for children, older people or local workers. Students revise their design and place signs explaining the factors behind their biggest changes. Each group ends with a walk-through city timeline that can be explored from street level. Minecraft's shared building space makes large-scale construction and revision practical.

Students map the natural and human features that help cities develop, including coastlines, rivers, terrain, roads and population patterns. They switch between data layers to work out why cities grow in some places more easily than others. Each pair chooses a location for a new city and challenges another pair to find a serious weakness in that choice. Students revise their decision and annotate the map with evidence for essential services, transport links and likely growth. Each pair ends with a labelled city-location map supported by geographic evidence. MapMaker's terrain, population and other data layers allow students to test rather than guess.

Students sort and compare Dollar Street images of homes, streets, transport and everyday services from cities around the world. The photographs show that income, climate, culture and access to services can shape how urban life looks and works. Groups choose two homes at different income levels and discuss one city improvement that would make daily life easier without assuming every family needs the same thing. They exchange comparisons with another group and check whether their claims match what is actually visible. Each group ends with a carefully selected set of photo evidence and spoken explanations. Dollar Street arranges homes by estimated monthly consumption, making differences and similarities easier to examine.

Students collect class ratings for local city features such as footpaths, parks, shops, public transport, housing and community spaces, then enter the results in Excel. Turning the responses into graphs shows which city functions Year 3 values most and where opinions differ. Groups receive the same limited city budget and use the data to choose three features they would fund first. They compare decisions and explain why the same evidence led to different priorities. Each group ends with a data table, graphs and a short written funding decision. Excel's chart tools make patterns in the class data easy to see.

s.t: Time-Travel City Layers: Light-Up Mini Metropolis
s.d: Students use the Design Cycle to investigate how cities grow, then design, build, test and improve a stacked 3D 'city through time' using cardboard, popsticks, recycled packaging, clay, foil, fabric scraps and paper roads. Each layer shows a different stage of city development, such as early settlement, growing town and modern city, with essential features like homes, transport, water, green spaces, markets and community buildings. They add simple paper circuits with copper tape, coin batteries and LED lights to highlight important city functions, then compare how the lights and layouts change as needs change over time. The final build becomes a hands-on timeline model that helps students explain where people live, why cities are built, and how place changes across time.

ci: Health and wellbeing are impacted by the choices we make
lo: How our body systems connect and function; How our choices affect physical, emotional and mental wellbeing; Strategies to measure and maintain the health of the human body

s.d: Students program a Micro:bit to count movements during short bursts of walking, dancing and stretching. They compare what the counter records and discuss why movement supports the heart, lungs, muscles and mood. Each student chooses a realistic movement goal, then adjusts the program so the LED grid signals progress towards it. Partners wear and test each other's devices, checking whether different kinds of movement are counted fairly. Students finish with a working wearable activity counter and a short explanation of its limits. The built-in movement sensor, buttons and LED grid allow the device to measure, reset and display a count.

Students draw a body outline and record themselves explaining how the heart, lungs, brain, muscles and digestive system help one another. This makes the connections between body systems visible rather than treating each system as a separate fact. Partners swap recordings and add one question about what might happen when sleep, food, movement or hydration changes. Students revise their explanation so it answers the question with a clear cause-and-effect chain. They finish with a narrated body-systems screencast that can be played at a family information evening. Explain Everything records each drawing and annotation in time with the student's voice.

Students record examples of three poses, active movement, quiet breathing and screen posture, and train Teachable Machine to recognise them. They test how reliably it sorts new poses and work out why balanced wellbeing cannot be judged from one body position alone. Groups exchange models and deliberately test different angles, bodies and backgrounds to find weak spots in the training examples. Similar pose recognition is used by physiotherapy and sports-coaching apps to give feedback on movement, so students can discuss why varied examples matter. Students finish with a tested pose model and a list of changes that improved its accuracy. Teachable Machine lets them add more pose examples, retrain the model and immediately test the result.

Students post one evidence-based wellbeing strategy for sleep, movement, food, feelings or balanced screen use on Padlet. They explain which part of physical, emotional or mental wellbeing the choice may affect and avoid claiming that one choice works for everyone. Classmates respond with a respectful question or a practical variation that would make the strategy easier for another child to try. Each student then selects one peer suggestion to test safely for several days and adds a brief reflection. The class finishes with a shared wall of realistic strategies, questions and student reflections. Padlet keeps the posts and peer responses together so patterns and gaps are easy to see.

Students write Kahoot questions that challenge common claims about hydration, sleep, exercise, emotions and screen breaks. They include believable incorrect answers, which requires them to understand why a choice may help or hinder wellbeing. Groups exchange quizzes and flag any question that treats health advice as a guarantee rather than a general strategy. Writers revise unclear questions before running the quiz with another Year 3 class. Students finish with a class-built wellbeing quiz that also reveals ideas needing further teaching. Kahoot gives immediate answer results so the teacher can pause and discuss surprising responses.

s.t: Body Systems Superheroes: Wearable Tech Workshop
s.d: Students design and build their own wearable 'super suit' accessories that represent and support a healthy lifestyle—think heart-rate monitor wristbands, lung-power capes, or balanced diet badges. Using recycled cardboard, felt, LED stickers, Velcro, and craft supplies, each student chooses a body system to highlight and integrates simple tech like Makey Makey or micro:bit for interactive features (e.g., a button that lights up when 'exercising'). Throughout the Design Cycle, students research their chosen system, prototype their wearable, and reflect on how their creation supports wellbeing. This project empowers students to express 'Who We Are' through imaginative, hands-on making that links body systems, wellbeing, and personal agency.

ci: The creative process involves understanding and applying artistic elements to communicate ideas and emotions across disciplines
lo: How colour, movement and music communicate character and mood; The creative process of making a multi-disciplinary presentation; The effort and commitment required to produce a live performance

s.d: Students paint several Beijing Opera-inspired masks, changing only the colours to show different characters and moods. This makes the link between artistic choices, identity and emotion easy to see. Classmates view each mask without its title and explain what kind of character they think it shows. The artist then adjusts one colour choice after hearing these different readings. Students finish with a set of original digital mask paintings and a short colour key. Layers let them refine details without repainting the whole mask.

Students compose a short piece of music for a character entering, facing a problem and leaving the stage. They choose tempo, instruments and changes in volume to communicate the character's shifting mood. Another group listens without seeing the story and arranges three mood cards in the order they hear them. Composers use that response to revise any section where their musical message was unclear. Students finish with a polished character soundtrack ready for a live performance. GarageBand's virtual instruments and loops make it possible to test several musical choices quickly.

Students photograph and sort body poses that communicate emotions such as confidence, fear, anger and curiosity. This helps them examine how movement can reveal character before a performer says a word. Classmates test the trained model with new poses and look for movements the computer confuses. They then add clearer examples and retrain the model, learning that both performers and computers need precise visual signals. Students finish with a working pose-recognition model and a live demonstration of its strengths and mistakes. Similar pose recognition is used in physiotherapy and sports-coaching tools to check how people move.

Students record and edit one dramatic scene three ways, changing movement, pacing and shot order to create different moods. This shows how performance and editing choices can change the meaning of the same script. Each group screens its versions to another class, which votes on the clearest mood and explains the choice. Students use that audience response to tighten pauses, remove weak moments and select their strongest version. They finish with a short film that shows both the first cut and the improved performance. IMovie's titles, transitions and editing tools allow students to shape the finished scene in one place.

Students build a virtual stage for an original character and code objects to move when the viewer interacts with the scene. They use colour, space and movement to show a change in mood across the performance. Groups swap scenes and test whether the character's feelings are understandable without a written explanation. Creators then revise one movement or visual choice that gave viewers the wrong message. Students finish with an interactive 3D performance that classmates can explore. CoBlocks let them program how stage objects move and respond.

s.t: Mask Makers' Puppet Parade: Stories on Strings
s.d: Students design and craft vibrant, expressive puppets inspired by Beijing Opera masks and their own cultural identities using cardboard, fabric scraps, yarn, and recycled materials. They integrate simple movement mechanisms—like hinged jaws or movable arms—using popsticks, split pins, and elastic bands, then embed a micro:bit or similar device to trigger light or sound effects that match their puppet's mood. Working in teams, students script and perform short scenes that showcase how colours, movement, and digital elements communicate stories and emotions. The project fuses physical making with coding, performance, and reflection, encouraging deep exploration of personal and cultural expression.

ci: Not-for-profit organisations exist to respond to a variety of needs within our community
lo: The function and purpose of not-for-profit organisations; How not-for-profit organisations respond to community needs; Our responsibility to take action and make a difference

s.d: Students build a short survey asking families which local community needs matter most and what action they could support. They collect responses without asking for names or private details. This helps students see that not-for-profit organisations listen before deciding how to respond. Another Year 4 class can complete the survey and suggest one need the students may have missed. The class ends with real response charts that can guide its fundraising or advocacy choice. Microsoft Forms automatically collects answers and displays simple charts.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion about how a not-for-profit should use a limited donation. They weigh choices such as immediate help, long-term support, staff costs and community education. This shows why leaders need clear purposes and responsible decision-making. Students swap their strongest reasons with a partner, then return to the chatbot to test whether their choice still holds up. Each student finishes with a written decision and reasons they can bring to a class planning meeting. The teacher can set up the Socratic Tutor scenario to ask questions without giving students the answer.

Students record a short interview with a local not-for-profit worker, volunteer or school community organiser. They ask how the organisation identifies needs, divides roles and knows whether its work is helping. Hearing a real person's answers makes organisational structures and responsibilities easier to understand. Small groups choose one answer that should influence the class's own community action. They produce an edited podcast episode with an introduction, selected interview sections and a closing question for listeners. Podcasting using Canva lets students record and edit the episode on an iPad.

Students map every job, decision and handover needed to run a class fundraising or advocacy event. They connect roles such as communications, finance, logistics and community contact with arrows showing who needs information from whom. This makes an organisation's structure visible before the event begins. Groups exchange boards and look for missing responsibilities, repeated jobs or points where a plan could stall. Each group finishes with a clear organisational map that can stay open during the real event. Freeform's shared infinite canvas allows students to move, group and connect ideas as the plan changes.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a short explanation of one essential role inside a not-for-profit organisation. They explain what that person does, who they work with and what could happen if the role were missing. This helps students understand that community action depends on coordinated people rather than one leader doing everything. Each group chooses a different role, then the clips are shown together as an induction for the class's own action team. Students finish with a set of talking-character clips that clearly explain how the organisation works. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically lip-syncs an on-screen character to each student's recorded voice.

s.t: Pop-Up Pantry Planners: Build & Code a Community Food Network
s.d: Students design and construct a 3D model of a community food support network using cardboard, recycled boxes, string, and art supplies to represent local food banks, community gardens, delivery routes, and collection stations. Teams use Ozobots or Sphero Indi robots, programmed via color codes or block coding, to simulate the movement of food supplies between their crafted locations, solving challenges like efficient delivery and equitable access. This project immerses students in the organisational roles, teamwork, and logistics that not-for-profits use to respond to real community needs. Through the Design Cycle, students prototype, test, and refine both their physical models and robot solutions, reflecting on leadership, resource allocation, and collaborative action.

ci: Engineers design and build structures using specific features and materials to make them strong, stable and fit for purpose
lo: Different types of bridges and their design features; How materials and engineering principles contribute to structural strength and stability; Testing and refining designs through experimentation

s.d: Students photograph a model bridge frame by frame as it bends, twists and finally collapses under an increasing load. This makes hidden forces visible and opens questions about why particular shapes and materials keep bridges stable. Groups swap animations, pause before the collapse and predict which part will fail first. They then remake the final frames to show one design change that could prevent the failure. Each group ends with a short before-and-after animation explaining structural failure and improvement. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame playback makes tiny changes in the bridge easy to notice.

Students build a bridge across a fixed Minecraft span using a strict block limit and requirements for pedestrians, boats and safe access. The constraints show that a bridge must be stable, economical and fit for a particular purpose. Another group inspects the bridge, follows every route and leaves specific feedback about access, supports and wasted materials. Students revise their structure while keeping within the original block budget. They end with a working virtual bridge and a clear record of the changes they chose to make. Minecraft's shared building world allows students to inspect a structure from above, below and inside.

Students measure how much load several classroom bridge prototypes hold and enter each result into an Excel table. Comparing the results helps them work out how span length, material and structural shape affect strength. Groups exchange data so the class can test whether a pattern holds across many bridges rather than just one. Students use the evidence to choose one feature they would keep and one they would change in their next design. They end with labelled graphs that reveal which designs carried the greatest load. Excel's chart tools turn repeated test results into patterns students can see quickly.

Students program a Micro:bit to show a warning symbol when a model bridge tilts beyond a chosen point during testing. This links structural stability to a measurement rather than relying only on what the bridge looks like. Each group chooses its own warning threshold, tests it on several slopes and adjusts the code when the alert comes too early or too late. Students then place the programmed board on different bridge prototypes and compare how each structure moves as load is added. They end with a working tilt-warning device and a table of observations from repeated tests. The Micro:bit's built-in accelerometer detects movement and tilt while the LED grid displays the warning.

Students record a narrated bridge analysis while drawing arrows over a diagram to show compression, tension, load and support. This helps them explain why arches, triangles, cables and beams behave differently instead of simply naming bridge types. Partners exchange recordings and identify one force explanation that is clear and one point that needs stronger evidence. Students revise the explanation by redrawing forces and adding the result of a classroom load test. They end with a short screencast that connects a bridge's visible features to its strength and purpose. Explain Everything records students' voices and on-screen drawing together, so their thinking unfolds step by step.

Students work in teams to design and construct model bridges using materials like popsticks, string, rubber bands, and recycled cardboard, focusing on stability and innovative structures. Once built, they mount their bridges onto a simple, student-made 'shake table' (crafted from cardboard, marbles, and rubber bands) and use an iPad to record slow-motion videos of their bridge during simulated earthquakes. Teams analyse footage to identify design strengths and weaknesses, then iterate their creations for improved resilience. This immersive project connects engineering, material science, and real-world problem-solving, making the forces that shape our world tangible and memorable.

ci: First Nations people have a deep connection to Country, language and culture
lo: The diversity of language and culture across First Nations communities in Australia; The significance of connection to Country as custodial responsibility; Listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives

s.d: Students map First Nations language regions, major waterways and terrain across Australia using information from teacher-checked Indigenous sources. This shows that First Nations cultures and languages are diverse and closely connected with particular Countries. Groups compare different map layers and choose one place where water, landforms or climate may shape custodial responsibilities. They swap maps and check whether boundaries are described as living cultural regions rather than fixed borders. Each group finishes with an annotated map that includes language names, environmental features and careful source notes. MapMaker's geographic layers let students test how cultural and environmental patterns sit alongside one another.

Students identify local Victorian animals that live around the St Kilda campus and research what each species needs to survive. This grounds care for Country in the habitats and wildlife students encounter nearby. Each group chooses one animal and writes a practical care recommendation after considering habitat, water, food and human impact. Groups compare recommendations and decide which action the school community could realistically take. The class finishes with a set of species profiles and evidence-based care recommendations. The app's Victorian species information keeps the investigation local and specific.

Students build a narrated book that explains what respectful listening to First Nations perspectives looks and sounds like. This helps them separate learning from Indigenous voices from speaking on behalf of First Nations people. Students select short ideas from teacher-approved First Nations sources, paraphrase carefully and record why each idea matters for caring for Country. A partner listens to every page and checks that the language is respectful, specific and properly attributed. Each student finishes with a multimodal book containing text, images and their own spoken reflection. Book Creator keeps the written, visual and recorded parts together on each page.

Students collect class data about water use, waste or habitat features around the school and enter the results into a table. This gives them evidence for discussing how everyday actions affect Country and local ecosystems. Teams choose the clearest category to investigate, then compare patterns across locations or days instead of guessing where change is needed. They exchange charts and ask one question that the other team must answer from the data. Each team finishes with a labelled graph and one realistic recommendation for caring for the school environment. Excel's tables and charts make patterns and differences easy to see.

Students program a Micro:bit to count two categories of litter during a school-ground survey, using one button for recyclable items and the other for non-recyclable items. This connects custodial responsibility with careful observation and action in a place students use every day. Pairs exchange devices, test the counting instructions and debug any program that records the wrong category. They then use the finished counters to compare which area needs the most attention and choose one practical response. Each pair finishes with a working handheld litter counter whose LED grid displays the recorded totals. The two buttons, variables and 5x5 LED grid make the counting visible while students are outdoors.

s.t: Water Wise Wonderland: Interactive Creek Quest
s.d: Students design and build a flowing creek ecosystem using cardboard, recycled materials, natural elements (pebbles, sticks, leaves), and craft supplies, creating habitats for native animals and plants. They embed Ozobot robots decorated as 'water droplets', programming them to travel along painted or marker-drawn water pathways, simulating the journey of water through different habitats and human interventions (like dams, pollution, wetlands). Along the route, students engineer interactive features—liftable floodgates, filtering stations, and bridges—using simple mechanisms and recycled parts. This hands-on project blends environmental science, First Nations water knowledge, and creative engineering, helping students understand sustainable water management and the importance of caring for waterways.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Exploration and discovery have led to changes that shape the world we live in
lo: The age of exploration and the reasons explorers set out on their journeys; How Australia changed through European arrival; Different perspectives on the consequences of exploration

s.d: Students program Sphero BOLT to follow a scaled floor route based on an explorer's journey, including planned stops for supplies and hazards. This shows how distance, direction and limited resources shaped exploration and its consequences. Groups swap routes and try to debug each other's code without being told where the hazards are. Students then change one waypoint to represent a decision that could have altered who was affected by the journey. Each group ends with a working coded route and a short explanation of its key decisions. BOLT's motors, movement sensing and programmable light grid make the route visible and testable.

Students map an Age of Exploration voyage and annotate the places where arrival brought major change. This helps them connect explorers' reasons for travelling with consequences for people and places, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia. Each group chooses a different journey, then compares its route with another group's map to find shared patterns. Students add terrain, climate and population layers to work out why particular routes and settlements were chosen. They finish with a labelled map that separates evidence about the journey from evidence about its effects. MapMaker's layers let students test geographic explanations rather than simply view a static map.

Students interview a teacher-created historical character about European arrival in Australia and ask follow-up questions about motives, choices and consequences. This gives them practice examining how the same event can be described from different perspectives. Students compare two carefully configured character interviews and flag any claim that still needs checking against classroom sources. Each student chooses one answer to challenge and writes a stronger question that asks for evidence or another viewpoint. They finish with a written conversation and a list of claims to verify. The teacher controls the character instructions, discussion rules, timing and level of support.

Students build an interactive 3D scene showing one Australian place before, during and after European arrival. This makes change over time visible while allowing students to show that exploration had different consequences for different groups. Groups choose which voices, locations and changes their scene will include, using checked historical evidence rather than stereotypes. They code objects to reveal short explanations when a viewer interacts with key parts of the scene. Students finish with a virtual tour that classmates explore and question. Delightex's 3D building tools and CoBlocks allow objects to move and respond inside the scene.

Students record a short podcast that compares two accounts of the same exploration event or European arrival in Australia. This helps them hear how word choice, missing details and the speaker's position can shape a historical account. Pairs choose which perspectives to compare and invite another pair to identify what each account includes or leaves out. They revise one section after hearing that response so the contrast is clear and respectful. Students finish with an edited episode containing an introduction, two evidence-based accounts and a closing comparison. Podcasting using Canva lets them record and edit the complete episode on an iPad.

s.t: Exploration Adventure Automata: Moving Moments Diorama
s.d: Students work in teams to design and build a kinetic diorama that brings a key moment from the Age of Exploration or early Australian encounters to life. Using recycled cardboard, popsticks, gears, cams, craft materials, and simple motors or hand-cranked mechanisms, they create a scene where explorers, Indigenous peoples, and landscapes physically move to tell their story. Students integrate a micro:bit (or similar) to trigger sound effects or light signals that enhance the narrative, blending historical research with creative engineering. This project encourages deep understanding of multiple perspectives and the impact of exploration, while making history literally move before their eyes.

ci: Leaders can help a group to function effectively
lo: Roles and responsibilities of effective leadership; Purpose of leadership; The strengths and qualities of a leader

s.d: Students record a group solving a tricky classroom decision, placing the Insta360 camera in the centre so every member can be seen. They watch the 360-degree recording and notice how leaders invite ideas, explain responsibilities and help the group move forward. Each group chooses one moment to revisit from several viewpoints and discusses whose voice was heard or missed. They record the decision again after changing one leadership behaviour. The class ends with paired before-and-after recordings that show how leadership choices affect a group. The 360-degree view lets students look around the whole discussion rather than seeing only the person holding a camera.

Students post examples of effective leadership from school, sport, books and community life on a shared Padlet wall. They sort the examples by purpose, responsibility, strength or quality and explain their choices in short notes. Another Year 4 class responds by naming the leadership quality they can see and asking one question. Students then revise one post when a response changes or sharpens their thinking. The finished wall becomes a growing bank of leadership evidence that can support later discussions and assessment. Padlet keeps notes, images, links and peer responses together in one shared space.

Students design a short leadership campaign for a positive change they want to make at school. They explain the change, the leader's purpose, the jobs a team would need and the personal strengths that would help. Students choose a real audience such as classmates, teachers or the Junior School Council and adjust their words for that group. Peers test each campaign by stating the action they think the leader wants them to take. Each student finishes with a clear poster, infographic or short promotional video. Adobe Express provides simple layouts for combining brief text, images and visual emphasis.

Students write short decision questions that ask what an effective leader should do in realistic group situations. Each question explores a responsibility such as listening, delegating, resolving disagreement or changing a plan. Groups swap quizzes and must explain why an answer is effective rather than relying only on the score. Students improve any question that produces confusion or more than one reasonable answer. The class ends with a student-made leadership quiz that can be used as a formative check. Kahoot gives immediate responses that help the teacher spot ideas needing further discussion.

Students create a visual profile showing how one leader's strengths match the needs of a particular group. They include evidence of the leader's choices, responsibilities and purpose rather than listing flattering adjectives. Each student then receives a different group challenge and adapts the profile to show which qualities would matter most in that situation. Classmates compare the two versions and point out how effective leadership changes with context. Students finish with a paired set of infographic panels suitable for a classroom exhibition. Canva makes it easy to arrange concise text, images and headings in a clear visual sequence.

Students design and construct a 3D maze representing their unique leadership journey, using cardboard, recycled boxes, string, and craft materials to build pathways and obstacles that symbolise personal strengths and challenges. They then code a Sphero Indi or similar robot to navigate the maze, with each section representing a leadership quality or decision point. Students decorate their maze with symbols, photos, and words that reflect their identity and leadership style, creating a physical and digital narrative of 'Who We Are'. The project integrates hands-on building, creative self-expression, and basic coding, making leadership personal, memorable, and interactive.

ci: Social norms and stereotypes can influence the way people express themselves
lo: How stereotypes and social norms form and persist in society; The impact of discrimination, prejudice and assumptions on individuals and communities; How people overcome stereotypes to express themselves and inspire change

s.d: Students train a pose model to recognise three body positions they think show confidence, then test it with classmates who express confidence differently. They see how stereotypes can form when a narrow set of examples is treated as the rule. Another class tests the model without being told which poses were used for training. Students end with a working classifier that sometimes gets people wrong and clear examples of why its training data matters. Teachable Machine lets them add new pose examples and retrain the model immediately. This works like pose-recognition systems used in accessibility, physiotherapy and sports-coaching apps, where limited training examples can also exclude people.

Students build an anonymous survey using short fictional situations about clothing, hobbies, jobs and ways of speaking. The responses show how group assumptions can persist even when nobody openly teaches them. Students send the survey to another Year 5 class, then choose one surprising result to discuss with that class. They end with auto-generated charts showing which stereotypes were common and which were challenged. Microsoft Forms collects every response in one place and creates charts automatically. Students revise one leading or unfair question after checking how its wording may have shaped the answers.

Students interview a teacher-set chatbot character based on a verified profile of a person who challenged stereotypes through art, activism or personal expression. Their questions explore the barriers the person faced, the choices they made and the change they inspired. Students swap transcripts and identify where two interviewers received different ideas because they asked different questions. Each student ends with a written conversation and a short reflection on one assumption they had to reconsider. The teacher controls the character information, discussion rules, timing and level of support. Students use the conversation to plan a stronger question they would ask the real person if they could.

Students compose two short pieces for the same identity statement, one showing pressure to fit a social norm and one showing freedom to challenge it. This lets them explore how music can communicate discrimination, resistance and self-expression without relying on appearance. Classmates listen without titles, explain what they assumed, and then hear the composer's intended message. Students end with a paired audio composition that can play beside their physical exhibition work. GarageBand lets them arrange musical loops, record original sounds and adjust layers within one project. They revise one section after listeners explain where the message was unclear or stereotyped.

Students build an interactive 3D scene showing a character facing a stereotype and two possible responses from the surrounding community. The scene makes the effects of assumptions visible through spaces, choices and consequences rather than a written definition. Another group explores the scene and chooses a path before the creator explains the intended message. Students end with a coded virtual scene that can be opened as part of the class exhibition. Delightex lets them use block coding so objects move or respond when a visitor interacts with the scene. Students test whether both paths work and revise any moment that makes the message confusing.

s.t: Wearable Voices: Message Maker Fashion Lab
s.d: Students design and construct expressive wearable art pieces—such as hats, capes, or badges—using recycled fabrics, LEDs, conductive thread, and simple microcontrollers (like Micro:bit or Circuit Playground Express). Each wearable broadcasts a personal or social message through patterns, scrolling text, or light effects coded by the students, reflecting their identities or challenging stereotypes. The project fuses hands-on sewing, crafting, and circuitry with digital coding, empowering students to literally 'wear' their stories and beliefs. The final showcase invites peers to decode each other's wearable messages, deepening understanding of how fashion and tech can be powerful tools for self-expression.

ci: Goods and services are exchanged within a marketplace
lo: The production of goods from raw materials through manufacturing to consumer; The exchange of currency for goods and services in a functioning economy; Ethics and responsible decision-making in the marketplace

s.d: Students run a class marketplace by entering each sale, cost, stock level and price into a spreadsheet. They can see how exchanging currency for goods changes profit, inventory and customer choices. Each business chooses when to change its price, then watches whether buyers move to a competitor. Students compare what happens when a popular item becomes scarce or a cheaper alternative appears. They finish with a working budget, sales table and graphs that show the story of their business. Formulas and charts update as new transactions are entered.

Students map the journey of a familiar product from its raw material source through manufacturing and transport to a Melbourne consumer. This makes the many places and services behind one marketplace item easier to see. Groups choose products with very different supply chains, then compare distance, terrain and population layers. They add labels showing where value is added, workers are involved and ethical questions may arise. Each group finishes with an annotated supply-chain map that supports a decision about whether the product should be sold. MapMaker's data layers let students test how geography can affect cost and access.

Students photograph and animate a product moving from raw material through manufacturing, packaging, sale and use. This slows down the production chain so every exchange and business role can be examined. Halfway through, groups swap animations and ask the creators to add one missing worker, cost or ethical choice. Students decide whether to show a responsible or irresponsible marketplace decision and animate its consequences. They finish with a short stop-motion film that explains how a product reaches a consumer. Frame-by-frame playback makes each stage of production visible.

Students record a narrated whiteboard explanation of an ethical marketplace dilemma, such as low prices supported by unfair wages. They draw the flow of money, goods and consequences while explaining who benefits and who carries the cost. A partner pauses the draft at the point where a business decision must be made and suggests a different choice. Students then revise their reasoning and show how that choice changes the outcome for workers, owners and consumers. They finish with a clear screencast that compares two possible decisions. Explain Everything records their voice while they draw and annotate on screen.

Students program a micro:bit to model changing prices when supply or demand rises and falls. Button A changes supply, Button B changes demand, and the LED grid displays a price or simple symbol. This turns an abstract economic relationship into a system students can operate, test and debug. Groups exchange devices and try to work out the pricing rule from the outputs they see. They finish with a working interactive model and a short live explanation of when its price changes. The buttons, variables and LED grid allow the whole simulation to run on one battery-powered board.

s.t: Supply Chain Showdown: The Automated Assembly Line Challenge
s.d: Students work in teams to design and build a miniature, multi-stage assembly line using recycled materials, cardboard, LEGO, and simple robotics (such as Sphero Indi or Ozobot) to transport and transform 'products' across stations. Each team creates stations (e.g., manufacturing, packaging, quality control, distribution) with physical mechanisms like ramps, levers, conveyor belts (rubber bands, popsticks, pulleys), and programs robots to move goods between them. Students must budget for materials, negotiate resource trades with other teams, and reflect on ethical dilemmas (e.g., fair wages, sustainable sourcing) as their assembly line grows. This hands-on project brings economic systems, supply and demand, and marketplace ethics to life through dynamic prototyping and collaborative problem-solving.

ci: Inventions and initiatives are a response to the changing needs of society
lo: How inventions have changed over time to meet the demands of society; The UN Sustainable Development Goals and the global problems they address; Using the design thinking process to create innovations that respond to real-world needs

s.d: Students draw and narrate how one invention changed as society's needs changed, revealing each improvement one step at a time. This shows that inventions are rarely finished ideas and often grow through repeated problem-solving. Students swap recordings and add a final question about the need that might drive the invention's next change. Each student then revises the last frame to show a possible future version linked to an SDG. They end up with a narrated visual timeline that moves from an early invention to a future redesign. Explain Everything records their voice and screen while they draw, move and annotate ideas.

Students build two versions of a Melbourne neighbourhood, one that struggles with a chosen social or environmental problem and one redesigned to address it. This makes the link between changing community needs and new infrastructure easy to see and discuss. Each team gives another team a tour, then receives one request from a resident's point of view and changes its design. Students must show how their solution supports a specific UN Sustainable Development Goal through visible features in the world. They end up with a walk-through model of a future neighbourhood and a clear before-and-after comparison. Minecraft Education lets teams build at full neighbourhood scale and test whether people can move through and use their design.

Students design and run a survey to find a real problem experienced by children, families or staff at Wesley College. This places people's needs before invention ideas, as required by the design thinking process. Students choose which survey result is important enough to guide an invention rather than simply selecting the most popular answer. They send a short follow-up survey later, asking whether their proposed solution would actually help. Each team ends up with a set of responses and automatic charts that support a precise design brief. Microsoft Forms collects all responses in one place and turns them into charts immediately.

Students program a Micro:bit device that responds to a chosen need, such as a light-level warning, movement reminder or radio alert between two locations. This shows how sensors, buttons and coded rules can turn an idea into a useful invention. Teams exchange devices without instructions and test whether another person can work out what each signal means. Students then debug the code or redesign the LED messages after watching the user test. They end up with a working battery-powered prototype and a record of the changes that made it clearer or more useful. The Micro:bit's LED grid, buttons, light sensing, movement sensing and radio link provide practical inputs and outputs.

Students interview an invented future user inside a multimodal book, using recorded questions and answers to explain a problem linked to one SDG. This helps them consider what a person might need before deciding what to invent. Another class listens to the interview pages and leaves one recorded request that the proposed invention must meet. Students add sketches, labelled explanations and a final page showing how the idea changed after that feedback.
