They end up with an illustrated and narrated design story ready for the Future Thinkers' Forum. Book Creator keeps text, drawings, images and voice recordings together in one book.

s.t: Inventors' Circuit Carnival: Power Up Your Problem-Solver
s.d: Students design and build imaginative, hands-on carnival games that solve a real-world challenge (e.g., recycling, clean water, renewable energy) using a mix of recycled materials, cardboard, motors, LEDs, and conductive tape. They sketch ideas, prototype physical game mechanisms, and wire up simple circuits with Makey Makey or micro:bit boards to add interactive features like buzzers, lights, or digital scoring. Throughout the process, students follow the design cycle to iterate and improve their inventions, learning how past innovations inspire creative solutions for today. The final 'Circuit Carnival' lets students showcase and explain their powered-up games, linking invention, play, and the impact of design on society.

ci: Communities interact with the environment in different ways
lo: How community values shape the management of the natural environment; The need for conservation and environmental stewardship; Ways in which First Nations land management practices can drive positive environmental change

s.d: Students build two versions of a local coastal habitat, one shaped by heavy development and one cared for through conservation and teacher-provided First Nations land management principles. This shows how community values can lead to very different environmental decisions. Groups visit each other's worlds and leave signs explaining which choices protect water, plants, animals and culturally significant places. Students then revise one part of their world after hearing another group's reasoning. They finish with a walkable comparison model that shows the consequences of each management choice. Minecraft's shared building world makes large environmental changes easy to see and discuss.

Students identify Victorian animals that could live around St Kilda's coast, wetlands and parks. This helps them work out how human actions affect the habitats of local species. Each group chooses one animal and checks what it needs before judging a proposed change such as brighter lighting, tree removal or wetland restoration. Groups swap animals and test whether the same decision helps or harms different species. Students finish with a set of evidence-based habitat recommendations for local planners. The app's Victorian species information keeps the inquiry grounded in animals students may encounter nearby.

Students photograph and sort clean examples of recyclable, compostable and landfill items, then train an image model to recognise the three groups. This makes waste management a practical example of how community choices affect the environment. Groups exchange unfamiliar items and test where each model makes mistakes or shows uncertainty. They improve the training set by adding clearer and more varied examples rather than simply accepting the computer's first answer. Students finish with a working classification model and a record of the changes that made it more reliable. Camera-driven sorting arms in recycling facilities work in a similar way, learning visual patterns so materials can be directed into different streams.

Students record a 360-degree view of a St Kilda outdoor space where people, plants, animals and built features meet. This helps them notice that one place can be valued for recreation, habitat, culture and community use at the same time. Groups position the camera at contrasting points and invite another class to look around each view before choosing what should be protected or changed. They record a second view after physically marking a proposed conservation change with removable signs or objects. Students finish with an immersive before-and-after tour of a real local environment. The spherical recording captures the whole setting, including details behind and beside the camera that an ordinary photograph can miss.

Students sort teacher-provided evidence about fire, water, habitat care and seasonal knowledge onto a shared Freeform board. This supports careful study of how First Nations land management practices can improve environmental health without treating them as one single approach. Groups connect each practice to possible effects on plants, animals, waterways and communities, then ask another group to challenge one connection. Students revise their board using arrows, notes and images so every claim has clear supporting evidence. They finish with a connected visual explanation of how knowledge, values, decisions and environmental change influence one another. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students rearrange ideas as their understanding changes.

s.t: Wildlife Corridors: The Sphero Safari Challenge
s.d: Students design and construct intricate 3D wildlife corridors using recycled materials, cardboard, fabric scraps, and natural elements to represent real-world habitats fragmented by human development. Working in teams, they map out safe passageways for native animals, then code Sphero robots (decorated as local fauna) to navigate through their hand-built corridors, overcoming obstacles representing roads, fences, and pollution. The project connects deeply to 'Sharing the Planet' by highlighting the importance of habitat connectivity, Indigenous land knowledge, and conservation strategies. Students iterate on their designs using feedback, blending digital programming with physical prototyping to create memorable, hands-on solutions for wildlife survival.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Colonisation has had a lasting impact on different countries and their people
lo: The reasons, methods and impact of colonisation; How colonisation transformed society and culture; The responsibility of colonisers and the perspectives of those colonised

s.d: Students map colonising journeys to Australia and another colonised country, then annotate key landing places, settlements and areas of resistance. They compare routes with terrain and population layers to work out how geography shaped the methods and impacts of colonisation. Each group chooses one route, then swaps maps with another group to check whose perspectives and places are missing. Students revise their labels so Indigenous place names, colonised peoples and colonisers are all clearly identified. They finish with two annotated maps that show both movement across land and lasting change within it. MapMaker's geographic layers let students test ideas rather than simply viewing a static map.

Students record a short podcast that places two sourced accounts of the same colonial event beside each other. This shows how colonisation can be remembered differently by Indigenous people, settlers and later historians. Pairs choose which voices to include, explain whose account has often been given more attention and ask another class to respond. Students revise any wording that treats one perspective as the complete story. They finish with a carefully edited episode containing an introduction, evidence, comparison and closing question. Canva lets students record and edit the full podcast on an iPad.

Students sort teacher-provided colonial sources onto a Padlet wall under reasons, methods, impacts and perspectives. They add a short note explaining who made each source, when it was made and whose voice may be missing. Groups then respond to another group's choices and challenge one source that could give a one-sided account. Students decide whether to move, relabel or qualify each challenged source after reading the feedback. The class finishes with a shared evidence wall that can guide later research and writing. Padlet's posts and peer responses keep the evidence and discussion together.

Students design a scrolling web page showing how one place changed before, during and after colonisation. They combine short text, sourced images and clear headings to show changes to land, language, law, work and culture. Each student chooses one change that still matters today and adds a question for families or another Year 5 class to discuss. Partners check whether the page avoids presenting colonisation as progress experienced in the same way by everyone. Students finish with a concise visual history that makes cause, change and responsibility easy to follow. Adobe Express supports simple web pages that can combine images, text and sections.

Students edit a two-minute historical documentary that answers whether a chosen impact of colonisation has truly ended. They use teacher-provided source images, recorded narration, titles and quotations to connect a past event with evidence from the present. Groups exchange rough cuts and identify any claim that lacks evidence or any perspective that has been left out. Students then re-record or reorder sections so the documentary makes its reasoning clear. They finish with a short film suitable for a class screening and evidence-based discussion. IMovie's voice recording, titles and timeline editing allow the whole film to be assembled in one place.

s.t: Journey Jigsaw: Build & Code the Paths of Change
s.d: Students will design and construct a large, interactive 3D map representing the journeys and encounters between Indigenous Australians and early settlers. Using cardboard, fabric scraps, natural materials, and craft supplies, they'll create landscapes, waterways, and key meeting points, then embed Makey Makey or micro:bit sensors beneath key locations. Students will code these sensors to play audio stories, music, or facts when touched, allowing users to experience different perspectives and pivotal moments in Australia's colonisation. This hands-on project lets students physically and digitally explore how place, time, and movement shaped identity and culture, making history tangible and multi-sensory.

ci: Values, beliefs and actions contribute to a diverse society
lo: How our values and beliefs shape our identity and interactions; Our responsibility to manage emotions and be safe online and in person; The importance of resilience, respect and positive relationships in a diverse community

s.d: Students hold a written conversation about a playground or online disagreement and explain which values should guide each response. This shows how beliefs shape actions, relationships and personal responsibility. The teacher sets the chatbot to question easy answers, while students must consider how someone with a different viewpoint may feel. Students then swap one key question with a partner and return to the conversation with a stronger response. They finish with a saved discussion that shows how their thinking changed. The teacher can assess whether each student explains a respectful and safe choice rather than simply naming a value.

Students compare photos of bedrooms, meals and treasured belongings from homes at different income levels and locations. This helps them notice diversity without assuming that possessions reveal a family's values or happiness. Pairs choose two homes that challenge an assumption they held and explain the evidence visible in the photos. Another pair checks whether their explanation is respectful and based only on what can actually be seen. Students finish with three carefully chosen on-screen comparisons for a class conversation. Dollar Street's category and income filters make it possible to compare everyday life across many communities.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a character explaining how they handled an emotional or online conflict safely and respectfully. This makes the link between values, self-management and actions clear through a believable first-person voice. Partners exchange scenarios, so each student must voice a viewpoint that differs from their own. Students re-record any line that blames, stereotypes or ignores the other person's feelings. They finish with a short talking-character video that models a resilient response. Adobe Express automatically lip-syncs the on-screen character to the student's recorded voice.

Students build an interactive 3D scene showing a group chat, friendship problem or unsafe online request. This lets them explore how one choice can strengthen or damage trust and relationships. Students swap scenes and test each other's choices before suggesting a more respectful pathway. They then code objects to respond when a viewer selects different actions. Students finish with a playable 3D situation that shows consequences and a safe way forward. CoBlocks make the scene interactive through programmed movement and responses.

Students write scenario questions in which several responses sound reasonable but only one best protects safety, respect and relationships. This asks them to apply values and beliefs rather than recall definitions. Small groups trial one another's questions and challenge any answer that depends on an unfair assumption. Each group revises its wording and adds feedback explaining why the strongest response is responsible. Students finish with a class quiz built from authentic Year 5 social and online situations. Kahoot's timed question-and-answer format gives the teacher an immediate check of which choices need further discussion.

s.t: MyStory Shadowbox Robots: Moving Scenes of Me
s.d: Students design and construct a dynamic shadowbox diorama that represents a key aspect of their identity, values, or community connection. Using cardboard, recycled plastics, coloured cellophane, and craft materials, they create layered scenes, then integrate a simple programmable microcontroller (such as a Micro:bit or Makey Makey) to add interactive movement or light effects—like a motorized figure, glowing symbol, or shifting background—triggered by touch or motion sensors. The design process follows the full Design Cycle: students ideate, sketch, prototype, test, and refine their creation, reflecting on how their chosen elements express 'Who We Are'. The final showcase lets students narrate their stories as their shadowbox scenes come alive with tech-powered motion and light.

ci: Understanding global issues and using effective communication empowers us to raise awareness and inspire action.
lo: Global issues are caused by interconnected factors that require collective solutions (Causation) ? Presentations in the media can reflect the perspective of the author rather than the truth (Perspective) ? We must make responsible choices when responding to and creating media (Responsibility) ? Messages can be expressed through a range of mediums and elements can be adjusted to enhance effectiveness (Communication) ? Design choices contribute to the effectiveness of a message (Influence)

s.d: Students question a teacher-set Socratic Tutor about whether a viral media claim on a global issue should be trusted or shared. This shows how wording, missing evidence and an author's perspective can change what people believe. Students then swap one claim with another group and compare how the chatbot challenges their reasoning. They must revise their judgement when stronger evidence or a different viewpoint appears. Each student finishes with a written conversation that traces how their thinking changed. The teacher controls the chatbot's rules, timing and level of support.

Students collect claims, evidence, causes, viewpoints and possible actions for their chosen global or local issue on a shared Freeform board. Connecting these items helps them see that global issues rarely have one cause or one solution. Groups invite classmates to mark weak links, missing voices and claims that need better support. Students reorganise the board until a visitor can follow the issue from cause to possible action. Each group finishes with a clear evidence map that can guide its Exhibition campaign. Freeform's infinite canvas lets students move, group and connect ideas as their inquiry develops.

Students build and run a short survey to find out what their audience knows, believes and would be willing to do about a chosen issue. Real responses help them choose messages that inform rather than assume, exaggerate or manipulate. Each group tests two differently worded questions and compares whether the wording changes the answers. Students use the results to decide which fact, viewpoint and action their campaign should emphasise. They finish with a survey and a set of response charts that provide evidence for their design choices. Microsoft Forms automatically collects responses and displays charts for quick analysis.

Students build two interactive 3D scenes that communicate the same global issue from contrasting perspectives. Comparing the scenes makes it clear that choices about setting, scale, objects and sequence can influence an audience. Groups exchange scenes and identify what each creator has highlighted, reduced or left out. Students then code one object in each scene to move or respond so the audience must explore before deciding what to believe. They finish with a virtual experience that reveals how media makers shape a message. Delightex provides 3D scene building and CoBlocks for coding object behaviour.

Students compose a 20-second campaign jingle or soundscape that encourages action on their chosen issue without using spoken explanation. This makes them consider how pace, repetition, silence and sound can influence emotion and attention. Another group listens without seeing the campaign brief and explains what issue, mood and action the music suggests. Students revise any section that sends an unintended message or overwhelms the purpose. They finish with a polished audio track that can open or close an Exhibition presentation. GarageBand lets students arrange recorded sounds and musical loops into a finished composition.

s.t: Light-Up Advocacy Parade: Message Lanterns in Motion
s.d: Students design and build expressive, hand-crafted lanterns using recycled bottles, tissue paper, wire, and LED circuits (simple soldering with supervision) to visually communicate their chosen advocacy message or global issue. Each lantern incorporates symbols, slogans, and design elements that reflect their research and campaign goals, integrating both artistic flair and persuasive communication. Students then choreograph a moving parade route for their lanterns, using programmable Sphero robots as mobile bases, and present their glowing creations in a collaborative exhibition. This hands-on project fuses physical making, circuitry, and robotics, empowering students to illuminate their voices and spark dialogue around meaningful causes.

ci: The way a country is governed impacts the lives of citizens.
lo: The key institutions and functions of Australia's democratic system of government (Function) ? How government decisions impact citizens at federal, state and local levels (Causation) ? The rights and responsibilities of Australian citizens and their obligations as global citizens (Equality/Citizenship)

s.d: Students draw and narrate how a proposed law moves through the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Governor-General. They add branches showing how the law could affect different citizens at federal, state and local levels. Pairs swap proposals and mark where public debate, voting or review could change the outcome. Each pair then revises its explanation after checking the roles of the institutions involved. They finish with a narrated screencast that follows one decision from proposal to impact. Explain Everything records their voice and screen while they draw, move and annotate each step.

Students build a survey asking families and staff which local, state and federal issues matter most to them. This shows how governments need evidence about citizens' needs before making decisions. Groups choose one fair question each and avoid collecting names or other personal information. They compare the automatic charts and discuss which level of government could respond to each priority. The class ends with a set of survey results that can support a realistic civic proposal. Microsoft Forms collects responses and turns them into charts automatically.

Students train an image model to sort printed photographs of public services into local, state and federal government categories. This makes them check who is responsible for services such as rubbish collection, public schools and national defence. Groups exchange photo sets to find examples that confuse their models, then retrain them with clearer and more varied images. Similar image recognition is used when council CCTV and emergency-dispatch systems identify vehicles or uniforms in camera footage. They finish with a working classifier and a record of the mistakes that helped them improve it. Teachable Machine lets students capture training images and test the model immediately.

Students record and edit a short news report about one government decision affecting citizens in Melbourne. They explain who made the decision, who is affected and what rights or responsibilities are involved. Each group includes two contrasting citizen viewpoints and asks another class to decide whether the report feels balanced. Students revise any section that presents opinion as fact or leaves out an important voice. They finish with a captioned news film suitable for a class screening. IMovie provides titles, transitions and video editing in one place.

Students write a quiz that challenges common mix-ups about Australia's Parliament, elections and three levels of government. This requires them to distinguish what each institution does rather than simply memorise names. Groups test one another's questions and reject any item that has an unclear answer or misleading wording. A partner Year 5 class plays the finished quizzes, giving Year 6 students a real audience to teach. Each group ends with a playable civic knowledge quiz and response data showing which ideas need clearer teaching. Kahoot gives immediate results after every question.

s.t: Parliament in Miniature: The Law-Making Board Game Build
s.d: Students will team up to design and construct a large-scale, interactive board game that simulates Australia's three levels of government and the journey of a bill becoming law. Using cardboard, recycled materials, paint, and craft supplies, they will physically build game boards, 3D government buildings, and creative playing pieces. They'll then use iPads to design and print QR codes or simple digital clues that trigger scenario cards or mini challenges, blending tech with tactile play. This hands-on project immerses students in the structures, roles, and decision-making processes of government, making abstract civic systems tangible, memorable, and fun.

ci: The relationships between the Earth, Moon and Sun create predictable patterns that shape life on our planet and are understood through both scientific and cultural perspectives.
lo: The movement of the Earth, Moon and Sun causes predictable patterns such as day/night, moon phases, tides and seasons (Causation) ? Different cultures, including Indigenous knowledge systems, interpret the night sky in unique and meaningful ways (Perspective) ? The Earth, Moon and Sun have specific structures, positions and relationships that can be represented through models and simulations (Form)

s.d: Students build a 3D Earth, Moon and Sun model and program each body to rotate or orbit. Moving the model helps them show why day, night, moon phases and seasons follow predictable cycles. Students choose one common misconception, such as seasons being caused by Earth moving closer to the Sun, and design the scene to correct it. Pairs swap scenes, follow the movement from different viewpoints and suggest one scientific improvement. Each team ends with an interactive simulation that includes labels and a short explanation. Delightex's block coding lets students adjust movement, timing and repetition as they refine the model.

Students enter teacher-provided monthly daylight data for Melbourne and turn it into a line graph. The changing values reveal the yearly pattern created by Earth's tilted axis and orbit around the Sun. Groups receive data from a different Southern or Northern Hemisphere location and work out why their graphs rise and fall at different times. They exchange graphs without location names and use the patterns to identify the likely hemisphere. Each group ends with an annotated graph and a written explanation supported by data. Excel makes it easy to change chart scales and compare several data series.

Students program a sequence of moon-phase images on the micro:bit's 5x5 LED grid. This shows that the phases repeat in a predictable order as the Moon changes position around Earth. Button A moves forward through the cycle, while Button B moves backwards so a partner can test any part of the sequence. Students swap devices, check the order and debug missing or unclear phases. Each student ends with a working handheld moon-phase guide. The programmable buttons and LED grid make the repeating pattern visible without needing a screen.

Students hold a teacher-guided written discussion that tests explanations for seasons, tides, day and night, and moon phases. The Socratic Tutor asks them to explain causes rather than simply name each pattern. Students choose one claim they initially believed and improve it as the questions expose gaps in their reasoning. Partners then read each other's discussion and identify the strongest piece of scientific thinking. Each student ends with a transcript showing how an explanation changed through questioning. The teacher can set the discussion rules, timing and level of support before students begin.

Students design an exhibition panel comparing a scientific explanation of the night sky with one teacher-curated Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander sky account. This shows that people can understand the same sky through scientific and cultural perspectives with different purposes and meanings. Students name the Nation or community, credit the approved source and avoid combining distinct knowledge systems into one general story. Another class views the panels and leaves questions for the creators to answer during a gallery walk. Each student ends with a clear visual panel using diagrams, short text and source credits. Canva's layout tools help students place the two perspectives side by side without suggesting that one replaces the other.

Students design and build intricate moving models (automata) that physically demonstrate the interactions between the Earth, Moon, and Sun—showing day/night, seasons, tides, and moon phases. Using cardboard, wooden dowels, gears, recycled plastics, and art materials, they construct layered scenes with rotating parts, then integrate micro:bit sensors or simple motors to animate their mechanisms. Teams prototype, test, and refine their automata following the Design Cycle, ensuring each model tells a story from both scientific and Indigenous sky knowledge perspectives. The result is a hands-on, visually stunning display that brings astronomical cycles to life in motion.

ci: Peoples' actions affect the balance of nature.
lo: What the environment is comprised of and how ecosystems function (Form) ? Our responsibility to care for and protect the natural world (Responsibility) ? The interdependence between humans, animals and the environment (Interdependence) ? The consequences of human actions on the balance of nature (Consequences)

s.d: Students build two versions of the same ecosystem, one balanced and one changed by roads, rubbish, farming or habitat clearing. This makes the consequences of human choices visible across the whole food web. Groups then exchange worlds and alter one feature to restore habitat without removing every human need. Classmates tour each solution and test whether animals can still reach food, water and shelter. Students end with a walk-through model showing damage, interdependence and a realistic conservation response. Minecraft's shared building space lets many parts of an ecosystem be changed and viewed together.

Students map the habitat of a threatened species and add climate, terrain and population layers to examine pressures on its survival. This shows how human communities, animals and environments depend on the same land and resources. Each group chooses one place where a wildlife corridor, protected area or changed human practice could make the greatest difference. Groups compare maps and challenge one another to justify that choice with visible evidence. Students end with an annotated conservation map that shows both the problem and a proposed response. MapMaker's data layers let students move beyond a static map and look for connections between real geographic patterns.

Students enter species counts or habitat observations gathered during the zoo visit, Camp Mallana or a school-ground survey into Excel. This helps them work out whether biodiversity is balanced or whether a few species dominate the area. Groups deliberately graph the same data in different ways, then decide which graph most honestly shows the environmental story. They exchange graphs and check whether another group reaches the same conclusion from the evidence. Students end with a table, chart and short written claim about the health of the observed ecosystem. Excel's formulas and chart tools make patterns and possible errors easier to spot.

Students photograph model animals or printed wildlife images and train Teachable Machine to sort them into categories such as local, introduced and threatened species. This opens discussion about how technology can support conservation while still making mistakes that people must check. Groups swap image sets and test whether each model can recognise examples it has never seen before. This works like image recognition in wildlife-monitoring cameras, where a computer sorts large numbers of animal images for researchers to review. Students end with a tested classification model and a record of which examples confused it. Teachable Machine lets students retrain the model with better or more varied images and immediately test whether its accuracy improves.

Students program a micro:bit to measure light levels at model nesting sites and show a warning icon when a site becomes too bright. This models how artificial light from human activity can disturb animals that need darkness for feeding, nesting or movement. Groups set different light thresholds for different species, then test one another's programs under changing classroom light. They debug the code when the warning appears too early, too late or not at all. Students end with a working habitat-monitoring device and a clear explanation of the conservation choice built into its code. The micro:bit's light sensing, LED grid and battery power allow the prototype to work away from the computer.

Students will design and build their own miniature 'Wildlife Rescue Rovers'—vehicles crafted from recycled materials, cardboard, and LEGO gears—that can navigate a custom-built, obstacle-filled habitat board representing real-world animal environments under threat. Using micro:bit controllers and simple sensors, students will program their rovers to detect and 'rescue' endangered animal tokens placed throughout the course. Teams will prototype terrain features like rivers, forests, and urban sprawl with mixed media, reflecting the challenges animals face due to human impact. This immersive project links hands-on engineering with digital tech, asking students to problem-solve and empathize with wildlife while exploring how innovative technology can support conservation in a changing world.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Human migration is a response to challenges, risks and opportunities.
lo: The causes for and consequences of migration (Causation) ? The changes in societies as a result of migration (Change) ? The impact of migration on the individual, both positive and negative (Impact) ? Migration results in a more diverse society (Diversity)

s.d: Students map a historical or contemporary migration journey and mark the challenges, risks and opportunities found along the route. They switch between population, climate and terrain layers to work out why people might leave one place and choose another. Pairs exchange maps and suggest one new piece of evidence that could strengthen the explanation. Students then revise their route so it distinguishes known evidence from reasonable conclusions. They end with an annotated migration map that explains both push and pull factors. MapMaker's geographic data layers let students test whether their first explanation fits the conditions along the route.

Students interview a family or community member about moving between countries, regions or neighbourhoods, then record selected parts of the story in Book Creator. This shows how migration can bring opportunity while also affecting identity, relationships and belonging. The interviewee chooses one detail, place or memory they feel is most important for readers to understand. Students combine careful writing, recorded narration and approved images while leaving out private information. They end with a multimodal biography that can join a class library of migration stories. Book Creator keeps text, images, audio and video together on each page.

Students examine homes, food, clothing and everyday objects from families living in two countries connected by a migration story. They look for differences caused by income as well as differences that may relate to place or culture. Groups compare choices and challenge any claim that treats one photograph as proof of how an entire country lives. Each group selects a small set of photographs and prepares spoken comparisons directly from the evidence on Dollar Street. They end with a teacher-observed visual comparison that separates economic conditions from cultural assumptions. Dollar Street arranges homes by estimated monthly consumption, helping students notice patterns that country labels alone can hide.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Students record a first-person migration monologue based on a researched historical account, using an animated character to deliver the words. This helps them explore how the same move can include fear, loss, hope and opportunity. A partner checks the script and asks the writer to replace one stereotype with a precise detail supported by research. Students revise the monologue so the character explains a difficult decision rather than simply listing events. They end with a short lip-synchronised character video for a class listening gallery. Adobe Express Animate from Audio automatically matches the character's mouth to the student's recorded voice.

Students draw and narrate a cause-and-effect chain showing how one migration movement changed both individuals and a receiving society. They connect each cause to consequences such as new businesses, languages, food, laws, tensions or community groups. Classmates pause the explanation and identify any arrow that needs stronger evidence or a clearer link. Students revise their diagrams and add a final section showing that consequences can be positive, negative or mixed. They end with a narrated screencast in which every claim is visibly connected to evidence. Explain Everything records the student's voice and on-screen drawing together, making their reasoning easy to follow.

s.t: Suitcase Stories: Interactive Migration Memory Boxes
s.d: Students design and build a physical 'memory box suitcase' representing a migrant's journey across time and place, using cardboard, fabric scraps, recycled materials, and small found objects to craft symbolic artifacts, landscapes, and personal treasures. Embedded inside the suitcase, students integrate simple circuits (LEDs, buzzers, or micro:bit with speaker) to illuminate or add sound to key artifacts when opened or touched, bringing stories to life. Each suitcase tells a unique migration narrative—real or imagined—highlighting push and pull factors, challenges, and cultural treasures. The project fuses storytelling, empathy, hands-on making, and basic electronics, allowing students to physically and digitally map the emotional landscape of migration.

ci: Understanding ourselves, our relationships and our wellbeing empowers us to thrive.
lo: The recognisable features of safe and healthy interactions (Form) ? The connections between emotions, behaviour, learning, interactions and goals (Connection) ? The tools and skills to stay safe online and in person (Safety) ? The active role we play in achieving and maintaining our wellbeing (Wellbeing) ? The strategies to achieve and maintain positive relationships (Relationships)

s.d: Students animate a common Year 6 interaction, such as being left out of a group chat, with one unsafe ending and one healthy ending. This makes the links between emotions, behaviour and relationships visible one small action at a time. Pairs swap unfinished animations and choose a respectful next move for the characters. Students explain how pausing, checking in or asking for help changes what happens next. They finish with a short animation showing the trigger, choice, consequence and repair. Frame-by-frame playback lets them adjust facial expressions, body positions and timing before publishing.

Students post short online-safety scenarios involving passwords, unwanted messages, screenshots, exclusion or pressure to share. They sort each scenario by the level of risk and add a safe action someone could take next. Another Year 6 class responds with one question or an alternative strategy, giving students a real audience beyond their friendship group. Students then revise any advice that is vague, blaming or unrealistic. The class finishes with a shared wall of practical actions for staying safe and seeking help. Padlet keeps scenarios, responses and revisions together where patterns can be compared.

Students record short interviews with classmates about ways people handle disagreement, stress, setbacks and changing friendships. This helps them hear that wellbeing strategies work differently for different people. Each student chooses one response that challenges their own assumptions and asks a respectful follow-up question. Small groups edit selected clips into an episode for families and the school wellbeing team. They finish with a podcast containing real voices, clear advice and a closing list of trusted support options. Canva supports recording and editing the whole episode on an iPad.

Students record 360-degree views of school spaces where belonging, privacy or safe interaction can be strengthened. Seeing the whole setting helps them notice how noise, sightlines, crowding and access can affect emotions and behaviour. Groups invite classmates to view each space and describe details the camera team missed. Students choose one realistic change, such as a quieter waiting point or a clearer place to seek help, and explain it during a second recording. They finish with paired 360-degree views that show the space before and after their proposed change. The spherical recording matters because viewers can turn around and inspect the full surroundings.

Students design a short online safety campaign that answers one difficult question, such as what to do when a friend asks them to keep an unsafe secret. This turns broad safety rules into clear choices that could be used in real life. Students test their first draft on younger students and note which message, image or instruction causes confusion. They revise the wording so it is calm, specific and free from blame. Each student finishes with a poster, infographic or short promo video that names the warning sign, next safe step and trusted support person. Adobe Express provides simple layouts for combining brief text and strong visuals.

Students design and construct a large-scale, interactive board game that explores real-life scenarios around wellbeing, digital safety, and positive relationships. Using cardboard, recycled materials, paint, 3D printed tokens, and craft supplies, teams create winding game paths, challenge spaces, and physical spinners or dice. They integrate simple Makey Makey circuits or micro:bit-powered buzzers/buttons to trigger digital prompts, reflective questions, or sounds when players land on key spaces. This hands-on project empowers students to collaboratively problem-solve, share strategies for managing emotions, and celebrate the diversity of the group — making abstract wellbeing concepts tangible, playful, and memorable.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time

s.d: Students use Seesaw to create a simple digital timeline of their lives, with teacher guidance. They take photos or draw pictures of themselves as a baby, a toddler, and now, then record their voices explaining each stage. This activity helps students sequence events and reflect on how they have changed over time, making connections between past and present in a play-based, age-appropriate way.

Students take a photo of a special family object or artefact using the iPad camera. Then, in ChatterPix Kids, they draw a mouth on the object and record a short message as if the object is telling its own story (e.g., 'I am Teddy. I belonged to you when you were a baby!'). This App Smash brings objects to life and encourages oral storytelling, supporting identity and belonging in a fun, creative way.

With teacher support, students use Puppet Pals to create a simple digital puppet show about their family or a special memory. They select characters and backgrounds, then record their voices to narrate a short story about something from their past. This playful, hands-on activity builds communication skills and helps students understand that everyone has a unique story worth sharing.

Students listen to a story about families or the past on Epic, then use PicCollage to create a digital collage about their own family. They can add photos, stickers, and drawings, and with teacher help, include a sentence about what makes their family special. This App Smash links reading and personal expression, helping students connect classroom texts to their own lives and histories.

Students use the insta360 camera to create a virtual 'Journey Jar' experience, capturing 360-degree scenes from different locations that represent key moments in their life stories, such as their home, favourite park, or a family celebration. Each child selects meaningful places or objects and, with teacher support, records short immersive videos that show what makes these moments special. The camera's all-around view helps students include family members, special items or environmental details that are important to their story. After filming, students add simple voice-over explanations about why each place or moment matters to them. The completed 360-degree journey jars are shared in a class showcase, helping students connect with each other's backgrounds and experiences. Teachers assess students on their ability to communicate personal history and connections through immersive storytelling.

s.t: Journey Jars: My Life Story Circuit Map
s.d: Students create a 'Journey Jar' diorama that tells their personal timeline using recycled jars, craft materials, and family artefact miniatures (drawn or modeled from clay). Each scene in the jar is connected with colourful paper 'timeline bridges' and simple LED sticker lights (with adult support) to highlight key life events. Children map out and sequence their stories, then use a Sphero Indi robot to travel along a large collaborative floor map, stopping at each jar to share and celebrate their unique journeys. This hands-on project blends crafting, basic circuitry, and robotics to help students see how their past shapes who they are today.

ci: Our experiences shape the way we grow and change over time
lo: Our community includes the people, places and environments that we visit and interact with.; Interactions and relationships within our communities can influence our growth and change over time.

s.d: Students photograph a treasured family object in Book Creator and record a short explanation of where it goes with them. This shows how people, places and experiences become part of who they are. Families can add a story about how the object or child has changed over time, with the teacher recording their words. Children handle each object, listen together and notice connections between the stories. The class ends with a narrated digital book about identity, family and belonging. Book Creator keeps the photographs and recorded voices together on each page.

Children build a shared picture map in Freeform showing places where they feel safe, welcome and connected, such as home, kinder, a grandparent's house or a local park. With teacher support, they add photographs, drawings, stickers and simple marks to represent paths between these places. Children move and resize items on the infinite canvas as they explain who they meet and what they do there. The group notices places that appear on several children's maps and respectfully discusses places that are special to particular families. Lines and arrows reveal how daily journeys connect people across the local community. The finished collaborative map becomes a visual conversation about identity, place and belonging.

Students act out a true story about a time when a family member, friend or educator helped them learn something new. This makes the influence of relationships visible through children's own experiences. Children first rehearse the story with their bodies and classroom props, then choose puppet characters and direct the teacher's recording. Another group watches and suggests one kind response a character could add. Each group ends with a short narrated puppet show about care, help or belonging. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and children's recorded voices in one scene.

Children take a supervised neighbourhood nature walk and use Seek by iNaturalist to investigate living things that belong in the local environment. They carefully observe plants, insects and birds near kinder, using the live camera identification feature with an adult to discover possible names. The group collects sightings rather than specimens, noticing examples such as gum trees, ants or native birds. Children compare where each organism was found and discuss how the place changes across weather and seasons. Seek's observation badges make repeated noticing feel like a gentle nature hunt while encouraging care for Country. Back together, children recall one living neighbour that helps make Glen Waverley feel like home.

Children create a short stop-motion sequence showing something they can do now that they could not do when they were younger, such as building a taller tower, putting on a coat or joining a group game. They arrange familiar objects or clay figures, move them a tiny amount and capture each frame with teacher guidance. Stop Motion Studio's onion-skin guide helps children see where an object was positioned before taking the next image. Children sequence a beginning, a helping moment and a successful ending to show how change can happen through practice and relationships. They replay the animation, spot any sudden jumps and retake frames where needed. Each silent mini-film becomes a concrete reflection on growth, persistence and the people who help us.

Children create big, friendly portraits of their families using paper plates, fabric scraps, yarn, and cotton wool for hair and features. With help, teachers add simple LED sticker lights (like Chibitronics) behind the eyes or smiles, so each portrait lights up when touched. The class displays their glowing faces in a gallery, celebrating everyone's unique family and identity. This hands-on project blends creative making with gentle technology, helping children share who they are in a bright, joyful way.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Our experiences shape the way we grow and change over time
lo: Our community includes the people, places and environments that we visit and interact with.; Interactions and relationships within our communities can influence our growth and change over time.

s.d: Students choose a familiar object from home or kinder, handle it, and record it talking about a community experience. A worn shoe might describe walks to the park, while a lunchbox might recall meals with family. Children tell the teacher what mouth to draw on the photo and speak the object's short message themselves. Families can send in an object with a story that matters to their child. The class ends up with a collection of talking objects showing how people, places and experiences help children grow. ChatterPix Kids makes each photo talk with a drawn mouth and a short voice recording.

Students arrange coloured tiles on the floor to make Indi travel between model community places built from blocks and loose parts. They explore how visits to kinder, a park, a shop or a relative's home become part of their growing story. Pairs choose a place that matters to them, test a tile path to reach it and change the sequence when Indi goes elsewhere. Children then walk beside another pair's route and listen to why each destination was chosen. The class ends up with a large, changing floor map of meaningful community journeys. Indi follows the coloured tiles without an app or screen.

Students act out a real moment when another person helped them learn, feel safe or try something new, then record it as a puppet scene. This shows in a concrete way how relationships can influence growth and change. Children choose the characters and backdrop while the teacher helps move and record the puppets. Another group watches the scene and suggests what the helpful character could say or do next. Each group ends up with a short animated puppet show based on a community relationship. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and children's recorded voices.

Students stand in different parts of the room to show where home, kinder and favourite community places belong, then direct the teacher to draw and label them in Freeform. They decide which places should be close together and describe the people they meet there. Children add lines by directing the teacher, showing journeys such as home to kinder or kinder to the garden. Families can suggest one more meaningful place for the class to add and discuss. The class ends up with one growing visual map of places, people and relationships. Freeform's infinite canvas allows the map to expand as new experiences are added.

Students repeat a familiar hands-on action over several weeks, such as pouring water, packing away or putting on a coat, while the teacher records short Seesaw clips. Looking back helps children notice that practice, encouragement and experience can change what they can do. Children choose an older clip, repeat the action and say what feels different now. A trusted adult can respond with a brief memory of when the child first began learning that skill. Each child ends up with a simple before-and-now journal entry containing video and voice. Seesaw keeps photos, video and recorded reflections together in a student portfolio.

Children work together to create a giant, soft floor map of their local community using felt pieces, fabric scraps, paper houses, and cotton wool parks. Each child adds a 'stop' that is special to them—like their house, a favorite playground, or a family shop—decorating it with tactile craft materials. Using Sphero Indi cars, children then guide their vehicles along winding felt roads to visit these meaningful places, learning about each other's stories as they travel the map. This playful project helps children connect their personal journeys to the wider world and understand how everyone is part of the community.

ci: People use a range of materials and resources to express ideas and respond to provocations.
lo: How properties of materials influence what we do with them; Ways in which a range of materials can be used to express our ideas; How materials can be repurposed

s.d: Students press, roll, drag and stamp clay, leaves, corks and recycled packaging, then direct the teacher to paint matching marks in Brushes Redux. They compare which real materials make dots, lines, scratches or broad prints and how those marks can carry an idea. Each child chooses one mark to change in size, colour or position while classmates copy its movement with their whole bodies. The class then places the digital painting beside the material collection so families can hunt for the matching textures. Students end up with an original layered painting inspired by marks made with real materials. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting on separate layers, so the teacher can preserve each child's contribution.

Students build faces from leaves, boxes, fabric scraps and bottle tops, then record each creation explaining what it wants to become next. This helps children see that discarded materials can carry new ideas and meanings. A partner chooses one material to swap, and the child records a second message showing how the character's idea has changed. The talking creations can be played to another Kinder group before the physical faces are rearranged again. Students end up with a set of short talking-image recordings and a table of reusable loose parts. ChatterPix Kids makes a photograph talk when the teacher draws a mouth and records the child's voice.

Students sort natural and recycled materials by what they can bend, stack, tear, roll or scrunch, then record a short spoken observation for each group. This makes the link between a material's properties and what children can do with it easy to hear and see. Children invite a classmate to choose an unexpected material and suggest a new use for it. The teacher adds each child's photo, voice and chosen material to a shared class book. Students end up with a narrated book families can revisit alongside a basket of the featured materials. Book Creator keeps images, audio and video together on each page.

Students arrange sticks, fabric, foil, cardboard and lids into temporary pictures, then ask the teacher to photograph each arrangement inside PicCollage. This shows that the same loose parts can express many different ideas without being glued down or thrown away. Children swap material trays and rebuild a classmate's picture in their own way before a second image is added. The paired images invite families to notice what stayed the same and what changed. Students end up with a visual collage comparing two responses to the same materials. PicCollage places several photographs in one clear grid with short teacher-added captions.

Students choose a material creation, hold it, move it or demonstrate how it works while the teacher records a brief Seesaw video. Talking while touching the materials helps children explain ideas that may be difficult to put into words alone. A classmate watches the recording and asks the maker one simple question, which the teacher captures in a second voice recording. Families can respond with another possible use for one of the featured recycled materials. Students end up with a multimodal journal entry containing the creation, the child's explanation and a peer question. Seesaw can keep photos, video and voice together in a child's portfolio.

Children work together to build a magical forest using big recycled boxes, fabric scraps, paper leaves, and soft natural materials. Each child decorates a 'feelings tree' by adding branches, leaves, and face features that show how they feel, using craft materials and expressive marks. With teacher help, they record their voice describing their tree and feelings using a simple talking button or sound recorder, which is attached to their tree trunk. This hands-on project lets children express their emotions creatively through both art and sound, celebrating different ways we communicate and connect.

ci: Light and shadows change in a variety of ways.
lo: The use of light for different purposes; How light can be changed; The ways in which light changes to affect the world.

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles to send Indi through pools of torchlight, under cardboard arches and past standing blocks that cast shadows. They move the light or blocks and watch how Indi's shadow changes in size, direction and darkness. One group rearranges the route while another group predicts where Indi's shadow will appear. Children then test the new path by pressing Indi onto the first tile and watching closely. They end with a physical route that shows several ways light can be blocked or changed. Indi follows the coloured tiles without a screen, keeping the investigation active and hands-on.

Students photograph a torch, lamp or sunny window and record a short message explaining what that light helps people do. This makes the different purposes of natural and artificial light easy to hear in children's own words. Children choose an audience such as a family member, cleaner, gardener or night-time worker and speak directly to them. They end with a set of talking light sources for a family display. The teacher operates the app while each child draws the mouth and records one clear idea. ChatterPix Kids turns each still photograph into a talking image with a short voice recording.

Students film a partner slowly moving a hand, toy animal or leafy branch between a torch and a plain surface. With teacher guidance, they replay the slow-motion footage and look for the moment the shadow begins to grow, shrink or change shape. Children point to where the light, object and shadow appear and predict what will happen during a second trial. They test ideas such as moving the object closer to the torch or turning it sideways. The class captures several short slow-motion shadow investigations for close observation and discussion. Frame-by-frame replay makes rapid changes visible to young children and supports careful comparison.

Students make finger drawings of shadows they observed outdoors in the morning, at midday or under clouds. They place each drawing beside a simple sun, cloud or lamp symbol on a teacher-prepared shared canvas. Another child moves the symbols and asks whether each shadow still belongs in that place. The class ends with one large visual board showing how changing light changes shadows. Children use the board briefly, then return outside to check one idea with their whole bodies. Freeform's open canvas lets the teacher collect and connect every child's drawing in one place.

Students direct the teacher to record close-up photos and short videos as they shine light through clear, coloured, cloudy and solid materials. They describe whether the light passes through, changes colour or makes a strong shadow. Each child chooses the most surprising test and records one spoken sentence for families. The class ends with a narrated book of real light experiments that can be revisited beside the materials. Pages can be arranged from most light passing through to least light passing through. Book Creator keeps images, video and children's recorded voices together in one simple book.

Children design and craft their own animal shadow puppets using safe materials like popsicle sticks, felt, paper, and cellophane, decorating them with collage bits and fabric scraps. With teacher help, they use a small flashlight or a child-friendly LED torch to project their puppets' shadows onto a DIY cardboard 'jungle' backdrop, exploring how different shapes and materials change the shadows. They experiment with moving their puppets closer or further from the light to see how the shadows grow or shrink, connecting to the unit theme of light and shadows. This hands-on project blends storytelling, imaginative play, and STEM discovery, sparking curiosity about 'How the World Works' through light.

ci: Connecting with others helps us to establish a sense of belonging.
lo: Identity: Understanding how our relationships shape our sense of belonging and identity.; Community: Exploring the impact of our contributions to groups and how they affect others.; Wellbeing: Developing strategies for conflict resolution and problem-solving to enhance self and others wellbeing.

s.d: Students choose puppet characters and record short friendship stories about joining play, feeling left out and finding a kind solution. This helps children see how words and actions can build belonging and wellbeing. Pairs first act out each problem with toys, then decide together what their puppets should say. They swap stories with another pair, who suggests a different peaceful ending. Each pair finishes with a short narrated puppet show for the class. Puppet Pals lets children move characters across a backdrop while recording their voices.

Students lay coloured tiles to send Indi between picture stations showing welcoming actions such as waving, sharing and inviting someone to play. The route opens discussion about how small contributions can help everyone feel included. Children work in pairs, taking turns to choose a tile, place it and explain the kind action at the next station. Another pair tests the route and changes any section that does not work. The class ends with a physical pathway that Indi can travel from 'alone' to 'belonging'. Indi follows the coloured tiles without children needing a screen.

Students sort family drawings, classroom photos and picture cards into groups that show people, places and actions that help them belong. This makes the links between identity, relationships and community visible to young children. The teacher operates Freeform while children move around the room, hold up a chosen item and direct where its matching idea should go. Families can contribute one word in advance that describes belonging, and children decide where each word fits. The class finishes with a shared visual web linking every child's ideas. Freeform's large collaborative canvas allows the web to keep growing across the inquiry.

Students design a 'Kind Words Toolbox' filled with photographed facial expressions, drawings and teacher-scribed phrases they could use during playground disagreements. They select and arrange examples such as 'Can I have a turn?', 'Please stop' and 'Let's play together' using PicCollage's grids, stickers and text labels. Children role-play a familiar friendship problem, then choose the phrase that could help resolve it safely. Each child personalises a collage with colours and images that make them feel calm, confident and included. The finished toolbox becomes a visual prompt that children can revisit before play or classroom discussions. PicCollage's image layering and movable elements make children's choices easy to rearrange as their social language grows.

Students record their voices beside teacher-added photos of hands-on moments when they helped, joined, comforted or solved a problem together. This shows that belonging grows through everyday relationships and contributions. Children choose which moment matters to them and dictate why it helped the group. The class listens to one page each day before play and looks for a new example to add. They finish with a narrated class book called 'How We Help Everyone Belong'. Book Creator keeps photos and children's audio together on each page.

s.t: Feelings Fort: Build Your Happy Hideaway
s.d: Children work together to design and build cozy 'Feelings Forts' using large cardboard boxes, fabric scraps, cushions, and soft decorations. Each child personalizes their section with drawings or collage portraits of themselves and family, then uses a Bee-Bot to deliver a 'kindness message' between forts. This playful, hands-on project helps children express their identity, explore emotions, and celebrate what makes them feel safe and special in their community. The Design Cycle guides them as they imagine, create, test, and share their unique spaces.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time
ci: Changes influence how we see ourselves and shape our future direction.
lo: How we grow and change over time: Exploring our development from birth to the present and recognising new skills and abilities.; Experiencing and understanding life transitions: Understanding transitions such as moving from kindergarten to prep and how these changes affect us emotionally and socially.; Discovering who we are through our experiences: Reflecting on how different experiences and changes shape our sense of self and identity.

s.d: Students animate a pair of shoes travelling from babyhood to kinder and towards prep, moving them frame by frame through miniature scenes built from classroom objects. They photograph each tiny movement with Stop Motion Studio's frame capture and use onion skinning to judge where the shoes should move next. Props such as a cot, family photo, kinder gate and school bag represent important transitions, people and places. Children test the sequence, notice jumps or missing moments and reshoot selected frames. Each group produces a short stop-motion journey showing 'then, now and next'. During a class screening, children identify the feelings and helpful routines represented in each scene.

Students compare a baby photo with a current photo and record one new ability for a teacher-made Book Creator page. Hearing their own voices helps children notice that growing changes both what they can do and how they see themselves. Each child also chooses something they hope to learn in prep, giving the book a genuine look towards the future. The class ends with a narrated book called 'Then, Now and Next' for families and prep teachers. Book Creator keeps photos, drawings and recorded narration together on each page. Children revisit the book in small groups and act out one another's past, present and future skills.

Students arrange teacher-provided pictures of a fictional child's first day at kinder into a visual story about facing change. Using PicCollage's grids, stickers, backgrounds and text labels, they sequence moments such as saying goodbye, finding a familiar activity and meeting a new friend. Children select emoji stickers to show how the character's feelings shift from worried to curious, safe or proud. They add images of people, objects and routines that could help during the move to prep. Each pair produces a 'Change Can Feel Like...' collage with a clear beginning, middle and end. The collages prompt a class conversation about different feelings and the many ways children build confidence and belonging.

Students look closely in mirrors, pose as a baby, as themselves now and as a future prep student, then direct short turns of digital painting in Brushes Redux. Three portraits help children show how experiences and new abilities can change the way they imagine themselves. A partner chooses one detail to add to the future portrait, such as a school bag, a friend or a skill the child hopes to gain. Each child ends with a three-part digital portrait showing past, present and imagined future. Brushes Redux supports expressive painting in layers, so each stage can be added without covering the earlier image. Children stand beside the finished portrait and explain one change using the words 'before', 'now' and 'next'.

Students sort printed photos and drawings of familiar Glen Waverley places, then direct the teacher to place matching images on a shared Freeform canvas. Linking home, kinder, local places and future school helps children see how places shape belonging and identity. Children choose one place that feels safe during change and explain which person, object or routine makes it welcoming. The class ends with a connected visual map of places, people, feelings and transitions. Freeform's open canvas lets the teacher move, group and connect images as children revise their ideas. Families can view the finished board while children trace a journey from home to kinder and towards prep.

s.t: Journey Jars: My Story in a Bottle
s.d: Children will create their own 'Journey Jar' by decorating a large plastic jar or bottle with fabric scraps, tissue paper, and stickers to represent their personal story. Inside, they will place soft, tactile objects like cotton balls, ribbon pieces, and photos (or drawings) of important moments, people, and places in their lives. Using a Bee-Bot, children will then create a simple map on a large mat, guiding the robot from one jar to another to share and hear each other's stories. This hands-on project helps children explore their identity, life transitions, and sense of belonging through creative building and collaborative storytelling.

ci: People express themselves in diverse ways, shaped by their imagination, culture, and personal experiences.
lo: How imagination and creativity influence the ways we express ideas; How materials and techniques help us share personal and cultural experiences; How we interpret and respond to expressions from ourselves and others

s.d: Students sculpt a clay face inspired by a family story, celebration or imagined character, then record it speaking in ChatterPix Kids. This shows how materials, imagination and personal experiences can work together to express an idea. Each child chooses the face's expression and the words it says, while the teacher operates the iPad. The class ends up with a collection of short talking sculptures to show families. ChatterPix Kids adds a moving mouth and a recorded voice to a photo. Children listen to several sculptures and explain what feelings or stories they noticed.

Students collect, arrange and photograph real materials that show a chosen feeling, such as soft fabric for calm or jagged cardboard for anger. This helps them explore how colour, shape and texture can communicate without words. Children swap collections and work out the feeling expressed before hearing the creator's idea. Each child ends up with a visual collage of materials and a short teacher-added caption using the child's own words. PicCollage makes it easy to place several photos together in a clear grid. Print the collages beside the real material collections for a family gallery.

Students paint, build or sculpt while the teacher captures brief photos, videos and voice reflections in Seesaw. This makes children's choices visible as they explain why a colour, tool or material suited their idea. Invite each child to choose one moment that surprised them and record what they changed next. Each child ends up with a short multimodal journal entry showing both the making and the finished work. Seesaw keeps photos, video and voice together in a student portfolio. Families can respond by discussing a material, technique or cultural connection they recognise.

Students use whole-arm movements to explore how sweeping, tapping, circling and zigzagging marks can express different music, memories or feelings in Brushes Redux. This shows that the same idea can look different when children choose different colours and gestures. Partners respond to each painting with a movement before the artist explains what inspired it. Each child ends up with an original digital painting for a projected class exhibition. Brushes Redux supports expressive digital painting with layered artwork. The teacher limits the screen session to a brief turn between active movement and discussion.

Students arrange puppets and backdrops, then record a short story based on a family tradition, personal experience or imagined event. This helps children see how voice, character and setting shape the way a story is understood. Pairs exchange one character and adapt their stories to include the new point of view. Each pair ends up with a narrated puppet show to play for another Kinder group. Puppet Pals combines movable characters, backdrops and recorded voices in one app. Before recording, children rehearse the story physically with toys and fabric scenery.

Children design and craft their own unique puppets using socks, fabric scraps, felt, yarn, buttons, and paper cups, expressing their feelings, stories, and cultural backgrounds through imaginative character creation. With teacher support, they use a simple programmable Bee-Bot as a 'parade leader,' decorating a large parade path on the floor with colourful paper, markers, and collage materials. Each child programs the Bee-Bot to guide their puppet along the parade route, introducing their character and sharing a story or feeling as their puppet 'marches.' This playful project blends hands-on making with basic robotics, celebrating diverse ways we express ourselves and connect with others.

th: Where We Are in Place and Time

ci: Human interaction with the natural world causes change.
lo:
The natural world
Human interaction with nature
Changes people can make

s.d: Students lay coloured tiles through a floor garden made from leaves, stones and toy animals, then change the route when cardboard paths, fences or litter are added. Moving the human-made pieces shows how people's choices can change natural places. Children swap one harmful change for a helpful one, such as removing litter or adding a wildlife gap, and rebuild Indi's route. They run alongside the car, watch what happens and move tiles when the route does not work. The class ends with two physical garden scenes showing nature before and after people act. Indi follows the sequence of coloured tiles without a screen.

Students collect a fallen leaf, stick or piece of litter outdoors, and the teacher photographs each item in ChatterPix Kids. Their short recorded voices explain what happened to the natural object and whether a person helped or harmed its surroundings. Children choose one item to speak to another Kinder group, asking them to make a small change such as using a bin or leaving living plants in place. They finish with a set of talking nature photographs for a brief class viewing. Drawing a mouth on each photograph turns the real object into the speaker. The activity keeps screen use brief while children's outdoor collecting, handling and speaking do most of the work.

Students move animal and human puppets across a chosen backdrop while recording a short story about a garden changing. The story shows that touching plants, dropping rubbish, planting flowers or making shelter can change what animals experience. Pairs first act out the same story with their whole bodies, then choose a different ending that helps nature. Another group watches the puppet show and points to the moment when the human choice changed the place. Students finish with a short narrated puppet show containing a problem and a caring response. Puppet Pals records voices and puppet movement together.

Students sort real classroom and garden items into 'helps nature' and 'hurts nature' hoops, then explain one choice while the teacher records them in Seesaw. Their words connect everyday human actions with visible changes to plants, animals and places. Families are invited to respond by trying one chosen action at home, such as refilling a water bowl or picking up litter. Children later add a second recording showing what changed after the action. Each child finishes with a two-part visual and spoken journal entry. Seesaw keeps the photographs, video and voice together in one portfolio.

Students arrange real leaves, bark, stones and recycled objects into two small scenes, one natural place and one place changed by people. The teacher photographs the scenes inside Book Creator while children record what changed and why. Each child chooses a final page showing one change people can make to care for the place. The class plays the recorded pages to another Kinder group, who copy one caring action using loose parts. Students finish with a narrated class book that can be revisited during outdoor play. Book Creator holds photographs and children's recorded voices on the same pages.

s.t: Little Rain Rescuers: Build a Squishy Creek
s.d: With close teacher support, children build a pretend creek on a shallow tray using paper plates, large sponge blocks, fabric scraps and recycled cardboard banks, secured with sticky tape and child-safe glue sticks. Following a simple Design Cycle, they notice how pretend rubbish blocks the creek, imagine a cleaner home for animals, and build sponge gardens that soak up small trickles of water. A teacher uses an iPad camera in slow motion to show water moving through their creations, helping children test, notice puddles and rebuild by moving their sponge gardens or widening the creek. Through sensory water play, children explore how people change nature and how keeping rubbish out of waterways helps us share the planet.
